chapters.chapter_key: the people of the house and the prophet's witness
chapters.before_md:
Ali (ع)'s role as a warrior is only one of the many things that account for his unique place in the Islamic tradition. Far more significant is his closeness, in every respect, to the Prophet, and the wisdom and sanctity that flowed from that nearness. Ali (ع) received the immense honor of marrying the Prophet's daughter Fatima, who — together with her mother Khadija, the Prophet's first wife — is regarded as the most saintly woman in Islam. One of the epithets the tradition gives Fatima is Majma' al-Nurayn, 'Confluence of the Two Lights', the two lights being nubuwwa (prophecy) and walaya (sanctity). After the Prophet himself, then, Ali (ع) stood at the head of what became known as the Ahl al-Bayt, 'the People of the House' — that is, the Prophet's family.

The Ahl al-Bayt are addressed in an important Quranic verse as having been purified of all defilement:

> وَقَرْنَ فِى بُيُوتِكُنَّ وَلَا تَبَرَّجْنَ تَبَرُّجَ ٱلْجَهِلِيَّةِ ٱلْأُولَىٰۖ وَأَقِمْنَ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَآتِينَ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ وَأَطِعْنَ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُۚۥٓ إِنَّمَا يُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ لِيُذْهِبَ عَنكُمُ ٱلرِّجْسَ أَهْلَ ٱلْبَيْتِ وَيُطَهِّرَكُمْ تَطْهِيرًۭا

'God only wisheth to remove from you all impurity, O People of the House, and to purify you with a complete purification' (Al-Ahzab: 33).

Several of the most authoritative early sources report that the Prophet called for Fatima, Ali (ع), and their two sons Hasan and Husayn, and declared, 'This is my Ahl al-Bayt.' On one well-attested occasion he gathered these members of his family beneath his cloak and recited the words of this verse. The event took place while a Christian delegation from Najran was engaged in religious debate with the Prophet, and a revelation was received calling for a challenge of mutual imprecation (mubahila) against the Christians. The Prophet brought forward the four persons named above for this mubahila, but the Christians declined the challenge.

The importance of the Ahl al-Bayt is expressed further in a verse in which the Prophet is instructed:

> ذَلِكَ ٱلَّذِى يُبَشِّرُ ٱللَّهُ عِبَادَهُ ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّلِحَتِ ۗ قُل لَّآ أَسْـَٔلُكُمْ عَلَيْهِ أَجْرًا إِلَّا ٱلْمَوَدَّةَ فِى ٱلْقُرْبَىٰ ۗ وَمَن يَقْتَرِفْ حَسَنَةًۭ نَّزِدْ لَهُۥ فِيهَا حُسْنًا ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورٌۭ شَكُورٌ

'Say: I ask you for no reward, save love of the near of kin' (Ash-Shura: 23).

Several of the most significant Quranic commentators identify 'the near of kin' in this verse as the Prophet's Ahl al-Bayt. Love of the Prophet's family is thus explicitly demanded by the revelation — without this excluding the verse's wider sense, which takes in love of all those bound to one by close kinship. The reverence due to the Prophet's family from every Muslim is shown further by the practice of invoking blessings upon his al, or progeny, as part of the blessings invoked upon him. The Quran instructs the believers:

> إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ وَمَلَٓئِكَتَهُۥ يُصَلُّونَ عَلَى ٱلنَّبِىِّۚ يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا۟ صَلُّوا۟ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلِّمُوا۟ تَسْلِيمًا

'Truly, God and His angels bless the Prophet. O ye who believe, bless him and greet him with peace' (Al-Ahzab: 56).

When this verse was revealed, the Prophet was asked how one should perform this blessing, and he replied that blessings were to be invoked upon him and his al in these words: 'O God, bless Muhammad and the progeny of Muhammad, as Thou hast blessed Abraham and the progeny of Abraham. Truly, Thou art the Praised, the Glorious ...' The importance of this blessing, which is recited during the canonical prayer, together with the obligation to love the Prophet's family, is beautifully expressed in the following lines by Imam al-Shafii, founder of one of the four schools of Sunni jurisprudence:

Loving you, O family of the household of the Prophet of God, is an obligation (fard) from God in the Quran which He revealed; Sufficient to show the grandeur of your dignity is that one who blesses you not, no prayer has he.

There is also a prophetic saying that underscores the spiritual significance of the Ahl al-Bayt:

Truly, I am leaving behind amongst you the two weighty things (al-thaqalayn): the Book of God and my Ahl al-Bayt. They will not be parted from each other until they return to me at the [paradisal pool] al-hawd.

Beyond these sayings about Ali (ع) as the foremost member of the Prophet's Ahl al-Bayt, there are sayings of the Prophet concerning Ali (ع) specifically that deserve to be cited in full, for only on the basis of these sayings can one begin to appreciate the immensely important role of Ali (ع) in the spiritual dimension of the Islamic faith. These traditions (ahadith, sing. hadith) are presented here as a list with minimal commentary, in the manner in which they appear in most standard hadith collections. Anyone who takes prophetic guidance seriously cannot but take Ali (ع) seriously, and it is largely for this reason that countless Muslims across the centuries have meditated on these sayings, drawing from them diverse interpretations and incalculable inspiration. In a certain sense, these sayings form the prism through which the tradition views Ali (ع), and they deepen one's spiritual receptivity to his teachings. The crucial importance of Ali (ع) in the spiritual firmament of nascent Islam emerges more clearly in the light of these prophetic descriptions, and they should therefore be regarded as a significant part of the 'prophetic background' to Ali (ع)'s seminal contribution to Islamic spiritual and intellectual life, whether in a Shii, Sunni, or Sufi context.

The traditions given below can be found in any standard Shii hadith collection. But to show that they — together with their implications and the devotion they have inspired — are not confined to Shii Islam, they are cited here from two of the most authoritative Sunni traditionists. The first is Ahmad al-Nasai, author of the Sunan, one of the six collections deemed 'canonical' in the Sunni corpus (al-kutub al-sitta). The second is al-Hakim al-Nisaburi, author of al-Mustadrak 'alal-sahihayn (Supplement to the Two Sound Collections), which gathers those prophetic traditions that meet the exacting criteria of authenticity established by Bukhari and Muslim, authors of the sahihayn, but were not included in their own collections. The sayings concerning Ali (ع)s distinctions, virtues, and merits — all conveyed by the Arabic word fadail (sing. fadila) — explain why Ahmad b. Hanbal, another leading Sunni traditionist and founder of one of the four Sunni schools of law, made the following statement: No companion of the Prophet has had such fadail ascribed to him as those which have been ascribed to Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع).'

The sayings are these:

'Truly, Ali (ع) is from me and I am from him (inna Ali minni wa ana minhu), and he is the wali (patron/spiritual master) of every believer after me.'

'Ali (ع) is with the Quran and the Quran is with Ali (ع), إِنَّ عَلِيًّا مَعَ الْقُرْآنِ وَالْقُرْآنُ مَعَ عَلِيٍّ، لَنْ يَفْتَرِقَا حَتَّى يَرِدَا عَلَيَّ الْحَوْضَ. They will not separate from each other until they return to me at the [paradisal pool] (al-hawd).'

'Three things were revealed to me regarding Ali (ع): he is the leader of the Muslims, the guide of the pious, and chief of the radiantly devout (sayyidul-muslimin, imamul-muttaqin, wa qaidul-ghurral-muhajjalin).'

'Gazing upon Ali (ع) is an act of worship (al-nazar ila Ali ibada).'

'May God have mercy on Ali (ع). O God, make the truth revolve around Ali (ع) wherever he turns (adiril-haqq maahu haythu dara).'

'I am the city of knowledge and Ali (ع) is its gate; so whoever desires knowledge, let him enter the gate.'

'O Ali (ع), you are a leader (sayyid) in this world and the Hereafter. Your beloved is my beloved, and my beloved is the beloved of God; your enemy is my enemy, and my enemy is the enemy of God. Woe to those who hate you after me [after I have passed away].'

'Whoever desires to live my life and to die my death and to take his rest in the eternal Garden my Lord has promised me, let him orient himself towards Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع), for truly he will never lead you away from right guidance, nor lead you into error.'

The Prophet said that Ali (ع) was 'as my own soul' (ka-nafsi).

He said to Ali (ع), 'You are from me and I am from you (anta minni wa ana minka), أنْتَ مِنِّی وَ أِنَا مِنْکَ.'

... whoever obeys Ali (ع) obeys me, and whoever disobeys him disobeys me.

'You will clarify for my community that over which they will differ after me (anta tubayyinu li-ummati makhtalafu fihi badi).'

'There is one amongst you who will fight for the tawil (تَأْوِيل) [spiritual interpretation] of the Quran as I have fought for its tanzil [literal revelation], عَلِیٌّ یُقَاتِلُ عَلیٰ تَاوِیلِہِ کَما قَاتَلْتُ عَلیٰ تَنزِیلِہِ.' Abu Bakr asked, 'Is it I?' The Prophet said, 'No.' 'Umar asked, Is it I?' The Prophet said, 'No, it is the one who is mending the sandal.' The Prophet had given Ali (ع) his sandal to mend.

'O Ali (ع), there is in you something akin to Jesus, on whom be peace and blessings. The Jews hated him so intensely that they slandered his mother; and the Christians loved him so intensely that they ascribed to him a rank he did not possess.' 'O Ali (ع), whoever separates himself from me separates himself from God, and whoever separates himself from you, O Ali (ع), separates himself from me.'

'Whoever curses Ali (ع) curses me, and whoever curses me curses God.'

The Prophet said to his wife 'Aisha, Call unto me the leader (sayyid) of the Arabs.' She asked, 'O Prophet of God, are you not the leader of the Arabs?' He said, 'I am the leader of the children of Adam, and Ali (ع) is the leader of the Arabs.' When some women asked Fatima why the Prophet had given her in marriage to a man as poor as Ali (ع), she related this to the Prophet. He said: 'Are you not pleased that God, exalted and glorified be He, surveyed the people of the world and chose two men from among them: one is your father, and the other your husband?'

'The first of you to reach the [paradisal] pool (al-hawd) is the first of you who entered Islam, Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع).'

'Ali (ع) is from me and I am from him (Ali minni wa ana minhu), and nobody can fulfil my duty but myself and Ali (ع).'

Ali (ع) himself relates that the Prophet told him that none but a believer will love him, and none but a hypocrite will hate him.

When the Prophet was about to depart on an expedition to Tabuk, he left Ali (ع) as his deputy in Medina. Ali (ع) was saddened not to be going with him. The Prophet said, 'Are you not content to stand in relation to me as Aaron stood in relation to Moses, except that there is no prophet after me?'

The Prophet prayed to God to bring 'the most beloved of Thy creatures' to share a meal of fowl with him. Only when Ali (ع) arrived did the Prophet invite him to join him.

Among the several Quranic verses on which the Prophet commented with reference to Ali (ع) is 13:7: 'Verily thou art a warner, and for every people there is a guide.' The Prophet said, 'I am the warner ... you are the guide, O Ali (ع). After me, the rightly-guided shall be guided by you.'

On the revelation of verse 55 of Sura 5 (al-Maida), 'Verily your wali is only God and His Messenger and those who believe, establish the prayer and give alms while bowing in prayer,' the commentators relate this to the occasion when Ali (ع), while bowing in prayer, extended his ring to a beggar who had asked for alms. On being told of the incident, the Prophet recited this verse, and then added — in what are perhaps the most celebrated words ever spoken about Ali (ع) — 'For whomever I am the mawla [guardian, master, close friend], Ali (ع) is his mawla (man kuntu mawlahu fa-Ali mawlahu).'

This last saying was uttered on a number of occasions, the most famous of which was after the Prophet's final pilgrimage to Mecca, in the year 10/632, at a pool midway between Mecca and Medina known as Ghadir Khumm. The Prophet assembled all the pilgrims, had a pulpit erected, and delivered an address to the thousands gathered there. The address culminated in the declaration: 'For whomever I am the mawla, Ali (ع) is his mawla.' For Shiis, this is regarded as an unambiguous designation (nass) of Ali (ع) as successor to the Prophet; for Sunnis it indicates the special closeness of Ali (ع) to the Prophet, but not his nomination as successor in the political domain. That the reference to Ali (ع) as mawla — in some versions as wali — is of the highest spiritual significance is, however, not seriously disputed. 'Umar is reported to have approached Ali (ع) and said, Bakh bakh', an expression of congratulation, 'you have become my mawla and the mawla of every Muslim.' The polemical debate that has exercised countless minds throughout history, and that continues to this day, turns on the political implications of Ali (ع)'s spiritual authority, his walaya.

The place of Ali (ع) within Shii Islam is not the subject here, yet his charisma was such that, even during the Prophet's own lifetime, a group came to be known as the shia, or 'partisans,' of Ali (ع). Al-Tabari, author of the first great commentary on the Quran, reports that the Prophet interpreted the verse:

> إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّلِحَتِ أُو۟لَٓئِكَ هُمْ خَيْرُ ٱلْبَرِيَّةِ

'Those who have faith and do righteous deeds, they are the best of created beings' (Al-Bayyinah: 7), as referring to Ali (ع) and his 'shia.'

Four individuals in particular were renowned for their devotion to Ali (ع) during the Prophet's lifetime and are regarded as the prototypes of early Shiism: Salman al-Farisi, Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, 'Ammar b. Yasir, and Miqdad b. Amr. This early love for Ali (ع) should not be identified with the theological doctrines that were elaborated in the Shii branch of Islam in later generations. It is nonetheless worth emphasizing that, at the core of Shiism in all its different expressions, lies the notion of fidelity to Ali (ع). This fidelity, loyalty, or love is one aspect of walaya; the other, complementary aspect is the spiritual authority or sanctity of Ali (ع). It is equally important to stress that neither devotion to Ali (ع) nor the spiritual orientation toward the walaya he embodies is the exclusive province of Shiism. Rather, it extends across the whole of the Islamic faith, for devotion to Ali (ع) as head of the Prophet's Ahl al-Bayt is found throughout the Muslim world and runs especially deep wherever Sufism flourishes. Ali (ع) is regarded as the first spiritual pole' (qutb) of Sufism after the Prophet himself, and he stands at the summit of all the spiritual chains (salasil, sing. silsila) through which the Sufi orders trace their lineage back to the Prophet. To speak of Ali (ع) is to speak not of exclusivist sectarianism but of universal spirituality.

The spiritual ethos of Ali (ع) has an intellectual heart. The intellect (al-aql) plays a pivotal role in the elaboration and assimilation of his spiritual teachings. To sketch some of the key dimensions of that ethos, with particular emphasis on its intellectual aspects, is to give a firmer grounding to the explorations offered in the chapters that follow. One aim here is to illuminate something of the 'spirit of the intellect', الرُّوحُ الْعَقْلُ — the term coined for the relationship between the intellect and the spirit as it appears in the Imam's worldview. This is a spirit that surpasses the activities of the rational mind while containing them, and that encompasses domains not associated with the intellect today, such as moral conduct and aesthetic sensibility. This spiritual understanding of the intellect is directly related to the Quranic conception of the spirit (al-ruh), and much of what follows explores the fruits of engaging deeply with this unifying spirit that belongs to the intellect.

It may help at the outset to explain why the English word 'intellect' is preferred over 'reason' as a translation of 'aql. What is meant to be evoked is the original meaning of intellectus in Latin Christendom, a meaning virtually identical to that of nous in the Patristic Greek tradition. The Latin intellectus means understanding', and it carries within it the sense of standing under a thing: to understand something is to stand beneath a perception of reality and let that perception overshadow and govern one's actions, since our actions are always performed in the shadow of how we perceive things. Intellectus, or nous, is thus the faculty capable of a direct, contemplative vision of transcendent realities — the very realities of which the Quran speaks, but which are hidden from the senses. Reason, which translates the Latin ratio and the Greek dianoia, is by contrast indirect and discursive; it works through logic and arrives only at mental concepts of those realities. The root of ratio denotes a relation or comparison between two numbers, and this captures how reason proceeds: by comparison, by a binary logic of affirmation and negation, weighing one thing against another until it has defined what it considers. Reason, so understood, is the instrument the intellect employs; but it can carry us only as far as the outward form of a thing, only as far as the mental concept or image of a reality. With the intellect one is able to contemplate or 'see' the Absolute; with reason one can only think about it. To know about a reality is one thing; to contemplate and experience it directly is quite another. It is the intellect, not reason, that is capable of that experience — even if it is through reason that the intellect is brought to it.

These preliminary reflections on the spirit of the intellect in the Imam's ethos turn chiefly on a short discourse of the utmost importance in the Nahj al-balagha: the discourse the Imam gave to one of his closest disciples, Kumayl b. Ziyad. The approach taken is that of an interpretive commentary on the Imam's words, drawing not only on his other sayings on the theme in question, but also on concordant Quranic verses and, at times, on traditions of the Prophet that either help to illuminate the meaning of the Imam's saying under consideration or are themselves elucidated by it. Before turning to that dialogue, however, three factors inherent in the spirit of this intellectual perspective must be stressed: the centrality of revelation; the harmony between revelation and the intellect; and the distinction between the intellect, conceived as the principle of the articulation of consciousness, and reason, understood as one expression of that principle.

To begin with the first: everything about the Imam's life and teachings is centred on the Quranic revelation and its embodiment in the Prophet's conduct. The Quran is the centre around which the intellect must revolve, for the intellect needs a centre — principles and definitions to which it can hold fast for proper guidance. Both the thought and the life of the Imam can indeed be read as a kind of spiritual commentary, a tawil, on the sacred text. On the doctrinal plane, it can be stated with confidence that Ali (ع) possessed an innate aptitude for the work of tawil. On the existential plane as well, his life — from his birth in the most holy shrine of the Kaba to his martyrdom in the mosque of Kufa — reads as a dramatic unfolding of the inner meaning of the revealed text. Ali (ع)'s refusal to stop short at the surface of things, whether religious, ethical, or political, showed an unflinching fidelity to the sacred substance of the religion, a fidelity that called for inward intellectual penetration and outward combative resistance alike. The saying of the Prophet cited earlier is highly significant here: Ali (ع) would fight for the tawil of the Quran just as he, the Prophet, had fought for its tanzil, عَلِیُّ یُقَاتِلُ عَلیٰ تَاوِیلِہ کَما قَتَلُ عَلیَ تَنزِیلِہِ. Ali (ع)s short caliphate was dominated by bloody civil wars, and a strong case can be made that all three of these wars — those of the Camel (al-Jamal), of Nahrawan, and of Siffin — were fought for the sake of the correct interpretation and application of the Quran, for the clarification of its fundamental message of tawhid (تَوْحِيد), and for the realization of that oneness on every level, spiritual and social alike. These were not political battles or mere power struggles; they were battles waged to clarify and enforce the oneness of God according to the principles of the Quran — in thought, in speech, and in action. This claim is vividly borne out by the Imam's response to a bedouin who, just as the battle of the Camel (al-Jamal) was about to begin, approached him and said, O Commander of the Faithful (یا أمیر المومنین)! Do you say that God is one?' Those present rebuked the bedouin, telling him that this was neither the time nor the place for such questions. The Imam, however, intervened: 'Leave him, for surely what the bedouin wishes is what we wish for the people.'

This response bears directly on the principle that right intention takes priority over outward action, whatever that action may be. Had the Imam been guided by reason alone, he would have agreed with those who rebuked the bedouin and told him to find a more fitting time and place; but he saw with the intellect that stands above reason. For the Imam, the most fundamental intention behind every action — whether religious in the ordinary sense or military, as here — is knowledge of the true nature of ultimate reality. What the Imam 'wishes for the people', then, is precisely this knowledge, which must lie at the very heart of all concerns, motivations, and actions, whether on the battlefield or the prayer-rug. There is therefore no time or place where the question 'What do you mean by saying God is one?' is irrelevant or out of place. It was for the sake of correct knowledge of the divine, and all its consequences in society, that the Imam was fighting, in fulfilment of the prophetic saying just mentioned. On the very field of battle, then, the Imam delivers a discourse on the meaning of divine oneness. The first part of his reply contains a key to his entire spiritual ethos. He refutes any notion that God's oneness is numerical or countable. He tells the bedouin that it is not permissible to say 'one' while holding any numerical conception in mind, for 'that which has no second does not enter into the category of numbers'. The moment a thing can be counted as 'one', it at once admits the possibility of 'two', 'three', and 'four'; a oneness understood in this numerical sense is thus undone by the very number that would affirm it.

'That which has no second' is not merely a divinity to which no partner can be ascribed, as a theologian might put it, but that reality which has no 'otherness' — the Real, al-Haqq, at once transcendent and immanent, beyond all 'things' and manifested by all 'things', at once inaccessible and inalienable. To say that God has no otherness is not to say that things exist which might have been His partners but which believers simply decline to associate with Him; it is to affirm that nothing whatever in existence bears His likeness, nothing that could conceivably be set beside Him. In these few words the Imam effects, for those who have 'ears to hear', a shift of consciousness — from the dogmatic notion of one God against many gods to the mystical apprehension of the one and only Reality, in the face of which everything else is mere appearance. All things come to be apprehended as outward phenomena that call out to be deciphered, as signs (ayat) pointing beyond themselves to That of which they are manifestations, for an aya is precisely a meaningful token that points beyond itself to another. Retracing these appearances back to their source and origin is the literal meaning of tawil: a going back to the awwal, 'the First' (عَودَۃ الی الاول). On the one hand, the Real is described as the beginning and end of all things, the apparent and the hidden; there is nothing in being but this one Reality: 'He is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward' (Al-Hadid: 3).

> هُوَ ٱلْأَوَّلُ وَٱلْآخِرُ وَٱلظَّهِرُ وَٱلْبَاطِنُ ۖ وَهُوَ بِكُلِّ شَىْءٍ عَلِيمٌ

On the other hand, apparent multiplicity is to be 'brought back' to real oneness: 'We shall show them Our signs (sa-nurihim ayatina) on the horizons and in their own souls, so that it be clear to them that He is the Real' (Fussilat: 53).

> سَنُرِيهِمْ آيَتِنَا فِى ٱلأٓفَاقِ وَفِىٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُمْ أَنَّهُ ٱلْحَقُّ

In one saying attributed to Ali (ع), the Prophet is described as the first of those whom God taught the science of tawil, and who in turn taught it to Ali (ع). According to the Prophet, 'Truly, Ali (ع) is with the Quran, and the Quran is with Ali (ع), أنَّ علیٌ مع القرآن، و قرآن مع العلی. In another famous saying, often quoted by Sufi commentators, Ali (ع) claimed that he could load seventy camels with the pages of commentary he could offer on the Fatiha alone, the opening chapter of the Quran. It is worth noting, too, that Ali (ع)s cousin, Ibn Abbas — often called the first commentator' — claimed to have learnt the science of interpretation from Ali (ع).

In this connection, the following saying of the Imam is of fundamental importance, and helps to explain why he is held in the highest esteem within the discipline of Quranic exegesis, tafsir: 'The Quran consists of a book inscribed, between two covers; it does not speak with a tongue, and it cannot do without an interpreter (la budda lahu min tarjuman).' The reciprocity between revelation and the intellect is underlined further in the saying, 'The prophet of a man is the interpreter of his intellect (rasul al-rajul tarjuman aqlihi).' Elsewhere there is an explicit correspondence between the intellect and the 'inner' messenger: the intellect is 'the messenger of the Real'.

The Imam's teachings, which express his spiritual ethos, should therefore be read essentially as creative interpretations of the Quranic revelation. They set in motion a movement from the letter of the revelation to its spirit, and from the spirit of the revelation to the spirit of the Revealer — a process of 'retracing', of returning to the source, the origin, the beginning, al-awwal, accomplished in proportion to how fully the spirit of the intellect is enlivened within the interpreter. Yet the Revealer remains necessarily concealed even as He is revealed through the revelation. He is concealed because the essence of what is revealed — the divine Reality in itself — is ineffable and inexpressible; only the forms of its manifestations can be revealed. This dialectical interplay between form and the formless, the evident and the hidden, the revealed and the concealed — such antinomies lie at the root of the paradoxical mode of expression for which the Imam is renowned, and which recurs throughout this book. The relationship that especially concerns the present discussion is the second of the three factors mentioned above: that between revelation and 'intellection', by which is meant the creative use of the intellect. This relationship takes on particular importance in a context substantially defined by fidelity to revelation. Whereas rationalists in the strict sense regard intellect and revelation as mutually exclusive, in this perspective they are seen as perfectly harmonious, subsisting in a state of creative reciprocity, each requiring the other for completeness, for integrity, for the 'making one' that is the very essence of tawhid.

Indeed, one of the most striking aspects of the Imam's perspective is the way it exposes the hollowness of many false or excessively polarized dichotomies that later came to characterize — or were imposed upon — Islamic thought. This is owing to the highly synthetic quality of the Imam's discourses, viewed as 'pre-philosophical' by some academics and as 'supra-philosophical', inspired and evocative, by those within the Islamic spiritual tradition. The apparently insuperable dichotomy between intellect and revelation appears in various polarized forms: reason versus faith, convention (sunna) versus nature (tabia), imitation (taqlid) versus verification (tahqiq), piety versus inquiry, and so on. In Ali (ع)'s ethos, however, intellect and revelation are not mutually exclusive but complementary, and at the highest level inseparable, since truth is one. While the human intellect clearly cannot be equated with divine revelation, the spirit that animates the intellect is not, in the final analysis, confined by human limitations. It is this spirit that perceives and grasps the divine quality of revelation.

The divine spirit that articulates the form and infuses the content of revelation must be fathomable, to some degree, by human consciousness; without this, revelation would amount to nothing more than a set of rules and regulations for the will, rather than a source of creative inspiration for the intelligence. It cannot be stressed too strongly that divine revelation, far from curtailing the operations of reason and imposing some unintelligible dictate, on the contrary presupposes a creative engagement with all the resources of the intelligence — in particular those processes of reflection and meditation for which the Imam himself is renowned, and which the Quran repeatedly calls for. It is precisely the opposite of a decree imposed from without: the Quran constantly demands fikr, deep and sustained reflection, and such reflection does not enclose the meaning of the text within its literal surface but discloses it, opening up the inner horizons of meaning folded within the letter.

For the revealed text is itself silent; it speaks only through its interpreter, the intellect. This understanding of the bond between intellect and revelation rigorously excludes all literalism and superficiality — every attempt to confine meaning within a flat, one-sided reading. How deeply the text's meaning is plumbed depends on the depth and penetration of the interpreter's own intellect, since the text carries multiple levels of meaning at once. At its most profound, this 'prophetic' intellect rejoins the very source of revelation itself; for it is this 'inner prophet', the inmost degree of consciousness, that is the ultimate ground on which a person is able to confirm the verses of the outer revelation as true — to validate them through lived experience, and not merely to affirm them by dogma. It is in this sense that the Imam says, in the first sermon of the Nahj, that one of the purposes of God's sending forth of prophets to mankind was 'to unearth for them the buried treasures of the intellects' (dafain al-uqul).

This saying is one of the keys to the spiritual ethos under consideration, and it returns again and again throughout these essays. The intellect is not stifled by revelation; it is brought to life by it. Revelation is a clarion call to the spiritual depths of the intellect. It cultivates and brings to fruition the seeds of consciousness — the seeds of توحید — that God has planted there and that lie buried within us. For the spirit of one's intellect already bears the first imprint of its Creator. In the world of the spirit it beheld its Lord and testified to His lordship, and revelation — the ذکر — does no more than remind it of that primordial testimony. A reminder is never a new piece of information. It is knowledge one already possesses but has forgotten, for one can be reminded only of what one already knows. We were created in this world in a kind of forgetfulness. A physician who treats a man who has lost his memory tells the family to surround him with familiar things, with signs (آیات) out of his past, so as to jog his memory; in the same way, God has set His reminders in the horizons and the souls (آفَاق وَ أَنْفُس). The spirit of one's intellect, then, cannot be alien to what descends as revelation from on high. On the contrary, it must be akin to it at the root, and it is precisely for this reason that one can be wholly certain that revelation truly comes from the Absolute. The point is not to set intellect against revelation, but to see the intellect as revelation, or at least as one mode of it: the God-given means by which a person comes to discern, affirm, and sound the depths of the divine 'revelations' outside himself — both those of scripture and those made up of the 'signs' (ayat) of the natural world. If the human intellect can perceive and recognize revelation, it is because both are rooted in one and the same ultimate source; we came from a spiritual realm, and so did revelation, sent to remind us of what we once witnessed and have since forgotten. Prophetic revelation awakens and quickens the depths of the human intellect; it does not replace or displace it. The messengers do for these buried seeds what the farmer does when he waters what lies hidden beneath the soil, what the miner does when he digs into the mountain for its gold and silver, what the diver does when he descends to the sea-bed to bring up its buried treasures. From this perspective the revealed text is not some foreign source set against the intelligence. It is rather the outward, objective expression of the very principles that the intellect itself yields up to the 'inner prophet'. The intellect serves as the inner messenger whom the outer messenger awakens and nourishes — and by 'intellect' is meant not simply the faculty of reasoning, but the source of consciousness that gives the human spirit its articulate form.

The intellect holds unsuspected depths and buried treasures. It is far from exhausted by its surface operations — the acts of cognition and reasoning proper to its purely mental dimension. A third matter now follows: the relationship between intellect and reason. Just as there can be no contradiction whatsoever between revelation and intellection, so too a false dichotomy between reason and intellect must be avoided. Reason should rather be seen as one of the modes of the intellect; reason no more contradicts intellect than intellect contradicts revelation. Reason is a mode of the intellect, but it is not to be equated with the intellect wholesale, just as one cannot reduce the universal objectivity of revelation to the subjective particulars of any one individual's intellection — to his or her own 'private' revelation. To equate reason with intellect would amount to denying that the 'buried treasures' of the intellect exist at all — those supra-rational dimensions that lie, at first, beneath the rational surface of the intellect, and so hidden from it. The revelation that the intellect constitutes is embedded within the creation of the human being, for the intellect is what most decisively defines the human being as human. Far from pitting intellect against revelation, each is to be seen in the light of the other. On one side, the substance of revelation cannot be engaged except through the intellect; on the other, the 'buried treasures' of the intellect cannot be disclosed except through revelation. The two are genuinely dependent on each other.

This understanding of the intellect stands close to what the Imam calls the 'heart' (قَلْب) — that innermost mode of perception able to 'see' God. It is the 'heart' that can 'see' God — not with eyesight, not with بصارۃ, but with insight, with بصیرۃ, that spiritual insight generated by the 'verities of faith' (haqaiq al-iman / حقائق الایمان). As the Imam says, in reply to the questioner who asked whether he had 'seen' his Lord: 'Eyes see Him not through sight's observation, but hearts see Him through the verities of faith.'

Between the spiritual depths of the intellect and its rational surface there is both continuity and discontinuity. The continuity shows itself in a plain fact: all thinking begins with concepts that carry intelligible meaning. Thought sets out from ideas that reason can discern, and these ideas must bear some relation to the realities they express, or else they collapse into ideas that lead nowhere. But there is also discontinuity between the spiritual and the rational aspects of the intellect, for reason stops short at the ideas it has 'de-fined'. The Arabic word for definition, hadd (حَدّ), like its English counterpart, holds both senses at once: a conceptual definition, and a limitation or boundary — the very boundary that reason draws around an idea by weighing its pros and cons until it is fixed and 'defined'. To go beyond the limits imposed by this rational act of definition, something more than reason is necessary; and it is this 'something more' that makes the ethos under consideration a spiritual one, and not a rationalistic one. It is certainly 'rational', in that the form of the ethos can indeed be examined by reason; but it is not 'rationalistic', since its essence does not rest on reason alone.

Now Ali (ع) often hints, in highly allusive terms, at the mysteries and marvels — the unearthed treasures of the intellect — that he has directly witnessed with the eye of his purified heart. He also alludes to this supra-rational mode of awareness indirectly, through a bewildering use of apophatic discourse and paradoxical utterance, of which the body of sayings attributed to him is full. In this ethos it seems that the higher the truth, the deeper the paradox. The sheer disproportion between reality as it is in itself and the human conceptions formed of it is powerfully evoked by this creative use of paradox. In modern parlance, each human conception of reality needs to be 'deconstructed'. But unlike a modern deconstructionism so radically destructive that it has nothing left to 'reconstruct', the Imam's apophasis feeds directly into modes of spiritual intuition, contemplation, and realization of what reason, on its own, cannot attain. It is this intuition and contemplation which 're-members', or 'reconstructs', if one likes, the spiritual realities that transcend the categories of reason. The value of the paradoxes, the antinomies, the apophasis, and the negation rests entirely on the eminently positive realities that the intellect can sound, and by sounding them becomes aware of its own hidden depths. The consciousness that results does not so much negate reason as place it, showing the limits of reason's proper sphere. It reveals that reason alone cannot 'comprehend' the higher realities, nor express them fully — however indispensable it may be in setting in motion the movement of the mind towards them.

Thus, when the Imam denies — as he so often does — that human conceptions can encompass the divine Reality, what he denies is the limitation that inescapably accompanies all such conceptions, and not the positive content, the mana or spiritual meaning, of the conception itself. For this conception is a necessary starting point for a process of assimilation that engages a deeper level of awareness than the one 'de-fined' by the mind, and that therefore reaches far beyond the domain of speculative thought. In this light, the negation of the limitations of human conception should be seen as the prelude to an absolute affirmation: the affirmation of the Absolute, which has no limitation. The spiritual negation of conceptual limitation is of an upward, 'constructive' order, not a nihilistic, deconstructive one. Nowhere is this style of discourse more apparent than in the famous opening lines of the first sermon of the Nahj al-balagha:

Praise be to God, whose laudation those who speak cannot deliver, whose graces those who count cannot number, whose rightful due those who strive cannot render; He who cannot be grasped by far-reaching aspirations, nor fathomed by profound intuitions; He whose attribute has no binding limitation, no existing description, no time appointed, no term extended.

The divine attribute (sifa) has no limit by which it can be defined — laysa li-sifatih hadd mahdud — and yet it is affirmed as real. It has no 'existing description', and yet in some sense it is described (mawsuf), by the very words of the Quranic revelation; for in the Quran God is described as having such attributes as mercy, compassion, and power. He is the Merciful, the Compassionate, the Almighty, and yet the Imam affirms that these very attributes cannot be defined, bounded, or described. The paradox sharpens still further when the Imam speaks of the perfection of ikhlas — the 'rendering sincere', the purification of one's devotion to God and of one's conception of Him. This perfection, he says, is to strip (nafy) God of all attributes. On the one hand the attributes are affirmed, and on the other they are to be negated. The rational mind can think of God only in terms of the attributes put into words in the Quran; and yet here the Imam appears to negate these same attributes, and so strips the mind of any convenient conceptual handle by which to grasp the nature of the divine Reality. The simultaneous affirmation and negation of the attributes raises an apparently irresolvable contradiction, and in so doing enhances receptivity to a deeper mode of knowing. This style of discourse appears designed to awaken in the listener some latent awareness inscribed in the heart or the depths of the intellect, and to invite the seeker to dive into those depths, into the knowledge 'buried' in the intellect. The very shock of the apparent contradiction in this apophasis seems meant to bring about a leap of consciousness — from the formal activity of reason to the supra-rational contemplation of the spirit.

The words spoken by the Imam immediately after affirming that his heart had indeed witnessed God, not by means of outward vision but through 'the verities of faith', run:

My Lord is not described in terms of dimension (bu'd), nor motion (haraka), nor rest (sukun) ... nor through coming or going: He is subtle in subtlety but not described by subtlety, magnificent in magnificence but not described by magnificence, great in greatness but not described by greatness ...

The attributes are again affirmed and denied. God possesses these attributes but is not reducible to them. The mind can begin to think of God in terms of these categories, but He is not reducible to such conceptions. The attributes give the mind something by which the divine nature can be understood, but this understanding is fragmentary, never complete, and it must be negated as the prelude to a fuller apprehension. The mind's first conceptual orientation towards the divine Reality must be both negated and sublimated: negated as a mental conception, while its positive content is sublimated through spiritual intuition. Only then can the two-dimensional 'portrait' drawn by reason be given a third dimension — that of depth. But this third dimension emerges only after the insufficiency of the rational depiction is understood — hence the need for the cognitive shock that paradox produces. That shock is meant to expose the pretension of reason as it strives to disclose the nature of the Absolute, the transcendent source of its own activities.

The Imam's discourses show a recurring combination of affirmation and denial, which mirrors the negation and affirmation found in the first testimony of Islam: la ilaha, 'no god', is the negation (nafy); then illaLlah, 'except God', comes as the affirmation (ithbat). This helps to show that the negation of the attributes mentioned by the Imam as being the perfection of ikhlas is in fact an affirmation of the infinitude of the divine Reality. Each of the attributes is to be 'negated', but only insofar as it is conceived by the mind. Such negation is necessary because, at the mental level, each attribute excludes the other attributes, and excludes the object of attribution itself — that is, the divine Essence. This exclusion follows inescapably from the very fact that the mind can distinguish, in concept, between the attribute and the object of attribution, between the divine quality and the divine Essence. For any conception to take place in the mind, defined ideas are necessary, and where there are definitions, there are limits and thus exclusions. The reality of the attribute, however, is unlimited, by virtue of its absolute identity with the Essence. The attribute that has been 'negated' is paradoxically affirmed, not in itself but inasmuch as it is nothing but God: illaLlah. Thus one can place each of the negated attributes in the position of the nafy of the first testimony, and so arrive at formulations such as la rahmana illaLlah, 'There is no All-Compassionate except God'; la rahima illaLlah, 'No All-Merciful except God'; and so on. The apparent negation of the attributes becomes, in fact, an affirmation of their true identity, shorn of any restrictive association with the poverty of mental conceptions. The attributes are not added on to the Essence but are absolutely one with it, distinguishable from it only in concept, not in being. The Essence does indeed comprise all the attributes mentioned, such as greatness, subtlety, and so on, but it is also infinitely more than these attributes; and, for their part, the attributes are infinite only within and as the Essence. The Imam's apophasis here can be seen as a commentary on the Quranic refrain, 'Glorified be God above what they describe' (Al-Mu'minun: 91). The infinitude of God strictly requires, on the human plane, the negation of all that the mind can conceive through reason, but not all that the heart can 'see' through spiritual vision. This very negation on the plane of reason calls out to something deeper, and that in turn can be understood only in the light of spiritual praxis — always assumed as the reflective, devotional, or contemplative setting of those who heard the Imam's sermons and discourses. The heart, the symbolic seat of the contemplative intelligence, calls out to be 'polished', and this is precisely what the 'remembrance of God' does — this dhikr Allah being, according to the Imam, the 'most excellent form of worship'. Even at this level of praxis there is a further paradox: the 'reality' of the remembrance is not attained until 'you forget yourself in your remembrance'.

It is not only the rational mind, and the determinate conceptions matched to it, that are to be negated or 'deconstructed', but the individual soul itself, as the seat of all cognition, whether rational or supra-rational. This final denouement, or fana, is the ultimate form of apophasis.

These considerations show the extent to which the spirit of the intellect, in Ali (ع)'s perspective, transcends the rational faculty. The intellect must be seen, first and foremost, as a spiritual faculty, and the spirit, in turn, must be appreciated as the source of the intellect, as well as the source of life. Without the intellect the spirit is reduced to unconscious existence; conversely, without the spirit, the intellect tends towards lifeless thought. These aspects of the spirit are clearly expressed in the first sermon of the Nahj, which can be read as a commentary on the Quranic verses that describe the creation of man in terms of God's breathing' of His spirit into man: 'He began the creation of man with clay ... He fashioned him and breathed into him of His spirit' (ثُمَّ سَوَّىٰهُ وَنَفَخَ فِيهِ مِن رُّوحِهِ).

The following lines, from the first sermon, form one of the many passages in which this infusion of the divine spirit into man is commented upon by Ali (ع):

> ثُمَّ جَمَعَ سُبْحَانَهُ مِنْ حَزْنِ الاْرْضِ وَسَهْلِهَا، وَعَذْبِهَا وَسَبَخِهَا۔ تُرْبَةً سَنَّهَا بالمَاءِ حَتَّى خَلَصَتْ۔ وَلاَطَهَا بِالبَلَّةِ حَتَّى لَزَبَتْ۔ فَجَبَلَ مِنْها صُورَةً ذَاتَ أَحْنَاءَ وَوُصُولَ، وَأَعْضَاءَ وَفُصُول۔ أَجْمَدَهَا حَتَّى اسْتَمْسَكَتْ، وَأَصْلَدَهَا حَتَّى صَلْصَلَتْ۔ لِوَقْت مَعْدُود، وَأجَل مَعْلُوم۔ ثُمَّ نَفَخَ فِيها مِنْ رُوحِهِ فَمَثُلَتْ إِنْساناً ذَا أَذْهَانُ يُجيلُهَا، وَفِكَر يَتَصَرَّفُ بِهَا، وَجَوَارِحَ يَخْتَدِمُهَا، وَأَدَوَات يُقَلِّبُهَا، وَمَعْرِفَة يَفْرُقُ بِهَا بَيْنَ الحَقِّ وَالبَاطِلِ۔

Then He, glorified be He, gathered up a quantity of dust, from some hard earth and some soft, some sweet earth and some salty, and poured water onto it until it was pure, then kneaded into it some moisture until it stuck together; then He fashioned from this a form with curves and joints, limbs and parts. He compacted it until it held tightly together, solidified it until it became as sounding clay, assigning to it a measured duration and a known consummation. Then He breathed into it of His spirit, and it stood up as a human being, endowed with intellectual powers with which to reflect, thoughts by which to conduct himself, limbs to put to service, instruments at his disposal, and knowledge with which to discern between the true and the false ...

The body had been fashioned entire — its eyes, its ears, the organ of thought all in place — and yet it could neither hear nor see nor reflect until God breathed His spirit into it. Only then did it stand up as a human being. It is this 'in-spiration' — literally the in-breathing, the insertion of the spirit — of God's breath that produces consciousness and life. Death, by contrast, is the 'ex-piration', the departure of the spirit. Life in the absence of 'aspiration', the intention to be true to one's spirit, is a kind of death. It is through the spirit that inanimate, unconscious matter is brought to life and to awareness of itself, generating not only knowledge but self-knowledge as well. This intimate intertwining of the gift of life and the capacity to know — existence that is conscious, and knowledge that is bound up with existence — is one of the foundations of any truly spiritual perspective. The question is not one of setting the spirit against the body, but of recognizing that the infusion of the spirit into the body is precisely what brings the body to life. And it is for this reason that knowledge gives life, in the very measure that it is spiritual: 'O ye who believe, respond to God and His Messenger when they call you to that which vivifies you' (Al-Anfal: 24). According to the Imam, one of the most important aspects of this call from God to human beings is to 'remind them of the buried treasures of the intellect.'

Existentiation is the bestowal of the spirit, which is consciousness. The 'aql, or intellect, is the principle by which the spirit is articulated, and so it is not merely a mental faculty but is itself constitutive of our true life. The intellect is that of which the mental faculty is one formal expression, one mode of its operation, but by no means the only one. The aql is many-sided, comprising aspects that in our times are rarely associated with intelligence. To be true to one's intellect — to the treasures buried deep within it, and not merely to the rational functions at work on its surface — amounts to being spiritual.

For Ali (ع), the true intellectual, al-aqil (الْعَاقِل), is one who not only thinks correctly but also acts ethically, and, at the deepest level, one who seeks to realize the ultimate Reality. The intellectual is defined as one who 'puts all things in their proper place' (العاقل من وضع شئی حق محلہ) — one who aligns his acts with the intentions of his Creator. This same alignment is the very definition of justice (عَدْل); only the true intellectual, then, can be fully just (عَادِل), for only one who sees things as they truly are is able to put them in their right place.

Thought, action, and realization are all the concern of the true intellectual, the 'aqil. Correct thinking, impeccable virtue, and authentic being are all inextricably bound up with the intellect in the spiritual ethos considered here. These aspects of the ethos come into sharper focus in the light of the Imam's discourse to Kumayl.

The discourse the Imam delivered to Kumayl brings these aspects of the ethos into sharper focus. Its importance lies above all in its deeply esoteric character. The Imam took his disciple Kumayl ibn Ziyad by the hand and led him out of Kufa to a graveyard; once the city lay behind them, he drew a deep breath and gave him the following private counsel.

> يَا كُمَيْل بْن زِيَادٍ، إِنَّ هذهِ الْقُلُوبَ أَوْعِيَةٌ فَخَيْرُهَا أَوْعَاهَا فَاحْفَظْ عَنِّي مَا أَقُولُ لَكَ۔ النَّاسُ ثَلاَثَةٌ- فَعَالِمٌ رَبَّانِيٌّ وَمُتَعَلِّمٌ عَلَى سَبِيلِ نَجَاةٍ، وَهَمَجٌ رَعَاعٌ أَتْبَاعُ كُلِّ نَاعِقٍ يَمِيلُونَ مَعَ كُلِّ رِيحٍ، لَمْ يَسْتَضِيئُوا بِنُورِ الْعِلْمِ، وَلَمْ يَلْجَؤُوا إِلَى رُكْنٍ وَثِيقٍ

O Kumayl ibn Ziyad, these hearts are truly vessels, containers for knowledge and wisdom, and the best of them are those that hold the most. So hold fast to what I say to you. People are of three kinds: a lordly knower ('alim rabbani); one who seeks knowledge (mutaallim) for the sake of deliverance; and the common folk (hamaj raa), the word naming the moth that hurls itself at any flame, who follow just anyone, sway with every current, and neither desire to be lit by the light of knowledge nor seek refuge in any strong support.

O Kumayl, knowledge is better than wealth. Knowledge guards you, while you must guard your wealth. Wealth shrinks as it is spent, but knowledge only grows as it is given away, replenishing itself the more it is disbursed. The fruits of wealth vanish when the wealth is gone — the friends that money bought and the comforts it purchased all fall away with it — yet no one can take a man's knowledge from him. O Kumayl ibn Ziyad, the wise apprehension of knowledge (marifat al-ilm) is a religion by which God is worshipped, for din, religion, is kin to dayn, a debt: by acquiring knowledge a man repays the debt his own intellect owes its Maker. Through it he gains obedience in his life and a good name after his death. And knowledge is a judge, while wealth is judged; knowledge is active and wealth passive. The one who knows takes command of what he owns, his knowledge directing him how to handle it, whereas wealth is forever ruled upon by the one who holds it.

O Kumayl ibn Ziyad, those who hoard wealth perish even while they live, but the knowers endure as long as time itself endures: their material forms are absent, yet their images are present in the hearts of men. Ah, what abundant knowledge is here (and he pointed to his breast), if only I could find someone to bear it. I did find one who was quick to understand, but he could not be trusted with it: he exploited the instruments of religion for worldly gain, using the graces of God against His servants and His proofs against His friends. When the vessel of the heart is corrupt, this knowledge, pure and precious as it is, becomes a weapon turned against the very friends of God. Then there was another, obedient to the bearers of truth but without insight of the heart, in whom doubt was kindled at the first appearance of anything obscure. So neither this one nor that! Nor one greedy for pleasure and submissive to passion, nor one obsessed with acquiring and accumulating — neither of them a guardian of religion in any respect. Such men resemble nothing so much as grazing cattle. So does knowledge die with the death of those who bear it, when its trust falls to the worthless and the self-serving.

But indeed — O my God! — the earth will never be empty of one who upholds the proof of God, whether openly and in plain view or in fear and obscurity, lest God's proofs and clear signs come to nothing. Yet how many are they, and where are they? By God, they may be the fewest in number, but with God they are the greatest in rank, for here authority does not belong to the many, and truth is not settled by counting those who hold it: the guardians of the proof are few, and it is they who stand highest in the sight of God. Through them God preserves His proofs and clear signs, so that they may entrust them to their peers and sow them in hearts like their own. Through them knowledge penetrates the reality of insight; they take hold of the very spirit of certainty; they make easy what the extravagant find harsh, and they befriend what estranges the ignorant; in their bodies they keep company with the world, while their spirits are bound to the transcendent realm. They are the vicegerents of God upon His earth, the summoners to His religion. Ah, how I long to see them! Go now, Kumayl, as you will.

Those whom the Imam names lordly knowers (alim rabbani) are the fewest in number yet the greatest in the sight of God, and through them His religion is sustained — His religion meaning the divine reality of religion, the pure and immutable essence of the faith, perfect and unchanging, as against religion in the ordinary sense, whose outward institutions are subject to the turns of human history. From Adam to the Seal of the prophets those outward institutions have shifted with the conditions of men, but the essence, the message, and the purpose have never altered: the salvation of the soul through willing submission to God, as the Quran declares: إِنَّ ٱلدِّينَ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ ٱلْإِسْلَمُ, "Truly, religion in the sight of God is submission" (Ali 'Imran: 19). It is through the knowledge of the true knowers that religion stays true to itself, and only through such sages does religion truly live in the world.

"Through them, knowledge penetrates the reality of insight." He does not say that their knowledge penetrates it, but that through them knowledge penetrates the reality of insight. Knowledge can remain merely abstract, far from the reality of insight. There is the outward, surface knowledge of a thing, its zahir, and the inner, hidden knowledge of the same thing, its batin. Yet knowledge holds a potential that calls out to be realized; it needs to be brought to life, so that it penetrates to something deeper than the words and concepts that give its outward form — the meaning that lies ready on the surface. A man may have a surface knowledge of a verse of the Quran, of a saying, of why he prays and fasts and how many cycles each prayer requires; but when he presses past that surface and asks what the bowing and the prostration truly represent, a world of knowledge opens that is nothing like the bare information he began with. Degrees of knowledge are plainly implied here, and with them the refusal of all literalism and superficiality, of the easy equation of factual information with actual knowledge, let alone with wisdom. The shift of consciousness this penetration requires is shown vividly by the Imam's gesture toward his breast: it is not the chest but the heart hidden behind it that holds knowledge. The chest is the outward form, the zahir that conceals the heart within its batin, and to reach the heart one must first pass through the chest.

The word chosen to translate hajama is "penetrate," but the primary sense of the verb is to assault, to take by storm, to charge. In the warfare of that age the battle lines were drawn as a right wing, a left wing, and a center — the heart of the army (qalb al-askar), where the king or commander stood. The aim of the assault was to break through the wings and reach that heart, for once the king was taken the battle was won, and the victor took command of everything the defeated had held: the kingdom, its treasury, its army, its people. The chessboard preserves the same rule. So the word shows that conceptual knowledge holds a latent force — one might almost call it an explosive power — deriving from the reality of knowledge, its haqiqa or spiritual essence. This is what calls out to be made real through tahaqquq, realization in depth rather than mere verification on the surface; and the striving by which one storms the outer wall of words to reach the heart of their meaning is tahqiq, investigation. This haqiqa can be pointed to, but never captured, by the words and concepts that make up its formal, communicable aspect, just as the chest can only be opened to reach the heart. By means of this inner force — which its outer conceptual form at once hides and evokes — knowledge can bring about a shift of consciousness from one degree of knowledge to another: a man begins to see the very realities of this world differently from those who rest in the surface play of cause and effect, so that the same act which is a burden to one is a delight to another. An indirect, mental conception of reality thus prepares the way for a penetrating, existential perception of reality. This is the difference between mere sight and true insight: sight reaches only the outward, superficial reality, whereas the reality of insight opens the intelligence to reality as such — ordinary insight, like abstract knowledge, remaining only at the superficial level of understanding. The same idea appears in a saying of Ali (ع) about the true understanding that comes to plumb, and so truly to know, the buried treasures of knowledge: "He who understands knows the depth of knowledge (man fahima 'alima ghawr al-ilm)." And the effort that true knowledge demands, as against the mere accumulation of facts, is likewise indicated: "Through learning and assimilating knowledge, until it becomes deeply rooted in one's consciousness, is knowledge attained (bil-taallum yunalul-ilm)."

The urgency of realizing this power latent within knowledge — of moving from the abstract to the concrete, the potential to the actual, the static to the dynamic, the formal to the essential — is powerfully evoked by hajama, a word bound up with battle. It warns against taking the first understanding of an idea for its full comprehension, and its full intellectual comprehension for its dynamic interiorization in the spirit. For when knowledge at last storms the surface of religion and takes its heart, a transformation begins from within: the heart, now lit by the realities it has seized, takes command of the limbs and their actions, which are the soul's own resources, exactly as the victor takes command of the kingdom he has won. This interiorization is a process of endless unfolding within, not the mere registering of some fact from without. It requires the effective integration of knowledge within being: knowledge from without must be transformed into being from within, woven into the deepest texture of one's existence. Knowledge thus demands not merely the attention of the mind but the total orientation of the soul.

In this ethos, then, the effective integration (تَوْحِيد) of knowledge within being cannot be reached without the participation of the whole soul; and this in turn requires the removal of every vice that flows from egocentricity. So the Imam describes the 'aqil, the true intellectual, as one constantly at war with his own soul — against its lower inclinations, its passionate whims, and the distracting caprices of the ego. These vices are not confined to the plane of morality; they encroach on the domain of knowledge, and this becomes clear precisely as knowledge is grasped as a concrete vision of things rather than a merely notional or conceptual apprehension. The vices are then seen as so many clouds obscuring the vision proper to the reality of insight. According to the Quran, evil deeds become a rust that covers the heart: "Nay, their hearts have become rusted by that which they have done" (Al-Mutaffifin: 14). The aqil, then, is engaged in a constant inner struggle against the tendencies that not only stain the soul but blind the heart. As a virtuous man he opposes vice on the moral plane, because it is contrary to virtue; but he opposes it for a further reason, on the higher plane of spiritual reality: vice contradicts the nature of the Real, it obscures the reality of insight, blinding the eye of the heart, which alone can see God.

This does not deny the validity of the moral perspective; the stress falls rather on the deeper motive that drives the 'aqil toward virtue — a motive that transcends the moral plane while including it. Here morality appears as the fruit or effect, and spirituality as the seed or cause. By drawing attention to the intellectual side of the aqil's motive for shedding the vices, the Imam shows more clearly how immorality is rooted in ignorance; and the uprooting of that ignorance, for the true intellectual, amounts to dissolving the very substance of the vices. This uprooting demands great effort — a relentless inner battle, indeed the most formidable of all battles, al-jihad al-akbar, the greatest struggle, as the Prophet defined it.

The following sayings of Ali (ع) bear on the importance of this inner struggle:

"Struggling against the soul through knowledge, such is the mark of the intellect."

"The strongest of people are those who are strongest against their own souls."

"Truly, one who fights his own soul in obedience to God, and does not sin against Him, has the rank of the righteous martyr in the sight of God."

"The ultimate battle is that of a man against his own soul."

"He who knows his soul fights it."

"No jihad is more excellent than the jihad of the soul."

In another saying the Imam clarifies what the Prophet meant by naming the greatest jihad the jihad of the soul (al-nafs). It is not so much a struggle against the soul as a struggle for the soul itself. This emerges from the metaphor by which the Imam defines the contest: al-aql, the intellect, leads the forces of al-Rahman, the Compassionate; al-hawa — whim, caprice, desire — commands the forces of al-shaytan, the devil; and al-nafs, the soul, wavers between them, pulled by both (mutajadhiba baynahuma), falling under the sway of whichever prevails.

These sayings make clear that for the true intellectual the soul in its entirety must be "conquered" and enlisted on the side of the intellect. The aim is not to destroy the lower soul but to free it from the destructive influence of its caprice, its egoistic whims, its subjectivism, its individualism — all of them carried in the word hawa. The Prophet, the Quran tells us, does not speak from hawa; rather: "It is naught but a revelation revealed" (An-Najm: 3-4). The divine objectivity of revelation is here set against the human subjectivity of passional whim. In the context of the holy war within, the Imam's sayings bring an analogous polarity into focus: the objectivity of the intellect must prevail over the subjectivity of individual caprice and egotistic desire. It is the intellect that represents — in the sense of makes present — the divine power of al-Rahman, and that combats the forces of al-shaytan embodied in al-hawa.

The word hawa is used further in the Quran to denote desires that spring from the ego, by which the ego becomes a kind of false god: "Hast thou seen him who maketh his desire his god?" (25:43; almost identical at 45:23). This is the subtle or hidden idolatry (al-shirk al-khafi) that the Prophet described as being more hidden than a black ant crawling on a dark stone on a moonless night. To root out this idolatry of the ego, a force higher than the ego itself must be brought to bear, since the ego cannot be controlled by anything belonging to it; and that higher force is the divine Reality, reached through the power of the intellect and the graces of faith. This complementarity — between the effort to overcome the egoism of hawa and the influx of divine grace — is well expressed in the Quranic verse: "As for he who fears the station of his Lord, and restraineth his soul from whim (hawa), verily, Paradise will be his abode" (An-Nazi'at: 40-41).

The soul's fundamental energy is not to be destroyed but converted and redirected — away from the fleeting objects of individualistic desire and the impulses of al-shaytan, and toward the one true object named by al-Rahman. This "conquest" of the soul involves far more than arriving at some mental conception. It is not only the mind, the will, and the character that must be transformed; the soul's very deepest disposition must be integrated into the truth the intellect perceives, if one is to be capable of perceiving that truth in all its dimensions and ramifications across the different planes of being.

For the Imam, the need to win the soul over in its totality follows naturally from his understanding of tawhid, the most fundamental principle of Islam. Tawhid is a verbal noun, and to translate it as mere oneness or unity misses its full force: it literally means "affirming one" — the affirmation of and belief in God's oneness, which is the outward, theological meaning — or "realizing one," the realization that there is but one reality, which is the inner, spiritual meaning. In the Imam's view, then, the absolutely Real is perceived not only as being one but also as making one, as integrating. The Real is not only unique; it is also unifying. Tawhid thus comes to mean not merely affirming the oneness of God, but being one oneself so as to reflect the One perfectly: to know God is to be "integrated." Here a link appears with the etymology of 'aql, whose primary meaning is "to bind." Yet whereas the later mystical tradition tends to stress the limiting side of this word — the intellect as that which defines and encloses meaning, in contrast to the heart, which intuits and discloses spiritual truth — here the intellect is that which "binds together" the disparate elements of the soul into an organic unity. This principle is expressed in the first of the following sayings of the Imam, each of which merits deep reflection:

"He who knows God integrates himself (man 'arafaLlah tawahhad)."

"He who knows his soul disengages himself (man 'arafa nafsahu tajarrad)."

"He who knows people isolates himself (man 'arafal-nas tafarrad)."

"He who knows the world withholds himself (man 'arafal-dunya tazahhad)."

Elsewhere the Imam describes this total adherence to the Real as "sincerity," sidq or ikhlas — terms that mean far more than simple truthfulness, as the root of ikhlas already shows. The verb khalusa means to be utterly pure, true to one's essence, unadulterated by any extraneous element. This sense comes through clearly in the following saying of the Imam: "Make purely for God (akhlis liLlah) your action and your knowledge, your love and your hatred, your taking and your leaving, your speech and your silence."

To be totally sincere, then, is to make oneself "purely" for God, to carry no "stain" of impurity — understood here as whatever is other than God — in one's devotion, action, intention, or even sentiment. One must love and hate only in relation to one's bond with God. Of all the tendencies that work their way into one's motives and intentions, the most pernicious is egotism. Ikhlas, pure sincerity, involves the active effort to be, think, and act purely for God — that is, with selflessness — which is why the Imam lays such stress on the holy war within the soul as the "ultimate battle." One who wins this battle attains the rank of the "righteous martyr," for the victor here is a martyr in the truest sense: he has sacrificed his lower life for the sake of God, with whom is the real life — the life witnessed by the intellect, the only element within human consciousness capable of looking upon the soul as "the other" with genuine objectivity.

As the saying holds, "struggling against the soul through knowledge, such is the mark of the intellect." The intellectual engaged in this battle is also one who bears "witness" (al-shahid, meaning both martyr and witness, as in the original Greek sense of the word). He bears witness to God through the intellect's sacrifice of whatever opposes the truth of God, and the chief opponent is his own egotism, his own "false life." To possess perfect ikhlas, then, is to be rid of all hypocritical self-preoccupation and to replace it with a sincere theocentricity, a way of being centered upon God rather than oneself. Ikhlas, therefore, means being for God, or belonging to God, in the sense pointed to by the Quranic verse: "Say: Truly my worship and my sacrifice, and my living and my dying, are for God, Lord of the universes" (Al-An'am: 162).

That worship is the first thing mentioned in this verse is of particular significance for understanding Ali (ع)'s spiritual ethos. Any account of that ethos must emphasize the indispensable role of worship and devotion — a role that belongs to the quest for the fundamental virtue of justice — while the ultimate fruits of worship and devotion have as their quintessence the remembrance of God. One of the defining features of the Imam's spiritual ethos is indeed the emphasis he places on prayer, taking that term in its widest sense to include all the means — from formal worship and supplication to meditation and reflection, remembrance and contemplation — by which the individual is oriented and attuned to the Real, al-Haqq.

Worship is therefore an integral aspect of ikhlas, precisely because it relates to and sustains a fundamental dimension of the human soul. That within the soul which yearns to worship, and is nourished only by worship, must be given its due. In a spiritual context, if worship is pushed to the margin, one's sincerity is compromised: one is no longer being sincere with God, no longer being "just" to God, no longer rendering God His due. And the spiritual logic of the Imam holds that if one is not just with God, one cannot be just to His creatures. "Whoso establishes well-being between himself and God," he says, "God establishes well-being between him and mankind."

The Quranic verse bears on this too: "Worship thy Lord until certainty cometh to thee" (Al-Hijr: 99). The quest for knowledge demands total dedication if it is to yield its inner riches, and that dedication includes the quasi-alchemical transformation of consciousness wrought by total concentration on the divine Reality — prayer in one of its deepest modes. In this form of prayer, the intensity of dedication is such that nothing else can occupy consciousness alongside its object: the "remembrance" (dhikr) of God strictly implies the forgetting of everything else, including, above all, oneself. The spiritual reality of the dhikr can only be attained when "you forget your soul in your remembrance." Concentration upon the divine Reality as the supreme object of knowledge, made present through the Name or Names of God, is thus a mode of prayer — one which, to be efficacious, requires both presence of mind and a genuine engagement of the will. To pray absent-mindedly or mechanically is far from sufficient. On this the Imam says, "He who prays without exertion is like one who shoots [arrows] without a bow." Equally, there is nothing passive or easy about acquiring knowledge: "Knowledge calls out for action; if it is answered [it is of avail], otherwise it departs."

The same idea is expressed more forcefully in another saying of the Imam: "When you hear knowledge [being imparted] cleave to it, do not mix it up with jest, lest hearts spew it forth." Knowledge that is not taken seriously will be of no avail; it remains "undigested" and cannot be assimilated by the "heart," that innermost faculty which has access to the "reality of insight" and which can thus "see" God. For it is the heart that sees Allah, not by eyesight, not by بصارۃ, but through the spiritual insight, the بصیرۃ, generated by the true principles of faith, the حقائق الایمان. Indeed, it is not the individual who "assimilates" knowledge to himself; it is knowledge — or rather the reality of being expressed through true knowledge — that assimilates the individual to itself: "Acquire knowledge, and [true] life will acquire you." The relationship between life and consciousness, so central to the intrinsic function of the spirit, lies again at the heart of this maxim. At first the individual seeks knowledge and cultivates consciousness; then life "seeks" the individual, as being makes itself more fully real within him. Put differently, the individual first makes an active effort to integrate knowledge within his being; but at a certain point this activity is transformed into passive receptivity, and being — "true life" — integrates the individual within itself. The Imam's counsel to Kumayl says the same: "Through them knowledge penetrates the reality of insight." It is not the knowers who penetrate; it is knowledge that penetrates to the reality of insight, doing so through them, and this in the very measure of their effacement within knowledge, an effacement that is the shadow cast by their effective integration within the life that "acquires" them.
