The discourse to Kumayl continues: "They rejoice in their intimacy with the spirit of certainty." This sentence bears directly on the sheer happiness that flows from the life of the spirit. In the Arabic phrase *wa basharu ruh al-yaqin*, the root meaning of the word *bashara* is to have intimate experience of something, to come into direct physical contact with it. The verb in this form also carries the sense of joy, so that "rejoice in intimate contact" conveys the single word more fully. To touch the spirit of certainty is not to arrive at a cold logical fact, the endpoint of a purely mental process. It means entering deeply into the very object of one's certainty, which is ultimately nothing less than the divine itself. That reality is infinitely more blessed than any imaginable bliss of Paradise, for the Quran affirms that the divine *ridwan* — beatitude and contentment — is "greater" than Paradise. It cannot, then, but bestow joy upon the soul that truly opens itself to it:

> وَعَدَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَٱلْمُؤْمِنَتِ جَنَّتٍۢ تَجْرِى مِن تَحْتِهَا ٱلْأَنْهَرُ خَلِدِينَ فِيهَا وَمَسَكِنَ طَيِّبَةًۭ فِى جَنَّتِ عَدْنٍۢ ۚ وَرِضْوَنٌۭ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ أَكْبَرُ ۚ ذَلِكَ هُوَ ٱلْفَوْزُ ٱلْعَظِيمُ

"God has promised the believers, men and women, gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they abide, and goodly dwellings in gardens of Eden. And beatitude from God is greater. That is the supreme triumph" (At-Tawbah: 72). In the words of Ali (ع), "Learning and reflecting upon knowledge is the delight of the knowers."

This is what one might call an epistemology of joy, for "the most joyous of mankind is the intellectual (*al-aqil*)." Such a joyous epistemology stands in sharp contrast to modern scientistic conceptions of knowledge as dry, cold, and abstract, and it deserves careful attention, for it reveals a crucial dimension of the spiritual knowledge proper to the Imam's perspective, and indeed to every spiritual tradition worthy of the name. Engaging with truths ought to bring happiness, and it does so in the measure that those truths are fundamental to one's own being, or to Being as such. These two modes of being are ultimately identical, given the uniqueness — the "one-and-onliness" — of Being. That which has no second and no other cannot fall under the category of number; being is indivisible. The being of the individual cannot, therefore, ultimately differ from Being as such, however great the gap in existence — or rather the incommensurability — between the individual and God. True knowledge is knowledge of Being, and so it is inevitably a form of self-discovery, even though knowledge of the Absolute is impossible without absolute self-abandonment. The highest discovery calls for the deepest effacement.

In the early stages of this process, however, the true knowledge the intellectual acquires is a kind of self-discovery that brings the happiness of a homecoming, a return from the exile of ignorance. This follows because "the most intellectual of people" is "the one who is closest to God" and "the one who is most alive." To be close to God is to be fully alive, and this true life gives profound joy — the *joie de vivre*, the sheer joy of living. It is a joy proper to existence itself, independent of any particular experience, whether pleasurable or not.

Here the crucial relationship between life and consciousness comes into view: between the fruits of the in-spiration of God's spirit on one side, and this life of spiritual consciousness and joy on the other. Those who are true to the spirit of God within them genuinely possess joy. The true *faqih* — not so much "the jurist" as "one who truly understands" — is defined by the Imam through that same intimate, unshakeable certainty of divine goodness and compassion: he is "he who does not make people despair of the mercy of God, and does not make them lose hope in the gracious spirit of God (*rawh Allah*)." So deeply is the sage immersed in the joyous certainty of God's mercy that no room is left for despair. To despair of this mercy is itself a mark of unbelief:

> قَالَ وَمَن يَقْنَطُ مِن رَّحْمَةِ رَبِّهِۦٓ إِلَّا ٱلضَّآلُّونَ

"And who despaireth of the mercy of his Lord except those who stray in error?" (Al-Hijr: 56). The divine assurances of mercy in the Quran come fully alive in souls that possess a profound knowledge — not a merely notional one — of the beatific nature of the divine Reality:

> وَٱكْتُبْ لَنَا فِى هَذِهِ ٱلدُّنْيَا حَسَنَةًۭ وَفِى ٱلْآخِرَةِ إِنَّا هُدْنَآ إِلَيْكَ ۚ قَالَ عَذَابِىٓ أُصِيبُ بِهِۦ مَنْ أَشَآءُ ۖ وَرَحْمَتِى وَسِعَتْ كُلَّ شَىْءٍۢ ۚ فَسَأَكْتُبُهَا لِلَّذِينَ يَتَّقُونَ وَيُؤْتُونَ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ وَٱلَّذِينَ هُم بِـَٔايَتِنَا يُؤْمِنُونَ

"My mercy encompasseth all things" (Al-A'raf: 156), and

> وَإِذَا جَآءَكَ ٱلَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِـَٔايَتِنَا فَقُلْ سَلَمٌ عَلَيْكُمْ ۖ كَتَبَ رَبُّكُمْ عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِ ٱلرَّحْمَةَ ۖ أَنَّهُۥ مَنْ عَمِلَ مِنكُمْ سُوٓءًۢا بِجَهَلَةٍۢ ثُمَّ تَابَ مِنۢ بَعْدِهِۦ وَأَصْلَحَ فَأَنَّهُۥ غَفُورٌۭ رَّحِيمٌۭ

"thy Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy" (Al-An'am: 54). These are the ones who truly understand, the true *fuqaha*.

This opening to joy through intimate knowledge of God's mercy cannot be separated from beauty, whose perception is another unexpected companion of the intellect in the Imam's perspective. The appreciation of beauty is not merely a matter of subjective taste; it is an objective part of the intellect's own working. Beauty also leads straight to the heart of ethics. The Arabic *ihsan* is often translated simply as "virtue" or "excellence," but one of its key literal meanings is "making beautiful," for *husn* means "beauty." Virtue, *ihsan*, can thus be understood as that which makes the soul beautiful. In this light the relationship among intellect, ethics, and aesthetics becomes far clearer. "The excellence of the intellect," says Ali (ع), "is in the beauty of things outward and inward (*jamal al-zawahir wal-bawatin*)." The outward beauty of forms and actions must be completed by inward beauty — beauty of soul, or virtue in its fullest and most penetrating sense. All this follows naturally from two sayings attributed to the Prophet: "Truly God is beautiful and He loves beauty," and "Assume the character traits of God."

To cultivate beautiful traits within oneself makes one lovable to God, since He loves beauty. And to make oneself lovable to God cannot be separated from emulating the virtues brought to perfection in the soul of the Prophet:

> قُلْ إِن كُنتُمْ تُحِبُّونَ ٱللَّهَ فَٱتَّبِعُونِى يُحْبِبْكُمُ ٱللَّهُ وَيَغْفِرْ لَكُمْ ذُنُوبَكُمْ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ غَفُورٌۭ رَّحِيمٌۭ

"Say: O ye who believe, if ye love God, follow me, the Prophet; God will love you" (Ali 'Imran: 31). This drawing down of God's love by making oneself beautiful in the fullest sense is hinted at in another saying of the Imam: "The foundation of the intellect is the assimilation of love (*awwal al-aql al-tawaddud*)." Rather than speak simply of love as such (*wudd/mawadda*), the Imam uses the form *tawaddud* to point to the need to make oneself lovable to God. The word alludes to a twofold process: integrating and realizing the principle of love within oneself, and expressing outwardly the love felt inwardly — for love is grasped at once as outward radiance and inner attraction.

To follow the Prophet, and so make oneself receptive to the divine inflow of love, means, among other things, cultivating the prophetic virtues. These virtues are prophetic not because they belong to the Prophet alone, but because he is held to have realized virtue in all its fullness and is therefore the exemplar, above all others, of virtue as such. Beauty and love are not the only qualities that give shape to the intellect's receptivity to the divine Reality: kindness and contentment, courtesy, generosity and modesty, and wise forbearance (*hilm*) are equally essential. Not one of these moral qualities is absent from the soul of the true intellectual, and there can be no wisdom or intellect in the fullest sense where the soul lacks them.

It is precisely the presence of these virtues that lets the intellect grow in depth and breadth. Without them it stays confined to the flat, horizontal plane of its own operations, confined to the activity of reason alone. Reason so confined, until it is touched by faith and deepened by grace, remains unaware of what lies beneath the surface of its own field, oblivious of the hidden treasures of the intellect, and blind to the need to gather the whole soul within the mould of that integral, unifying virtue which bestows integrity upon intelligence. Such integration — this making-one — is absolutely fundamental to *tawhid*, now grasped as a dynamic process of spiritual unification demanded by the very idea of God's oneness. Truth must, plainly, inspire the soul; but it is equally necessary that virtue, in turn, aerate the intelligence, providing the leaven that allows it to expand to its full dimensions.

In this perspective, sinful and immoral qualities are understood not only as vices but as so many blind spots and failures of the intellect. Vice makes the heart diseased; it blinds the heart's eye and so leaves it unable to see the Real. As the Quran says:

> فِى قُلُوبِهِم مَّرَضٌۭ فَزَادَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ مَرَضًۭا ۖ وَلَهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌۢ بِمَا كَانُوا۟ يَكْذِبُونَ

"In their hearts is a disease and God increased them in disease" (Al-Baqarah: 10), and

> أَفَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا۟ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ فَتَكُونَ لَهُمْ قُلُوبٌۭ يَعْقِلُونَ بِهَآ أَوْ آذَانٌۭ يَسْمَعُونَ بِهَا ۖ فَإِنَّهَا لَا تَعْمَى ٱلْأَبْصَرُ وَلَكِن تَعْمَى ٱلْقُلُوبُ ٱلَّتِى فِى ٱلصُّدُورِ

"It is not the sights that are blind, but blind are the hearts" (Al-Hajj: 46).

All the vices are gathered together within egotism, which is in turn often described simply as caprice (*hawa*). In one saying, the Imam treats the conquest of caprice as equivalent to salvation: "He attains deliverance whose intellect dominates his caprice." Deliverance, *falah* — a word that carries the sense both of salvation and of beatitude — is thus to some degree within reach here and now; it is not a grace granted only after death. It involves tasting the joy that flows from certainty, from intimate contact with the spirit of that certainty. As for cultivating receptivity to this spirit of certainty: beyond obedience to the rules and regulations of the revealed Law, what is required is that union of pure intention and sincere devotion expressed by the word *ikhlas*. Without such sincerity or purity, obedience to formal rules is nothing but hypocrisy (*nifaq*) and pretension (*riya*) — which the Imam in turn defines as the gravest of all sins, *shirk*, the ascribing of partners to God: "Know that the slightest pretension (*riya*) is polytheism." This saying can be read as a commentary on one of the Quran's most important condemnations of hypocrisy. The verses in question speak of those who deny the essence of faith while outwardly conforming to it:

"Hast thou seen the one who belieth religion? He is the one who repelleth the orphan and urgeth not the feeding of the poor. So woe be to those who pray, those who are heedless of their prayer, who want only to be seen, and withhold small kindnesses" (Al-Ma'un: 1-7).

This short sura makes clear that formal acts of devotion have no value at all unless they are woven into a life of virtue, and unless they are performed with the right intention — that is, with *ikhlas*. It also helps explain why the Imam's ethos is described here not merely as religious but as spiritual: it carries the ideals of religion through to their deepest application. To be spiritual in this sense is precisely to be true to one's intellect, true to the treasures buried deep within it, and not merely to the reasoning functions working on its surface. Without this dimension of depth, religion is empty. "There is no religion for one who has no intellect," says the Imam. Likewise: "Action without knowledge is error." What counts is the intention behind an action, for "action, all action, is dust, except what is purified within it." This turning away from action as such, and toward instead an inner state of being from which good actions cannot but arise, clearly reflects the Quranic teaching:

> لَن يَنَالَ ٱللَّهَ لُحُومُهَا وَلَا دِمَآؤُهَا وَلَكِن يَنَالُهُ ٱلتَّقْوَىٰ مِنكُمْ ۚ كَذَلِكَ سَخَّرَهَا لَكُمْ لِتُكَبِّرُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ مَا هَدَىٰكُمْ ۗ وَبَشِّرِ ٱلْمُحْسِنِينَ

"It is not their sacrificed flesh nor their blood that reacheth God, but it is piety from you that reacheth Him" (Al-Hajj: 37).

"There is no religion for one who has no intellect." Perhaps no group better illustrated the principle in this saying than the Kharijites. Among those who rebelled against the Imam were many readers (*qurra*, sing. *qari*) of the Quran — men who enjoyed considerable religious prestige for their knowledge of the Quran and their intense worship. Their piety, however, was more apparent than real; it was, in truth, a zeal of bitterness, a caricature of true piety. When his supporters spoke of the long night vigils kept by members of this group, the Imam answered sharply: "Sleeping with certainty is better than praying with doubt." Certainty brings peace and joy, and so sleep, for one immersed in what the Imam calls the spirit of certainty, is a bodily rest that only deepens the happiness flowing from a good conscience and spiritual certitude — a certitude that is itself a kind of unbroken wakefulness, a being awake to higher realities. Bodily sleep, then, does not contradict spiritual wakefulness. As the hadith of the Prophet has it: "My eyes sleep, but my heart sleeps not."

In matters of formal worship, the true intellectual, the *'aqil* — whom the Imam defines as the one who puts each thing in its proper place (العاقل من وضع شئی حق محلہ) — is one who obeys the divine command to pray. Yet he does not pray in a mechanical way, supposing that the act alone is enough. He knows that such obedience is necessary but not sufficient for becoming receptive to grace. There must be awareness of what one is doing and why; and it is this awareness, together with virtue — inward beauty — that draws divine acceptance. "The most worthy knowledge for you," says the Imam, "is that by virtue of whose presence action is accepted by God."

"They make easy what the extravagant find harsh; they befriend that by which the ignorant are estranged." This sentence bears, among other things, on the mark left upon the soul of true sages by their remembrance of the inevitability of death and the renunciation of this world that must follow from it. In the first place, what the extravagant — the greedy, worldly sort — find harsh is outward adversity, hardship, and loss. The Quran views all these as the trials that inevitably accompany life in this world:

"And We shall try you with something of fear and hunger and loss of property and life and fruits; but give glad tidings to the patient, those who, when struck by affliction say: 'Verily, we belong to God and verily unto Him we are ever-returning.' These are the ones upon whom there are blessings from their Lord, and mercy; and these are the ones who are rightly guided" (Al-Baqarah: 155-157).

The wise, the rightly-guided (*al-muhtadun*), perceive the blessings showered upon those who are patient in the face of affliction — a patience that itself naturally accompanies their knowledge of the truth: "By the Age, truly man is in a state of loss, except those who believe and do virtuous deeds and exhort one another to truth and exhort one another to patience" (Al-'Asr: 1-3). These are the believers who remain steadfast in the face of trials, firmly rooted in their awareness of their origin and end, and in the knowledge that unto Him we are ever-returning. For this reason they can make the trials and difficulties of life easy to bear, whereas the extravagant experience them only as harshness and bitterness. The ease that lies within every difficulty is hidden from the ignorant but discerned by the wise: "Verily, with hardship cometh ease; verily with hardship cometh ease" (Ash-Sharh: 5-6). The wise go further still than merely anticipating ease as the inevitable fruit of hardship; they taste that fruit already as the seed hidden within hardship itself, for they actually befriend that by which the ignorant are estranged.

One level of meaning here is illuminated by this saying of Ali (ع): "Death is more intimate to me than the breast of the mother is to the suckling babe." In the verse cited above, the mention of trials and difficulties is preceded by a reminder that those slain in the path of God are not truly dead, "nay, they are alive but ye perceive not." This is not simply an affirmation of the life hereafter; it is also an allusion to the esoteric meaning of being slain for God: *al-fana fiLlah*, extinction in God. The Imam's intimacy with death can be understood in relation to this death while still alive, which he alludes to in another saying as well: "I am the death of the dead." Life in the world is itself a kind of death — a limitation, and therefore a privation — set against the infinite plenitude of the divine realms; and so to die to this death is tantamount to true life:

> وَمَا هَذِهِ ٱلْحَيَوٰةُ ٱلدُّنْيَآ إِلَّا لَهْوٌۭ وَلَعِبٌۭ ۚ وَإِنَّ ٱلدَّارَ ٱلْآخِرَةَ لَهِىَ ٱلْحَيَوَانُ ۚ لَوْ كَانُوا۟ يَعْلَمُونَ

"And the life of this world is nothing but sport and play," says the Quran, "and verily, the abode of the Hereafter, that is true life, did they but know" (Al-'Ankabut: 64).

It is not the physical world as such that is to be negated; rather, it is worldliness, egotistic attachment to the world, that must be overcome. One of the key principles of the Imam's perspective, stressed repeatedly throughout the *Nahj al-balagha*, bears directly here: the principle of *zuhd*, which no single English word can render adequately. It comprises several meanings: asceticism, austerity, abstention, detachment, doing without, and making little of. The following passage from the *Nahj* conveys well the attitude of the *zahid* toward this world:

The world is an abode for which annihilation is ordained, and for its people departure from it is decreed. It is sweet and green, and it hastens to one who seeks it, and confounds the heart that gazes upon it. So set out from it with the best of the provision available to you, and ask not from it above what suffices and seek not from it more than what can be attained.

What is this best of provision, this *zad*? In many places in the *Nahj* it is described as *taqwa*, another word that resists simple translation, its meaning encompassing piety, fear of God, awe, and God-consciousness. "I exhort you, O slaves of God, to *taqwa*, which is the provision," says the Imam. This provision for the next world is attained only in the measure of one's detachment from the perishable aspects of the life of this world, for "whoso desireth that which hasteneth away, in that We hasten for him what We will":

> مَّن كَانَ يُرِيدُ ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ عَجَّلْنَا لَهُۥ فِيهَا مَا نَشَآءُ لِمَن نُّرِيدُ ثُمَّ جَعَلْنَا لَهُۥ جَهَنَّمَ يَصْلَىٰهَا مَذْمُومًۭا مَّدْحُورًۭا
>
> "Whoever desires the fleeting life, We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We intend; then We appoint for him Hell, wherein he burns, disgraced and rejected." (Al-Isra: 18)

The despicable aspect of the world is described in vivid terms by the Imam. "By God, this world of yours is more contemptible in my eyes than a chewed-up bone of a pig in the hand of a leper." "An image of the world is the snake, soft to touch, but virulent poison within." The world is "as worthless to me as that which drips from the nose of a goat." It is the grandeur and beauty of God that renders the world insignificant and distasteful; only in the light of the Absolute do the pleasures and attractions of the world appear fleeting and illusory: "The greatness of the Creator for you belittles creatures in your view." In a similar vein, the Imam speaks of a brother in God: "What made him great in my eyes was the smallness of the world in his eyes (*kana yuazzimuhu fi 'ayni sighar al-dunya fi aynihi*)."

This, according to the Quranic usage of *zahid*, is the real meaning of *zuhd*. In the sura named after Joseph (*Yusuf*), the brothers of Yusuf deemed him of little value in selling him for a small price, and they are described in relation to him as *zahidin*:

> وَشَرَوْهُ بِثَمَنٍۭ بَخْسٍۢ دَرَهِمَ مَعْدُودَةٍۢ وَكَانُوا۟ فِيهِ مِنَ ٱلزَّهِدِينَ
>
> "And they sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams counted out, and they were of those who deemed him of little worth." (Yusuf: 20)

In the Imam's perspective, the world is likewise deemed of little value — not altogether valueless, but rendered all but insignificant in relation to the Hereafter, to eternity, to ultimate reality. All created things are reduced to infinitesimal, fleeting shadows destined for annihilation: "Everything perishes except His Face":

> وَلَا تَدْعُ مَعَ ٱللَّهِ إِلَهًا آخَرَ ۘ لَآ إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ۚ كُلُّ شَىْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُۥ ۚ لَهُ ٱلْحُكْمُ وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ
>
> "And do not invoke with God another deity. There is no deity except Him. Everything will perish except His Face. His is the judgment, and to Him you will be returned." (Al-Qasas: 88)

Yet the world is not deprived of all value; indeed, its significance lies precisely in what it cannot help but signify: "And there is nothing that does not hymn His glory with praise":

> تُسَبِّحُ لَهُ ٱلسَّمَوَتُ ٱلسَّبْعُ وَٱلْأَرْضُ وَمَن فِيهِنَّ ۚ وَإِن مِّن شَىْءٍ إِلَّا يُسَبِّحُ بِحَمْدِهِۦ وَلَكِن لَّا تَفْقَهُونَ تَسْبِيحَهُمْ ۗ إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ حَلِيمًا غَفُورًۭا
>
> "The seven heavens and the earth and whatever is in them exalt Him. And there is not a thing except that it exalts Him by His praise, but you do not understand their way of exalting. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving." (Al-Isra: 44)

Everything in the world, every creature in existence, proclaims the infinite creativity of the Creator. That the imagination might fathom the mystery of this universal praise, the Quran says: "And the birds in flight, each one knoweth its prayer and glorification":

> أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُسَبِّحُ لَهُۥ مَن فِى ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ وَٱلطَّيْرُ صَٓفَّتٍۢ ۖ كُلٌّۭ قَدْ عَلِمَ صَلَاتَهُۥ وَتَسْبِيحَهُۥ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمٌۢ بِمَا يَفْعَلُونَ
>
> "Do you not see that God is exalted by whoever is within the heavens and the earth and by the birds with wings spread in flight? Each one has known its prayer and its exalting, and God is Knowing of what they do." (An-Nur: 41)

It is therefore not at all contradictory for the Imam to despise the world and yet wax lyrical in his descriptions of the beauties of virgin nature, including that unsurpassable marvel, the peacock. This comes in a sermon that also includes descriptions of birds in general, as well as ants, serpents, and elephants. The sermon concludes with a galvanizing description of Paradise, setting the marvels of this world beside the delights of the next; in the light of the latter, all terrestrial phenomena pale into insignificance. For once the eye of the heart is directed toward Paradise, "your soul would become averse to the marvels of this world, its passions, its pleasures and its embellished scenery."

It might seem contradictory to bring together such apparently opposed qualities as joy in certainty and the befriending of hardship. But the latter is in fact the fruit of the former. All difficulties without exception are endured through the spiritual resources made available by faith combined with intellectual assimilation — or rather, in the measure that faith is intellectually assimilated and thus becomes *marifa* or gnosis, comprising a certainty so deep and so complete that "even if the veil be lifted" it cannot increase, according to the famous saying. It is possible to believe, at one level of the mind, that there is no god but God. The Imam, however, draws attention to what this apparently simple belief should imply when it is sincere or pure: "I bear witness that there is no god but God alone Who has no partner, a testimony whose sincerity has been tested and whose essence has been assimilated with conviction (*mutaqadan musaffaha*)."

The word *musaffa* refers to the choicest and purest part of any substance, its very essence. The root *massa* means "to suck," the idea being that the liquid or juice of a substance or fruit holds its essence, that which is extracted from it. In the present context, the Imam is stressing the spiritual substance of the testimony, as distinct from mere verbal affirmation or mental comprehension of the words. He affirms a heartfelt connection with the reality to which the testimony bears witness; the words that define it are an echo of the reality they convey, and are not to be confused with that reality itself. He continues: "We cling to it always, for as long as we endure, storing it up as protection against the terrors that will befall us. For truly, it renders faith resolute, opens up spiritual virtue, pleases *al-Rahman* (the All-Compassionate), repels *al-shaytan* (the devil)."

Returning to "befriending that by which the ignorant are estranged," one might say that this points not only to the trials of life — which are a source of strength for the wise and a source of repulsion for the ignorant — but also to the inevitability of death. For the wise, death means release, the encounter with God, blissful eternity — in short, a mode of *tawhid*, whereby the soul enjoys ever deeper degrees of integration within higher principles. For the ignorant, by contrast, death is perceived as a frightful disintegration, the end of their world rather than the beginning of endless life. There is also the prefiguration of death in life: *fana*, "extinction," "effacement," the "perishing" of egoistic consciousness before the Absolute. The ignorant recoil in horror at the prospect of losing what they falsely take to be their life, not realizing that this sacrifice of egoistic and limited self-consciousness is the very ground on which infinite consciousness is glimpsed or tasted. One can only taste the ocean of the Real by being drowned in it.

The means to this ultimate attainment is likewise embraced by the wise and feared by the ignorant, namely, the act of pure prayer, total concentration on the Real. This concentration strictly precludes all worldly or egotistic preoccupations; the sheer intensity of focus upon the Absolute burns away thoughts of the relative, and for those who ignorantly identify with relativities, both inward and outward, this amounts to a kind of death. For the wise, by contrast, this concentration on the Absolute — the unsullied remembrance of God — is a joyous contemplation of reality before which the ego is displaced and all illusions are dispelled. The passage continues: "With their bodies, they keep company with the world, while their spirits are tied to the transcendent realm."

This sentence becomes more concrete when read alongside another well-known expression of the Imam. He describes himself as belonging to a group whose spiritual degree is such that "their hearts are in the Gardens of Paradise while their bodies are at work." Being tied or attached to that realm — which encompasses the paradisal abodes and extends up to the divine Presence itself — means that they are already within that transcendent realm more fully than they are within this earthly one. This helps explain the saying: God keeps man perpetually in that which his soul desires. Those whose hearts or spirits are in the transcendent domain are those whose consciousness is substantially, not merely conceptually, determined by transcendent realities. Those whose consciousness, by contrast, is shaped by worldly concerns are in this world in the sense of being enclosed by its formal limitations; their orientation and imagination are trapped within a worldly framework. Their actions bear the mark of this worldliness, whereas the actions of the wise are the fruits of their immersion in a higher reality. One might say that their outward actions in the world belie their inward transcendence of all action; they act, yet are not bound by the fruits of their action. They know that action, all action, is dust, except what is purified — accomplished sincerely — within it.

The notion of the Hereafter deserves consideration within the Imam's ethical framework. The Hereafter is repeatedly invoked in the Imam's discourses. Is this simply a matter of holding out a heavenly reward and threatening a hellish punishment in order to enjoin the good and forbid the evil? Even if the answer is partly affirmative, there is a deeper dimension to this apparently straightforward use of divine warnings and promises as levers for moral action.

The ethical orientation here is defined not merely by belief in God but by the spiritual reality of the Hereafter as well — both objectively, in itself, and subjectively, insofar as it is assimilated by the individual. It thereby becomes a dynamic dimension — a process, an orientation, a reflux — within the believer's own soul, rather than a bare belief or hope. Anticipation of the Hereafter characterizes every believer in principle; its realization characterizes the soul of the *wali Allah*, the friend of God, the saint and the sage. The Imam speaks in a famous sentence that bears witness to his total immersion in the reality of which he is certain: "Were the veil to be removed, I would not increase in certitude (*law kushifal-ghita, ma azdadtu yaqinan*)." The anticipation — or better, the foretaste — of the Hereafter deepens, rather than diminishes, in proportion to one's virtue, piety, and sanctity; it does not become a merely heuristic device whose value is exhausted once its moral impact is achieved. The following moving passage from the *Nahj* deserves reflection in this light. What appears in it is the description of a blissful vision of the reality of Paradise, not merely a rhetorical flourish in the service of moral exhortation:

If you were to cast the eye of your heart towards what is described for you of the Garden, your soul would become averse to the marvels of this world, its passions, its pleasures and its embellished scenery. And your soul would be rapt in contemplation of the swaying trees whose roots lie hidden in dunes of musk on the banks of the rivers of the Garden, and the clusters of dazzling pearls hanging down from the branches of its trees …

It is, of course, true that the highest degree of spirituality transcends the desire for Paradise and the fear of Hell, along with the moral conduct proportioned to them. But this means that when such higher degrees of realization are attained, the soul's state can properly be described as paradisal — that is, as being already so utterly content in the beatific presence of God that it desires nothing more. This state of soul is called in the Quran *al-nafs al-mutmainna*, "the soul at peace in absolute certainty":

> يَٓأَيَّتُهَا ٱلنَّفْسُ ٱلْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ
>
> "O reassured soul." (Al-Fajr: 27)

The Imam frequently echoes, implicitly if not explicitly, the Quranic principle that "the Hereafter is better and more lasting":

> وَٱلْآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌۭ وَأَبْقَىٰٓ
>
> "But the Hereafter is better and more enduring." (Al-A'la: 17)

The Hereafter is not only the time at which divine warnings and promises reach their consummation; it is also the space in which all positive qualities — human, angelic, divine — are manifested in their fullness. These are the qualities that appear on earth as reflections of higher realities, and that encompass and subtly penetrate the entire sphere of earthly existence. The Quran, perhaps more than any other scripture, furnishes the imagination with numerous and complex descriptions of paradisal bliss. One of the key functions of these descriptions is alluded to in the Quran itself: "Assuredly, We purify them with a pure quality, remembrance of the Abode of the Hereafter":

> إِنَّآ أَخْلَصْنَهُم بِخَالِصَةٍۢ ذِكْرَى ٱلدَّارِ
>
> "Indeed, We chose them for an exclusive quality: remembrance of the Home of the Hereafter." (Sad: 46)

The mere thought of Paradise is itself a purification of the mind and heart, a means of guarding the soul against the ever-present temptation to seek its ultimate happiness and well-being in this world alone. Conversely, one's well-being in the herebelow, in regard to action, lies in the performance of good deeds, and such well-being is proportioned to the depth of one's belief that "Whatever good ye send before for your souls, ye will find it with God, better and more tremendous as reward":

> إِنَّ رَبَّكَ يَعْلَمُ أَنَّكَ تَقُومُ أَدْنَىٰ مِن ثُلُثَىِ ٱلَّيْلِ وَنِصْفَهُۥ وَثُلُثَهُۥ وَطَآئِفَةٌۭ مِّنَ ٱلَّذِينَ مَعَكَ ۚ وَٱللَّهُ يُقَدِّرُ ٱلَّيْلَ وَٱلنَّهَارَ ۚ عَلِمَ أَن لَّن تُحْصُوهُ فَتَابَ عَلَيْكُمْ ۖ فَٱقْرَءُوا۟ مَا تَيَسَّرَ مِنَ ٱلْقُرْآنِ ۚ عَلِمَ أَن سَيَكُونُ مِنكُم مَّرْضَىٰ ۙ وَآخَرُونَ يَضْرِبُونَ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ يَبْتَغُونَ مِن فَضْلِ ٱللَّهِ ۙ وَآخَرُونَ يُقَتِلُونَ فِى سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ ۖ فَٱقْرَءُوا۟ مَا تَيَسَّرَ مِنْهُ ۚ وَأَقِيمُوا۟ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَآتُوا۟ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ وَأَقْرِضُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ قَرْضًا حَسَنًۭا ۚ وَمَا تُقَدِّمُوا۟ لِأَنفُسِكُم مِّنْ خَيْرٍۢ تَجِدُوهُ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ هُوَ خَيْرًۭا وَأَعْظَمَ أَجْرًۭا ۚ وَٱسْتَغْفِرُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ ۖ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورٌۭ رَّحِيمٌۢ
>
> "And whatever good you put forward for yourselves, you will find it with God. It is better and greater in reward." (Al-Muzzammil: 20)

In other words, a sincere orientation toward the Hereafter is transformed into a perception of heavenly beatitude already in the herebelow, in the form of those very acts and attitudes which, being good, share the same nature as the felicity to which they lead. In this light, morally good actions and noble intentions are grasped by one who sees beyond the veil of this world as vivid prefigurations of heavenly realities, not merely as ethical prerequisites for salvation. Goodness, in other words, does not simply lead to a heavenly reward; it already participates in that reward: "Is the reward of goodness (*ihsan*) aught but goodness?":

> هَلْ جَزَآءُ ٱلْإِحْسَنِ إِلَّا ٱلْإِحْسَنُ
>
> "Is the reward for good anything but good?" (Ar-Rahman: 60)

The Imam's saying, "The fruit of good action is like its root," can be read as an echo of the idea that the end is already present in the means that lead to it. Fitting to close is the following verse of the Quran, which also introduces what follows:

> وَبَشِّرِ ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّلِحَتِ أَنَّ لَهُمْ جَنَّتٍۢ تَجْرِى مِن تَحْتِهَا ٱلْأَنْهَرُ ۖ كُلَّمَا رُزِقُوا۟ مِنْهَا مِن ثَمَرَةٍۢ رِّزْقًۭا ۙ قَالُوا۟ هَذَا ٱلَّذِى رُزِقْنَا مِن قَبْلُ ۖ وَأُتُوا۟ بِهِۦ مُتَشَبِهًۭا ۖ وَلَهُمْ فِيهَآ أَزْوَجٌۭ مُّطَهَّرَةٌۭ ۖ وَهُمْ فِيهَا خَلِدُونَ
>
> "And give good tidings to those who believe and perform virtuous deeds, that for them are Gardens underneath which rivers flow. Every time they are given to eat from the fruits thereof, they say: This is what we were given to eat before. And they were given the like thereof." (Al-Baqarah: 25)

The fruits of the paradisal gardens are thus experienced already in the herebelow, in the form of all goodness, beauty, and truth, and the diverse modes of happiness that flow from them. All such experiences are so many foretastes of the ultimate beatitude in Paradise. On the ethical plane, the performance of good deeds — and, even more directly, the realization of intrinsic virtue, *ihsan* — is therefore not simply a prerequisite for posthumous salvation, but is already a kind of deliverance, here and now: a deliverance from the imprisonment of sin on the outward plane, and from the bondage of egocentricity on the inward plane. This theme of salvation here and now, grounded in unshakeable certitude, is fundamental to the spirit of the Imam's teachings and will be explored further throughout the rest of this book. In the following chapter, the cardinal virtue of justice will be considered within Ali (ع)'s perspective, rooted as it is in *ihsan*, a virtue defined by the Prophet as worshipping God as if one saw Him, and concretely affirmed by the Imam as real and not merely hypothetical, for God is indeed seen by the pure of heart through the verities of faith.

The discussion of justice that follows is not theoretical speculation about what justice means in Ali (ع)'s letter to Malik al-Ashtar, written fourteen centuries ago. Neither is it the kind of definition found in a dictionary, where justice amounts to little more than fairness, equality, and fair play. Its aim is, first and foremost, to bring justice into alignment with the concept and the reality of the sacred — the reality of the sacred One, القدس. The principle of justice carries a sacred and spiritual dimension that contemporary discussion so often overlooks. At the same time, a sensitive grasp of what the sacred means opens a deeper understanding of the roots of justice within the divine nature itself, and a fuller awareness of why justice is necessary, in the world and in the soul.

The basic argument is this. In Ali (ع)'s view of the world, a commitment to justice is deepened beyond measure once it is consciously joined to the spiritual teachings of the Islamic faith. The spirit that underlies moral rules and ethical values grows stronger through a commitment to transcendent principles — even though, or rather precisely because, those principles rise above the realm of action in which the rules themselves operate. The شریعۃ may be pictured as having a body and a spirit, as a person does. Its body is made of actions — prayer, fasting, the paying of زکوۃ — but the spirit that animates those actions rests on the nature of the divine, which is justice. To follow the شریعۃ is therefore to train oneself in becoming like the divine through the principles of justice, so that action must be completed by contemplation of the divine. Here contemplation and action complete one another rather than conflict, for their union lies at the very heart of the Islamic message of tawhid, توحید — an integrating oneness that makes theory and practice a single thing, so that a person becomes a true موحد. This unity is embodied with dazzling clarity in the life of the Imam, as it is in the life of the Prophet. The harmony between the two — contemplation and action, being and doing, theory and practice, ideal and reality — runs through the whole of the remarkable document these reflections concern.

These reflections stand against the background of contemporary ethical thought and may be seen as a modest contribution, from an Islamic perspective, to the scholarly debate on virtue and ethics. They should be understood above all in light of one of the most serious and far-reaching critiques of modern and postmodern ideas of virtue in general, and of justice in particular: that of Alasdair MacIntyre. His critique, put simply, holds that for several centuries ethical thought in Western society has drifted far from its moorings in absolute values. He argues, and argues convincingly, that debates about morality and ethics, along with their philosophical foundations, are no longer grounded in any conception of 'the good life' or of 'the Good' as such. The result, on his account, is that various shades of relativism, nihilism, utilitarianism, and opportunism have become, in practice, the shifting bases on which ethical values are formed — if they are formed at all. Relativism holds that knowledge, truth, and morality are not absolute but relative, existing only in relation to a culture, a society, or a historical context. Nihilism rejects all religious and moral principles and takes life to be essentially meaningless. Utilitarianism counts an action right only if it is useful or benefits a majority, so that good and bad rest on nothing more than a calculation of greater benefit or loss. Opportunism seizes whatever advantage circumstances offer, without regard to any plan or principle — the way of the manipulator, who flatters, performs, or deceives to get what he wants.

Whatever worth these human-made theories occasionally yield, none of it is rooted in the divine; and so, even where they happen to mirror the values of faith, they are baseless, without spirit, dead corpses. Virtue practised piecemeal is not virtue properly so called; it is a series of pragmatic adjustments to changing circumstances, made in the absence of any genuine principle of virtue. Truthfulness illustrates the point. Suppose a person resolves always to speak the truth without grasping the reason that underlies it — that truth is the very nature of our Creator, الحق, the absolute truth, and that our purpose in this world is to take on the virtues of our Creator. Then truthfulness will in the end become situational and self-serving, a thing to be compromised whenever circumstances seem to warrant it, spoken when it profits and abandoned when it costs. But once truth is seen as the nature of the divine, it becomes everlasting and eternal, indifferent to consequence, because one speaks it in imitation of the immortal nature of God. The virtue itself becomes immortal, and the need to practise it piecemeal falls away. 'We are looking,' writes MacIntyre, 'for a conception of the good which will enable us to order other goods, for a conception of the good which will enable us to extend our understanding of the purpose and content of the virtues, for a conception of the good which will enable us to understand the place of integrity and consistency in life ...'

It is at this level in particular that the insights of Ali (ع) and other sages of the Islamic tradition prove especially relevant. MacIntyre's proposed solution to the crisis — a reformulation of an Aristotelian ethics grounded in a Thomistic worldview — shares a great deal with the Islamic tradition of ethical thought (akhlaq). Yet a careful engagement with the Imam's legacy yields far more than a merely theoretical approach to justice, and it does so in two respects. First, the Imam was himself a paragon of justice, and so a living embodiment of this virtue and of the other fundamental virtues. His life shows a perfect, indeed unflinching, adherence to this cardinal virtue — a life governed not by his نفس but entirely by the divine nature of God. The remarkable actions recorded of him, over which readers marvel, are the fruit of his irresistible attraction toward the nature of الحق, for his whole being was perfectly oriented toward God. His attention rested never on the action itself but on the source of the principles that gave rise to it; fixing upon the beauty of the divine nature and striving to take it on, he found that good actions arose from him naturally and inevitably. This work does not enter into many of the details of his life and their lessons, though certain incidents and events that help to illustrate the point will be recalled. Second, and more important for the present purpose, the discourses, letters, and sayings attributed to Ali (ع) offer a rich source of reflection on the living spirituality that lies at the root of a life of virtue. They afford a glimpse into a way of life wholly governed by the sacred — one in which the desire for the 'good life' emerges as the fruit of an irresistible attraction toward the Good as such, which is identical to the absolutely Real, al-Haqq.

In other words, a person is ethically inspired by 'the Good' in direct proportion to how far his very existence is oriented toward the Real. If moral rules rest on ethical outlooks, and those outlooks rest in turn on a conception of the 'good life', then that conception of the Good derives from the moral agent's most basic understanding of what life means. Amyn B. Sajoo, in a recent thoughtful work on Muslim ethics, draws a careful distinction between ethics and morals. Ethical thought, he argues, is concerned more with conceptions of 'the good', while morals pertain more narrowly to rules about right and wrong. Ethics deals with the soul and the spirit of the good, the باطن, and it is out of ethics that morals are born. 'Certainly,' he continues, 'the concepts overlap substantially in theory and practice; but it is well to bear in mind the more encompassing sense of reality that typifies ethics.' To set ethics within the wider frame of spiritual virtue — in the sense of ihsan, احسان — widens the reach of both ethics and morality still further, lending each a dimension of existential depth and grounding both in a more organic and all-embracing whole. For the spiritual life has three components: اسلام, which supplies the outer aspects of morality; ایمان, which is the framework of ethics; and the union of the two, serving as their underlying principle, which issues in احسان, the good life, the beautiful life. Abstract questions of right and wrong thus come to rest on the more decisive principle that emerges in answer to the question: what is reality?

The previous chapter's discussion of the deeper meanings of divine unity bears on this. In the Imam's spiritual vision of tawhid, a person perceives, according to his capacity, an ultimate reality that not only 'has no second' but also has no moral 'opposite'. People tend to picture the world as good against evil, God against شیطان, forever thinking in opposites; yet the Imam teaches that God has no opposite at all. ابلیس does not stand against God, for nothing has the power to stand against God. He stands against God's creation, and his whole endeavor is to drive people away from their innate divine nature by making its opposite beautiful — making arrogance attractive where God's nature is modest, lewdness where it is decent, boastfulness where it is humble. For the goodness proper to God is not the moral opposite of evil; it belongs to an altogether different plane, that of al-Haqq, الحق, the absolutely Real, whose only 'opposite' is unreality or nothingness. Goodness is at one with the pure positivity of the Absolute, whereas evil arises solely from a negative power to negate the Real, the Good. In other words, the essence of all goodness and beauty is identified with the Creator, while evil is a mode of the created — the corrupted condition of a creation that has strayed from the divine nature. This is strongly implied in the Quranic verse of سورۃ الفلق, which calls the believer to seek refuge in God from 'the evil of that which He created' (Al-Falaq: 2):

> قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلْفَلَقِ ۱ مِن شَرِّ مَا خَلَقَ ۲

'Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of the daybreak, from the evil of what He has created.'

The verse is often mistranslated as 'from the evil which He created', a rendering wrong both in theology and in language. The expression 'min sharri ma khalaqa', مِن شَرِّ مَا خَلَقَ, plainly refers to the evil that derives from creation, not to creation itself. In theological terms, God creates morally free agents, and it is they who author the evil found in creation; when creation, of its own free will, chooses to negate the divine nature of its Creator, evil is born. God may be said to 'create' all actions only in the metaphysical sense that He is the source of all being, and so of every mode within being, of which action is one; He cannot be said to have created evil as such, only the conditions within which evil arises. Evil is therefore the negation of the Good, which is at one with the Real, and as such it has no ultimate ontological principle. It is only a temporary state of deviation from that pure and divine nature, an illusion witnessed by the 'eye of the heart'.

The verse, then, may be understood as a call to seek refuge in the Real from the unreal, since between goodness and evil there is no common measure of being. Goodness can be opposed only by the appearance of evil — an appearance that the 'eye of the heart' grasps as illusion, that eye which truly 'sees' God through 'the verities of faith'. This vision of the merely relative reality of evil, far from breeding indifference toward it, greatly strengthens the spiritual resolve to overcome it, for the moral effort to be good intensifies in proportion to one's conviction of accountability to that goodness. That conviction is carried inward, from the mind to the heart, by the certainty that goodness is 'more real' than evil; and this certainty is itself nourished by the spiritual vision of the good as the Real. To perceive the radical incommensurability of good and evil therefore leads not to indifference in the face of evil but to an orientation toward the good that grips one's very existence. In the Imam's view, the notions of 'right' and 'rightful due' contained in the meaning of haqq, حق, are charged with an aura of absoluteness: to understand what is right leads to a commitment to fulfil one's obligations, while what is rightfully due is the restoration of reality through the removal of illusory evil — and both alike are infused with reality, which is justice. The moral notions of rectitude and propriety are expressions of a principle that transcends morality, a principle belonging to ultimate reality. A person's commitment to fulfilling his obligations, to giving every being its rightful due, is charged likewise with a powerful current of reality; the resolve to be just is made more absolute by the very absoluteness proper to the Real.

This duty to give each and every being its due connects to the most explicit definition of justice the Imam offers, وَضَعَ الشَّئُی حَقَّ مَحَلِّہِ, 'Justice puts everything in its right place.' A person is 'just' insofar as he gives everything its proper due, rendering the haqq owed to each person — indeed to each and every thing in existence; and the capacity to be 'just' in this demanding and universal sense grows in proportion to one's attunement to al-Haqq, the Real. As the previous chapter makes clear, this spiritual conception of virtue not only takes in one's duty to all but engages all that one is. One must be good before one can do good; and the only way 'to be' is to be at one with the Real, that which alone truly 'is'.

The Imam's remark on justice recalls the more famous definition of Plato: ...we have laid down, as a universal principle, that everyone ought to perform the one function in the community for which his nature best suited him... that principle, or some form of it, is justice. There are indeed many remarkable parallels between Plato's *Republic* and the Imam's letter to Malik al-Ashtar. Some of the more obvious correspondences deserve attention, along with the way the Imam's explicit spirituality illuminates what stays implicit in Plato's philosophy — namely, how one may actually attain the vision of the Real, which Plato calls 'gazing upon the Good'. It is this contemplation of the Good as such that serves as the source of one's capacity to act ethically at every level, for it allows one to take the Good 'as a pattern for the right ordering of the state and of the individual'.

The influence of Platonic and Neoplatonic conceptions of justice upon the shaping of ethical discourse in Islam is amply attested in the sources. Within that discourse, justice is not one virtue among several. It is the perfection, or the sum, of all the other virtues — above all the three principal Platonic virtues of temperance, courage, and wisdom, which must govern the concupiscent, the irascible, and the rational dimensions of the soul, each in its own place. When every dimension of the soul, filled out by its proper virtue, stands in its right place, the soul may be called 'just'.

What has not received sufficient attention, however, is the spiritual correspondence between Plato's chief means of arriving at the vision of the Good — anamnesis — and the cardinal role of dhikr (ذِکْر) in Islam. Both words may be rendered in English as "remembrance." And how is this justice achieved? Its power is unlocked by precisely this remembrance, this recollection of ultimate reality and of the immutable principles that apply at their several levels. It is not a matter of learning things afresh, but of recollecting principles already inherent in the very substance of the intellect — principles by which all things can be understood, and which are rooted, in the end, in the Sovereign Good itself. Such remembrance is the cognitive and philosophical foundation of ethical thought. That its importance has been largely ignored is a symptom of the severing of ethics from spirituality in modern discourse, which treats each discipline as though it were sealed off from the other. Ethics is still taken seriously as a branch of philosophy and as a discipline in its own right; spirituality, by contrast, is all too often dismissed as irrelevant to serious scholarship and consigned to the realm of the imaginary, the vague, and the mythological. This exclusion of spirituality from what passes for serious discourse is closely bound up with the reductive view of knowledge that has increasingly marked Western thought since the Renaissance — a reduction that goes hand in hand with the steady emptying out of the sacred dimension of life.

In the Islamic tradition the realms of ethics and spirituality are intimately connected. Nowhere is this clearer than in the Sufi tradition, now increasingly, and most aptly, called the ihsani tradition — taking the word ihsan (احسان: excellence, virtue, goodness) in the sense the Prophet gave it in a hadith of central importance concerning the three fundamental aspects of the Islamic way. It is known as "the hadith of Gabriel," for the questioner in the exchange — unknown to the Companions who were present — was the angel Gabriel (جبرئیل) in human form. He approached the Prophet as he sat among his Companions and said:

'O Muhammad, tell me about submission (al-islam),' يَا مُحَمَّدُ، أخْبِرْنِي عَنْ الإسْلاَمِ.

The Prophet replied: الإِسْلاَمُ أَنْ تَشْهَدَ أَنْ لاَ إِلهَ إِلاَ اللهُ وَأَنَّ مُحَمَّداً رَسُولُ اللهِ، وَتُقِيمَ الصَّلاَةَ، وَتُؤْتِيَ الزَّكَاةَ، وَتَصُومَ رَمَضَانَ، وَتَحُجَّ الْبَيتَ إِن اسْتَطَعْتَ إِلَيْهِ سَبِيلاً, 'Al-islam is to testify that there is no god but God and Muhammad is the messenger of God, to perform the prayers, to pay the poor-due (al-zakat), to fast in Ramadan, and to make the pilgrimage to the House if you are able to do so.'

'You have spoken truly (صَدَقْتَ),' Gabriel said. The Companions, who saw only a man and did not know he was an angel, were astonished that he should question the Prophet and then declare that he had spoken truly.

'Then tell me about faith (al-iman),' he said, فَأَخْبِرْنِي عَنِ الإِيْمَانِ.

The Prophet said: أَنْ تُؤْمِنَ بِاللهِ، وَمَلاَئِكَتِهِ، وَكُتُبِهِ، وَرُسُلِهِ، وَالْيَوْمِ الآخِرِ، وَتُؤْمِنَ بِالْقَدَرِ خَيْرِهِ وَشَرِّهِ, 'It is to believe in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day, and to believe in divine destiny, both the good and the evil thereof.'

'You have spoken truly (صَدَقْتَ),' he said.

'Then tell me about virtue (al-ihsan),' he said, فَأَخْبِرْنِي عَنِ الإِحْسَانِ.

He said: أَنْ تَعْبُدَ اللهَ كَأَنَّكَ تَرَاهُ، فَإِنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ تَرَاهُ فَإِنَّهُ يَرَاكَ, 'It is to worship God as though you see Him, and if you see Him not, yet truly He sees you.'

The word ihsan may also be translated literally as "doing what is beautiful," its root (حَسَنَ) being bound up above all with beauty, husn. In Islamic ethical discourse virtue and vice are often called husn and qubh (قُبْح) — literally, beauty and ugliness. In the end it is the vision of divine beauty that inspires virtue, which is beauty of soul, just as it is the departure from the divine qualities that leaves the soul ugly (قُبْح). It is unsurprising, then, that in broad terms the specialists in outward action have been the jurists, the fuqaha, and the specialists in formal belief the theologians, while it fell to the mystics to be the custodians of spiritual virtue, of "making beautiful." It is no coincidence, either, that the great majority of artists in the Islamic world — calligraphers, painters, poets, musicians, and the rest — have been practising Sufis.

The Prophet's definition of ihsan as "worshipping God as if one could see Him" makes the crucial relationship plain — between worship and virtue, between spirituality and ethics, between devotion to the Creator and goodness toward creatures. One cannot have the one without the other. This relationship lies at the very heart of the spiritual tradition in Islam. And it is the denial and subversion of that tradition by some modern Muslims which, more than any other single factor, lies behind the atrocities now committed by Muslims in the name of Islam.

Both the theory and the practice of ethics have always been integral to Sufism. Even some who wrote in more philosophical and less explicitly spiritual terms, such as al-Farabi, were known also to be practising Sufis. The most influential figure in whom spirituality and ethics meet is, of course, al-Ghazali, whose magisterial Revival of the Sciences of Religion stands as a monument to the impress of Islam's deepest spirit upon the ethical temper of the believing soul. He has aptly been called the greatest thinker on ethics in Islam; and since his thought is shaped so thoroughly by Sufism, this alone testifies to the close bond between Sufism and ethics. It would be no exaggeration to say that the majority of treatises written by Sufis are in fact treatises on "ethics" — if ethics is understood not merely as akhlaq in the narrow sense, but also as the fruit of ihsan, or spiritual virtue. The various spiritual stations (maqamat) the Sufis describe often bear the names of particular virtues, such as patience (sabr), gratitude (shukr), contentment (rida'), generosity (karam), and so on.

The thread running through all these stations is a transforming awareness of God — the principle of being and acting "as if you could see God," that is, of conducting and composing oneself in the consciousness of standing always in the divine presence, for even if one cannot see Him, "He sees you." The imperative of ihsan thus lies at the very root of a life of virtue in the spiritual universe of Islam. In his sermons in the نھج البلاغۃ, Ali (ع) repeatedly draws the reader back to the "vision" of God, at whatever degree, as the true basis of a life of virtue, and repeatedly warns against its opposite, the engrossing vision of oneself, as the source of all vice. On the one hand, the Imam says, "Know that your every action is dependent upon your prayer" — that is, upon one's way of "gazing upon the Good," to use the Platonic terms. On the other, he warns against vanity, conceit, and the lavish praise of oneself by others, for these are Satan's (شیطان) surest openings for effacing the virtue, the ihsan, of the virtuous (المُحسنین). The true and objective vision of al-Haqq (اَلْحَقّ), the Real, attained through the effacement of oneself in prayer — for in the prostration (سجدۃ) of prayer one effaces one's own ego, one's nafs (نَفْس) — is here set against the distorted, subjective vision of the ego, swollen by pride, which is precisely what Iblis (اِبْلِیس) desires. The first leads to justice — the placing of all things in their proper place, and, most fundamentally, of the ego itself; the second leads to all the injustices that flow from self-aggrandizement, fanaticism and bigotry among them. For Satan, the epitome of pride and disobedience, is described as "the leader of the fanatics and the forerunner of the proud" (امام المتعصبین و سلف المستکبرین, imam al-mutaassibin wa salaf al-mustakbirin). Bigotry is intolerance toward those who hold different opinions; and fanatical bigotry is a peculiarly intense form of injustice, for it carries that pernicious prejudice which subordinates the objective demands of justice to the supposed prerogatives of one's self — whether that self is defined as the individual, the family, the clan, the tribe, the nation, or the religion.

The Imam's letter appointing Malik al-Ashtar as his governor of Egypt appears as letter 52 in most editions of the نھج البلاغۃ. It has been a source of inspiration across the centuries, read as an ideal constitution for Islamic governance. With its fairly detailed account of the duties and rights of the ruler, of the various officers of the state, and of the main classes of society, it complements the more general framework of principles enshrined in the famous "Constitution of Medina" dictated by the Prophet. Yet the counsel in the letter far exceeds the bounds conventionally set by political or legal texts on governance. Though addressed in the first place to the ruler or governor of the polity, much of that counsel in fact concerns universally applicable ethical principles, and it is therefore as relevant to the governed as to those who govern. The letter is as much a statement of ethics as of politics — not a systematic "theory" of ethics, to be sure, but an inspiring expression of the spiritual ethos the Imam embodied and radiated. That ethos flows directly from the sources of the Islamic revelation, and so the letter discloses the roots of virtue and ethics within a climate governed by the all-embracing principle of revelation. It can accordingly be read as a commentary on that revelation as well, one that in turn draws the reader more deeply into the meanings enshrined in the revealed texts. Malik al-Ashtar was a long-standing and devoted follower of the Imam, spoken of as one of his "right-hand" men. Muawiya — the Imam's chief antagonist in the civil war that dominated his caliphate — was among those who used the term, notably on hearing that his plot to have Malik poisoned before he could take up his post in Egypt had succeeded. Tabari reports him as remarking: "Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع) had two right hands. One of them was cut off at Siffin, and the other today." The Imam, for his part, responded to the news of Malik's assassination thus: "Malik, and what was Malik! By God, were he a mountain, he would be the solitary one soaring above all others, and were he a rock, he would have been impenetrably solid. No horse could ascend such a mountain, no bird could fly up to it."

The Imam's definition of justice stands at the center of what follows: "Justice puts everything in its right place." In everyday speech justice means little more than fairness, equality, and fair play — a serviceable but essentially formal account of the word. The conception at work here is of an altogether different order. It aligns justice with the sacred, with القدس, the All-Holy, and locates the very roots of justice within the divine nature itself. What binds this conception of justice to the sacred is the imperative of first putting one's relationship with God in its right place; everything else follows from that spiritual imperative. The same order of precedence is clearly set out in an important statement in the Imam's letter to Malik: "Be just with God and be just with people [giving them what is their due] from yourself."

Being just with God means, among other things, conforming as far as one can to His own nature — which is not merely the source of justice but is justice. The weight falls on that word is: justice is not simply one attribute among His many, standing alongside His mercy, His wrath, and His love. It is the very essence of His nature, so that all His other qualities flow from it. His mercy is an expression of His justice, and so too are His anger, His love, His creating, and His destroying. "I bear witness," says the Imam in one of his sermons, "that He is Justice ('adl) and He acts justly."

It might be objected that between the divine reality of justice and its human expression there is a radical gulf. In God, justice means that everything is in its right place; in man, justice means the effort to put everything in its right place — an immutable metaphysical quality on the divine side, a dynamic effort of the will on the human side. One reply runs thus: man's moral effort to act justly in a world where things are not in their right place is itself rooted in an innate spiritual disposition toward justice. Just action thus expresses the principle of justice, which, in man as in God, is that immutable principle by which everything is in its right place. As divine action in creation, judgement, and the rest is an expression of absolute justice, so in man just action expresses not only a moral, volitional, and intellectual effort to realize justice, but also a spiritual affinity with the ultimate nature of reality — with things as they truly are in God, and therefore as they ought to be here on earth.

Applied to state and society, one of the plainest consequences of this conception of justice is the necessity of piety and rectitude in rulers. As the Imam says in another sermon: "The most momentous of the reciprocal rights that God has made obligatory is the right of the ruler over the subjects, and the right of the subjects over the ruler, a reciprocal obligation which God has ordained for them." He then makes a point altogether indispensable to any discourse on good governance in Islam: "The subjects will not be righteous except through the righteousness of the rulers, and the rulers will not be righteous except through the uprightness of the subjects. So if the subjects render to the ruler his rightful due and he renders them theirs, then will right be honoured among them, the ways of religion will be upheld, and the banners of justice will be erected." This insistence on the piety of the ruler is, as one would expect, central to the Imam's message to his governor; but it involves far more than a simple exhortation to abide by the formal rules of Islamic law.

The whole of the Imam's life may be seen as a quest to conform as perfectly as possible to the divine nature, and to this quality of justice in particular. The dimensions of this principle as they appear in his life and teachings — social, economic, political, juridical — are far too many to treat within a brief compass. One defining moment in his caliphate shows the rigour with which he held to justice at whatever cost. The revolt of Muawiya, and the civil war into which the fledgling Muslim empire was thereby plunged, may be seen as having begun not at Siffin but in Medina. On assuming the caliphate, Ali (ع) was advised by his cousin Ibn al-Abbas to confirm all of 'Uthman's governors in their posts for the time being, and then, once the new order was secure, to remove them. The Imam's reply to this proposed course was reported thus: "I do not doubt that this would be best for the sake of reconciliation in this world. But there is my obligation to the Truth (alladhi yalzamani min al-haqq) and my knowledge of Uthman's governors, so, by God, I shall never appoint one of them."

Thus was the die cast: the Imam dismissed Muawiya together with all of his predecessor's governors. He saw clearly that Ibn al-Abbas' proposed solution had every chance of success; he knew that all Muawiya wanted was worldly power, and that Muawiya would have been content to govern Syria had the Imam allowed it. Commentators have cited this episode — which made the revolt of the governors all but inevitable — as evidence of Ali (ع)'s want of political acumen and his intransigence. It ought instead to be understood as an expression of his disdain for worldly ease when that ease can be bought only at the price of essential principles. As he says in one of his aphorisms: "People renounce no part of their religion for the sake of rectifying their world without God opening them up to something worse than it" — worse, that is, than the very defect they were seeking to rectify.

Plainly, to confirm in power governors whose corruption was beyond both doubt and remedy would have meant, for the Imam, "renouncing" a part of his religion — for religion without justice is not religion. To support unjust governors, even as a tactical manoeuvre, was a compromise of religious principle simply inconceivable to him. This disposition was embodied in countless episodes of his life, all of which show that the principles enshrined in the letter to Malik al-Ashtar were far from merely theoretical.

What follows examines one particular dimension of justice — political on the surface, ethical in its outward expression, but spiritual in its depth: the justice of the political ruler, taken in relation to its most clearly definable opposite, which is injustice, tyranny, oppression, and corruption. A deep assimilation of the Imam's spirituality can lend an existential power to the moral effort to live justly, a power that is absent when justice is conceived only in individual or horizontal terms — that is, as a secular moral philosophy divorced from religious or spiritual principles. The crucial role of devotion and worship, both formal and supra-formal, belongs to this same inquiry. Contemplation of the divine Reality is the wellspring from which integral virtue flows freely and without ceasing — a point sharpened by comparison with Plato's "gazing" upon the Sovereign Good as the source of all virtue.

The inquiry that follows takes its bearings from a single document above all others: the letter of Ali (ع) to Malik al-Ashtar. It is there that a sacred conception of justice is set out most fully, and it is from its key passages that the present analysis draws.

Around that letter stand the Imam's other writings. His further letters, his sermons, and his sayings are gathered here as they bear upon the same theme, extending and deepening what the letter to Malik sets down. Justice, treated in this way, is not read out of a single text in isolation but heard across the whole body of his counsel.

Beyond the words of Ali (ع) himself, the analysis turns to certain traditions of the Prophet and to verses of the Quran. These are brought forward not as ornament but as illumination, for they cast light on the very themes the letter raises and disclose the ground on which its conception of justice rests.

The letter is addressed to one of the Imam's closest and most trusted companions. For that reason his warnings against injustice and oppression carry a very precise force, over and above the universal theme they express. Such warnings apply to everyone who is bound by Islam and its laws, and who begins with every right intention, yet still stands open to the temptations of political power. They reckon fully with a truth that is unfortunate but well proven, the truth caught in the maxim that power corrupts, or, in the Imam's own words, 'he who rules, appropriates (man malaka istathara).'

The Imam's understanding of justice plainly reaches beyond its own historical moment and beyond the formal boundaries of the Islamic faith. The letter can be read as speaking not only to those who wish to govern by just principles, but to everyone who, though not corrupt at the start, can be corrupted — and that includes the great majority of humankind.

A note of sober realism sounds from the very opening of the letter. What dominates the tone of the preamble is the capacity for evil in a person left to his own devices and cut off from divine grace, and this is why the preamble stresses obedience to God's wajibat, the religious obligations binding on every Muslim. Malik is instructed to place obedience to God above all else, 'to abide by what He has commanded in His Book ... for no one prospers except through abiding by them, and no one is wretched except through repudiating and neglecting them'. The preamble introduces, but it is far from a formality: obedience to the divine commands is to be understood not merely as legally binding but as spiritually liberating. Such obedience plays a crucial part in freeing a person from the tyranny of the 'soul which incites to evil' (al-nafs al-ammara bil-su), which the Imam names immediately after calling Malik to obedience: 'For truly, the soul incites to evil, unless God has mercy.' This sentence is almost identical to the words of the Prophet Joseph in the Quran (Yusuf: 53), and it matters greatly, for it sets the scene for the ethical commands and the social and political instructions that follow. The one relationship that decides the spiritual substance of the soul, and still more its moral conduct, is the relationship between the human soul and divine grace. Without grace the soul leans toward evil; with God's help it is freed from its base inclinations and guided back to its true, original nature, its fitra, which the Quran names in the following verse:

So set thy purpose for religion with unswerving devotion: the nature of God (firat Allah), according to which He hath created man. There is no altering God's creation. That is the right religion (al-din al-qayyim), but most men know not. (Ar-Rum: 30)

The present state of the fallen soul, then, is called to give way to the ideal state of original human nature. That nature is both the origin and the end of the human condition, and at the same time the true substance of every human soul. It is always within reach in principle, even if, for most people, fallen human nature keeps it clouded in practice. To revive this original nature, one turns back to the two functions that complete each other, the human intellect and divine revelation. In the first sermon of the Nahj, the Imam states that God sent to mankind 'His messengers, dispatching prophets in succession, in order to claim from them [His creatures] the fulfilment of the covenant of His creation; to remind them of His forgotten graces; to remonstrate with them through communication [of His revelation]; to unearth for them the buried treasures of the intellects (dafa in al-uqul).'

These 'buried treasures' can be identified with the original, God-given knowledge that belongs to the fitra. Out of this whole and undivided human nature, in full harmony with the divine nature, all the essential virtues flow freely and without hindrance. 'Let your most beloved treasure be the treasure of virtuous acts', the Imam writes. Virtue will indeed be the 'most beloved treasure' for the person who reverses the natural inclinations of the self-centered soul and sets it, by a movement above the natural order, toward its own deepest nature, and by that very token toward the divine Reality that is the ground of being of all authentic virtue. For al-Haqq, the Real, is not only the deepest foundation of virtue; it is the true substance of every good quality, and, in the end, of every single thing that exists. As one of the most celebrated supplications attributed to the Imam puts it:

By Thy tremendousness (bi-a matika), which has filled all things ... by Thy Names which have filled the foundations of all things, by Thy knowledge which encompasses all things, by the light of Thy face, through which all things are illumined ...

From this vantage point, every virtue can be seen as the reflection, on the human plane, of a divine attribute — of what is called a divine 'Name.' So the central theme of the ihsani tradition — the path of spiritual excellence (احسان), which the Prophet defined as worshipping God as though one could see Him, knowing that even if one does not see Him, He sees him — finds its expression in the saying: 'Assume the character traits of God (takhallaqu bi-akhlaqiLlah).'

In the Imam's view the bond between human virtue and divine reality is wholly indispensable. From the side of the person, the practice of virtue draws down the matching divine quality; from the side of the reality itself, the divine quality is the source, and, in keeping with true tawhid, the very substance of all human virtue. Every good quality, whether in itself or as it shows forth, belongs to God, the One who 'has no partner' in the language of theology and 'has no second' in the language of being. This mystical absorption of the principle of tawhid is strongly implied in the Quranic verse, 'And thou threw not when thou didst throw [a handful of dust], but God it was who threw' (Al-Anfal: 17). These divine qualities are not to be seen as purely transcendent, as though they were wholly one with the divine essence and entirely beyond the reach of the human soul. They are also to be grasped as models, as patterns of perfection for the soul to imitate as fully as it can. The goal is to grow as 'like' God as possible, yet this growth can unfold only within the bounds of one's servitude to Him. A person is generous for the sake of God, because God is الکریم, the Generous; he is compassionate and merciful because God is الرحمن الرحیم — never out of any claim that 'I am generous' or 'I am merciful,' for the aim is to imitate the qualities of God, not to claim to embody Him. The individual must therefore be effaced before God if he is to be truly virtuous. At the same time he must share in and embody the very qualities he wishes God to show toward him, staying lowly, humble, and effaced throughout. He does so in the certainty that no measure of virtue or intelligence can ever lessen or match the qualities of God, since there is no proportion between the Absolute and the relative, the Creator and the created. His effort to embody these qualities gains its power in the measure that he grasps the divine attributes — by direct insight and in his very being, rather than by reasoning alone and in theory. It is like gazing into a mirror: what one sees is a reflection, but an inverted one. The aim is to catch, on the human plane, the inverted reflection of divine transcendence. For man is at once خلیفۃ اللہ, God's vicegerent upon the earth, and عباد اللہ, His slave. The awareness of servitude makes sure that, even as he represents God, man does not slip into rivalling Him in grandeur; and the active commitment to represent God's attributes keeps him from the spiritual paralysis of neglecting his duties toward the world. Such is the meaning of the verse, يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ أَنتُمُ ٱلْفُقَرَآءُ إِلَى ٱللَّهِۖ وَٱللَّهُ هُوَ ٱلْغَنِىُّ ٱلْحَمِيدُ, 'O mankind, you are the destitute before God, and God is the Self-sufficient, the Praiseworthy' (Fatir: 15). There must be a joining of the active human virtues with the spiritual awareness of one's own nothingness before the divine Reality. The bond between intelligence and humility deserves stress here: the mind's perception of the divine attributes gives rise to humility, and the effacement of the soul in turn draws attention away from the ego and toward the transcendent reality as the source of all virtue and truth.

The idea of the 'soul which incites to evil,' and the Quranic story of Joseph (Yusuf) in which it appears, deserves closer attention. The Imam could take it that his readers knew this context, and he plainly meant it to be kept in mind by Malik, and by anyone else reading this letter on governance.

Joseph gives this account of man's base inclinations after his innocence of every charge has been established before the Egyptian king. Even so, he says, 'I do not exonerate myself. Truly, the soul incites to evil, unless my Lord has mercy.' On the two occasions when Zulaykha's seductions were set before him, the Quran makes clear that his successful resistance came not from his own moral resources but from the grace of God.

This theme of human helplessness before gratification that is attractive but immoral is strongly implied when the Imam repeats the Quranic phrase, 'Truly the soul incites to evil, unless God has mercy.'
