These, then, are the two poles that draw the ordinary soul, the soul not yet 'at peace': on one side its own base inclinations, pulling toward the negative possibilities of the fleeting world of appearances; on the other the higher pull toward the grace of God, which draws the soul back toward the pure positivity of ultimate reality. The sheer sharpness of the contrast in this powerful Quranic sentence awakens an awareness of the soul's absolute and unconditional need of God in every circumstance. It is a most fitting way to open a letter of instruction to a man about to be given authority over a vast and wealthy country, where temptations lie in wait on every side. It stands as a solemn reminder that the soul can be lured on every plane, the gross and the subtle alike, and that this weakness cannot be overcome by the soul itself, but only by the mercy and grace of God. And yet, to return to Joseph's words, the 'vision of the evidence' of God implies active discernment, and, as its moral fruit, resolute self-control. The human effort to avoid sin therefore does not contradict the fact that grace is necessary for virtue; rather, that effort expresses a grace already given, already present within the conscientious soul. The very capacity of the human will to strive for virtue is itself a grace that was there beforehand, set within the spiritual constitution, the fitra — though it is a grace that must be made present, or brought into act, through the sincere effort to draw upon this God-given power.

How this grace enters the soul and becomes a deciding element of moral and spiritual life is made clearer later in the Imam's letter. For now the negative side of the question needs more work, for the ever-present temptation of the ruler to abuse his power and commit injustice and tyranny deserves more than a passing mention. It could indeed be argued that the question of how to hold back from injustice is far harder and more subtle than its positive counterpart, how to act with justice. The Imam lays out the positive rules of governance in a direct and plain manner. Far less plain is whether any holder of political office can actually stay faithful to those rules when faced with the temptations that power offers. One can frame laws to punish corruption, but no law can supply the will or the strength to stay incorruptible before the enticements of political power. This helps explain why the Imam's exhortations take on such a strongly negative cast in the early part of the letter, as in the command to 'break the soul in the face of passionate desires,' to 'dominate your inclination,' to 'withhold yourself from that which is not lawful for you.' It also explains why the ethical demand of justice must be set firmly within a lived spirituality. Without that grounding, commands to be fair, just, and honest will lack the quality of lived reality that turns them from abstract propositions into unquestionable realities, and that changes a formal obedience to rules imposed from outside into a spiritual kinship with the source of those rules.

Living by just precepts then stops being a matter of complying with something imposed from outside, and becomes instead the moral accompaniment of one's inner being. In other words, a whole and integrated approach to justice leads to an identification with what is right, with al-Haqq itself, rather than merely to the doing of what is right. There is a shift of consciousness from doing to being, from action to contemplation, without this in any way weakening or undermining action. On the contrary, action comes to reflect, on its own plane, the divine object of contemplation, and by that very fact becomes more effective, not less. An orientation toward the Real gives a deeper degree of reality both to what one does in the realm of action and to one's own manner of being. One does what is right in the measure that one is real; this process of realization is named in the Islamic spiritual tradition tahqiq, 'making real.' One's ethical conduct is 'made real' through spirituality, and spirituality, for its part, is voiced and made more concrete through the practice of virtue.

The Imam then issues a stern warning: وَلاَ تَنْصِبَنَّ نَفْسَكَ لِحَرْبِ اللهِ, 'Do not set your soul up for war with God.' One may well ask what this means, and what kinds of acts or attitudes set the soul at war with God. The reference seems to reach deeper than simple disobedience, deeper than the many breaches of religious obligation named at the letter's outset. That is the most obvious meaning of 'fighting' against God, but it does not rule out subtler forms of opposition to divine reality: attitudes that may go along with outward acts of obedience yet contradict their very spirit. One example is the cardinal vice of pride (takabbur, or kibr), against which the Imam warns again and again — the inner state in which a person feels superior and behaves highhandedly toward others, its signs so plain in his conduct that they cannot be hidden. A ruler's pride is a theft of a divine attribute, a seizing of a greatness that belongs to God alone, who declares: الْكِبْرِيَاءُ رِدَائِي، وَالْعَظَمَةُ إِزَارِي، فَمَنْ نَازَعَنِي وَاحِدًا مِنْهُمَا، قَذَفْتُهُ فِي النَّارِ, 'Pride is My cloak and greatness is My robe; whoever contends with Me over either of them, I shall cast him into the Fire.' God alone has the right to takabbur, and God alone may be called, without offence, al-Mutakabbir, 'the Proud.' To vaunt oneself before others is as good as defying God's authority within, and so amounts to an implicit denial of His unique and incomparable majesty. This denial of something that belongs to divine sovereignty can itself be understood as a kind of 'war' with God, for a subject who openly defies his king is, in effect, waging war against him. In short, enmity toward transcendent reality is the invisible substance that runs through all pride, and through every act of arrogance or oppression that a ruler commits against those beneath him.

The paradox here, which only a sense of spiritual values can make visible, is this: an attitude of superiority toward those 'below' is in fact an act of rebellion against that which is 'above'. An injustice done to creatures does not merely draw down upon its author the justice of the Creator; it is also, in itself, open opposition to the Creator. So what looks like a horizontal vice — 'horizontal' in the sense that it belongs to this world — is in truth a spiritual disorder. The outward wrong of corruption is only the symptom of an inner sickness of the spirit: an unspoken denial that the source of all power and authority is absolute, and therefore unique; a forgetting of the truth stated in the Quranic verse, لِّمَنِ ٱلْمُلْكُ ٱلْيَوْم لِلَّهِ ٱلْوَحِدِ ٱلْقَهَّارِ, 'To whom belongeth the dominion this day? To God, the One, the All-Conquering' (Ghafir: 16). This truth ought to sound without pause in the ears of every ruler, where 'this day' means every day, and not the Day of Judgement alone. In the Imam's sermon known as al-Qasia (القاسیۃ), 'the Abasement' — so named because it abases the proud — Iblis (Satan) is described as the first of those who 'competed with God' in grandeur, and so as the very embodiment of pride and arrogance. When commanded to prostrate before Adam, Iblis refused, as the Quran recounts:

إِذْ قَالَ رَبُّكَ لِلْمَلَٓئِكَةِ إِنِّى خَلِقٌۢ بَشَرًۭا مِّن طِينٍۢ ۝ فَإِذَا سَوَّيْتُهُۥ وَنَفَخْتُ فِيهِ مِن رُّوحِى فَقَعُوا۟ لَهُ سَجِدِينَ ۝ فَسَجَدَ ٱلْمَلَٓئِكَةُ كُلُّهُمْ أَجْمَعُونَ ۝ إِلَّآ إِبْلِيسَ ٱسْتَكْبَرَ وَكَانَ مِنَ ٱلْكَفِرِينَ, 'When your Lord said to the angels: Truly I am going to create man from clay; and when I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down before him prostrate. So the angels prostrated themselves, all of them together; save Iblis: he was proud and was one of the disbelievers' (Sad: 71-74).

He refused because 'vehement passion' overcame him. He judged himself higher than Adam on the grounds that he was made of fire while Adam was made of clay, خلقتنی من نار و خلقتہ من طین. Taking pride in this supposed superiority, and so rebelling against God's command, Iblis is not only the first 'enemy of God' but also 'the leader of the bigots and the forerunner of the proud' (imam al-muta assibin wa salaf al-mustakbirin, امام المُتَعَصِّبِین و سلف المستکبرین). The Imam warns his listeners: 'Beware lest he infect you with his disease' through his insinuations, whisperings, and machinations. And he urges them: 'Be resolute in placing self-abasement over your heads, casting self-glorification beneath your feet, and removing pride from your necks. And take up humility as the fortified watchtower between you and your enemy.'

Humility is the chief weapon in the war against Iblis, whose own aim, conversely, is to plant pride, for pride is not only the worst of the vices but the poison that infects and destroys every virtue. The moment pride keeps company with a virtue, the virtue turns into a vice. 'The sin that grieves you is better, in the sight of God, than the virtue that makes you proud.' Bound up with this is what was noted earlier about the dangers of excessive praise and the conceit it breeds, these being among 'Satan's most reliable opportunities to efface the virtue of one who is virtuous'.

Taken together, these statements form a commentary on the Quranic account of the disgrace of Iblis. They seize a simple act of disobedience at its spiritual root, and in doing so bring home how ever-present is the danger of falling into that 'hidden' form of shirk (polytheism) to which the Prophet refers in these words: الشِّرْكُ فِي هَذِهِ الْأُمَّةِ أَخْفَى مِنْ دَبِيبِ النَّمْلِ علی حَجَرِ الأَسوَد فِی لِیلَۃِ الظُّلْما — 'The creeping of shirk in my community is more hidden (akhfa) than the creeping of a black ant over a hard rock on a dark night.' The surface notion of shirk as the worship of material idols, شرک الجلی, the open and manifest form, must be grasped more subtly as شرک الخفی, the hidden form: false gods concealed within one's intentions, attitudes, and orientations — all the makings of hidden pride, vanity, ostentation, and pretentiousness. As the Imam says, 'Know that the slightest pretension (riya — ریا) is polytheism.' To act in order to earn the praise of others is to act for others rather than for God, and so to ascribe partners to God by implication: 'Whoso acts for other than God, God entrusts him to those for whose sake he acted.'

Seen in this light, the meaning of Iblis' disobedience opens more deeply. It is the outward moral result of an inner sickness of the spirit, one rooted in that pride which amounts to 'hidden polytheism' and which brings a shameful humiliation in its train. Iblis is disgraced because he disobeyed God, and he disobeyed God because of pride. Pride is therefore, in and of itself, a disgrace — a state of 'dis-grace', a warping of the human condition that carries within it the seed of its own certain reversal. 'Do you not see how God humiliated him through his pride?' the Imam asks. To be proud is already, in reality, a form of humiliation, for to exalt the self is to destroy the self.

Returning to the pride of those in power, the Imam states in a few words the train of thought that sets itself running in the mind of a ruler who is stepping onto the slippery slope toward oppression: وَلاَ تَقُولَنَّ: إِنِّي مُؤَمَّرٌ! آمُرُ! فَأُطَاعُ! إِنَّ ذلِكَ إِدْغَالٌ فِي الْقَلْبِ، وَمَنْهَكَةٌ لِلدِّينِ — 'Do not say, "I have been given authority, I order and am obeyed", for this leads to corruption in the heart and the erosion of religion.' Such self-glorification is seen to produce first an inner, spiritual corruption, that of the 'heart', and only then the ruin of religion. This order of priority makes plain that the outward prescriptions of religion require the right inward attitude if they are to be applied with integrity and held steady over time. The Imam's thought might be put another way: when power goes to the head, faith departs from the heart; and conversely, for faith to be rightly shown in the world, it must flow from a heart filled with humility. This is another face of 'putting each thing in its proper place', وضع کل شئی حق محلہ.

The Imam continues: وَإِذَا أَحْدَثَ لَكَ مَا أَنْتَ فِيهِ مِنْ سُلْطَانِكَ أُبَّهَةً أَوْ مَخِيلَةً، فَانْظُرْ إِلَى عِظَمِ مُلْكِ اللهِ فَوْقَكَ، فَإِنَّ ذلِكَ يُطَامِنُ إِلَيْكَ مِنْ طِمَاحِكَ، وَيَكُفُّ عَنْكَ مِنْ غَرْبِكَ،يَفِيءُ إِلَيْكَ بِمَا عَزَبَ عَنْكَ مِنْ عَقْلِكَ — 'If the authority of your position engenders vanity and arrogance, then look at the grandeur of God's dominion above you … this will calm your ambition, restrain you from your own vehemence, and restore to you what had strayed from your intellect.' The bond between intellect and humility deserves close attention here. The part of the intellect that 'strays' when vanity and arrogance take hold is precisely the part that is aware of God's absolute reality, and of the relative, derivative, and finally illusory character of everything else. It is telling that the word for 'arrogance', makhila (مَخِيلَةً), comes from the same root as the word for imagination, khayal (خَیَال), and is thus closely tied to the realm of the imaginary, the fanciful, the illusory, and the unreal: when imagination fastens upon the unreal, it becomes charged with pride and turns into مخیلۃ, arrogance. Arrogant pride is therefore an intense form of self-delusion rooted in a defect of the intellect. It shows itself as a vice, but its cause lies deeper than the moral level, for it involves not merely an overestimation of oneself but, more fundamentally, an underestimation of the Absolute. In this light, the open egotism of the tyrant can be seen as a heightened form of the inborn egocentricity that clings to anyone who has not realized the truth of God's sole reality and the finally illusory nature of all else. The sage alone takes fully into himself the truth stated in such Quranic verses as: كُلُّ شَىْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُ — 'Everything is dying away except His countenance' (Al-Qasas: 88); كُلُّ مَنْ عَلَيْهَا فَانٍۢ ۝ وَيَبْقَىٰ وَجْهُ رَبِّكَ ذُو ٱلْجَلَلِ وَٱلْإِكْرَامِ — 'Everything that is thereon is perishing, and there subsisteth but the Face of thy Lord, possessor of Glory and Bounty' (Ar-Rahman: 26-27); and وَقُلْ جَآءَ ٱلْحَقُّ وَزَهَقَ ٱلْبَطِلُ ۚ إِنَّ ٱلْبَطِلَ كَانَ زَهُوقًۭا — 'The Truth hath come and falsehood hath passed away; indeed, falsehood is ever passing away' (Al-Isra: 81). Only the sage draws from this truth the humility that dissolves all individualism and egocentricity — the roots of pride, vanity, and arrogance, which are in turn the lifeblood of tyranny and oppression.

The Imam's warning can now be better appreciated: إِيَّاكَ وَمُسَامَةَ اللهِ فِي عَظَمَتِهِ، وَالتَّشَبُّهَ بِهِ فِي جَبَرُوتِهِ، فَإِنَّ اللهَ يُذِلُّ كُلَّ جَبَّار، وَيُهِينُ كُلَّ مُخْتَال — 'Beware of comparing [yourself] with God in greatness and likening [yourself] to Him in might, for God abases every tyrant and disgraces every braggart.' The one who does not act justly toward God and His creatures — for the Imam commands, أَنْصِفِ اللهَ وَأَنْصِفِ النَّاسَ مِنْ نَفْسِكَ، وَمِنْ خَاصَّةِ أَهْلِكَ، وَمَنْ لَكَ فِيهِ هَوىً مِنْ رَعِيَّتِكَ، فَإِنَّكَ إِلاَّ تَفْعَلْ تَظْلِمْ — will find that not His creatures alone but God Himself becomes his adversary: وَمَنْ ظَلَمَ عِبَادَ اللهِ كَانَ اللهُ خَصْمَهُ دُونَ عِبَادِهِ، وَمَنْ خَاصَمَهُ اللهُ أَدْحَضَ حُجَّتَهُ، وَكَانَ لله حَرْباً حَتَّى يَنْزعَ وَيَتُوبَ — 'He remains at war with God until he desists and repents.' The tyrant will in the end be forced to repent, even if only at the moment of death, with judgement close at hand. And even if he seems to have escaped the consequences of his tyranny in this life, he cannot escape them in the Hereafter.

As for the nature of the tyrant's war against God in this world — that is, before repentance or judgement overtakes him — it lies in his unspoken opposition to ultimate reality, his violation of the deepest nature of things, of the true nature of his own being, his فطرۃ. This war takes several forms.

One form lies in the very persistence of tyranny itself, for the longer it lasts, the more wretched the tyrant's soul becomes, and the more firmly the seeds of misery take root in his being. This is what the Quranic doctrine of istidraj (اِسْتِدْرَاج), the drawing out of punishment by degrees, implies. The word derives from درج, meaning stages, as even in Urdu one says درجہ بدرجہ, step by step. God uses it in Surat al-Araf: ‏وَمِمَّنْ خَلَقْنَآ أُمَّةٌۭ يَهْدُونَ بِٱلْحَقِّ وَبِهِ يَعْدِلُونَ ‎۱۸۱‏وَٱلَّذِينَ كَذَّبُوا۟ بِـَٔايَتِنَا سَنَسْتَدْرِجُهُم مِّنْ حَيْثُ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ ‎۱۸۲ — 'Of those We have created are people who guide with truth and dispense justice therewith. But those who reject Our signs, We will lead them on by degrees [to punishment] from whence they know not' (Al-A'raf: 181-2). The punishment dealt out by degrees can take the shape of apparent worldly success, as the following verse makes clear: ‏وَلَا تُعْجِبْكَ أَمْوَلُهُمْ وَأَوْلَدُهُمْ ۚ إِنَّمَا يُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ أَن يُعَذِّبَهُم بِهَا فِى ٱلدُّنْيَا وَتَزْهَقَ أَنفُسُهُمْ وَهُمْ كَفِرُونَ ‎۸۵ — 'Let not their wealth nor their children please thee. God desireth only to punish them thereby in the world, that their souls shall pass away while they are disbelievers' (At-Tawbah: 85). A tyrant or oppressor can be a Muslim in the formal sense and yet be guilty at the same time of a mode of disbelief — taking the word kafir in its strict etymological sense, as one who 'covers over' the truth and its moral demands, both in his very being and in his actions. This connects directly with the contrast drawn in the verses just quoted (Al-A'raf: 181-2): between those who dispense justice in accordance with the truth and 'those who reject Our signs' — the oppressors and tyrants, precisely.

chapters.chapter_key: prayer, remembrance, and gazing on the good
chapters.before_md:
The most important part of the whole letter now comes into view: prayer, the chief means by which the ruler takes into himself the sacred substance of all the virtues. At the opening of the letter, the Imam began with a counsel to observe the obligatory prayers. Here, after stressing that every task of government must be done at its proper time, he instructs Malik to set aside the best portion of his available time for what lies between him and God — that is, for worship and devotion. Malik is urged to give special care to the obligatory prayers, the means by which he purifies his religion for God and makes his devotion to Him sincere. This is not merely a call to perform the formal prayers. It must be understood above all in light of the deeper meaning of purifying one's religion for God: the purifying of the very substance of the relationship between the soul and God, for the depth of that relationship is what determines the quality of all human virtue. As the Imam put it in a saying already noted, "Know that your every act is dependent upon your prayer." Every action, in other words, depends upon the way one gazes upon God, who is the source of all good. What matters is not only the formal performance of the prayer, in body and word, but the inward quality that accompanies it and gives it life from within. Sincerity, intensity, and frequency are essential to its power. The Imam continues, "Give unto God of your vital energy in your nights and your days, and perform fully that by which you draw near to God, doing so perfectly, without becoming dull or deficient, taking your body to its limits (balighan min badanika ma balagha)."

The whole emphasis here falls on the word taqarrub, drawing near. One attains divine nearness most directly through deep devotion, offered up alone, in the dead of night, with all one's heart. Once that nearness is realized, all one's other actions in the world are imbued with something of the spiritual quality gained through closeness to God. In this way all action can be drawn into devotion in the wider sense, since every outward act is then governed by the sincere intention to give oneself to God. If the inner life is ruled by prayer, prayer comes to penetrate the outer life as well. Hence the Imam, immediately after telling Malik to set apart the best of his time for God, adds, "all times [and the actions performed therein] are for God if the intention underlying them is good and if your subjects derive security as a consequence." All the actions of a ruler, in other words, will partake of the sacred to the degree that his devotion truly reaches into the source of the sacred. One may then envisage an overflow, as it were, from the fountain of obligatory and voluntary prayer into the outward domain of action. This subtle truth is expressed in the famous hadith qudsi of the Prophet, often referred to as the hadith of taqarrub:

> My slave draws near to Me through nothing I love more than that which I have made obligatory for him. My slave never ceases to draw near to Me through supererogatory acts until I love him. And when I love him, I am his hearing by which he hears, his sight by which he sees, his hand by which he grasps, and his foot by which he walks.

To see and to act through God can be understood, at one level, as seeing things as they really are and then acting upon that vision — which is to say perfect justice, the placing of each thing in its proper order. This is why the Imam repeatedly draws those who read his sermons back to the vision of God, setting that vision as the true foundation of a life of virtue. In prayer the ego is effaced through prostration, and this submission to God through self-effacement is itself what puts all things in their right place, including, and especially, the ego. The hadith qudsi marks a distinction between the obligatory and the supererogatory acts of devotion. Both are means of drawing near, but it is primarily through the latter that the slave comes to perceive and act through the divine. The Imam's phrase, taking your body to its limits, carries the same weight. Strenuous effort is called for, and it is far from enough to perform the prayers and devotions in a mechanical or perfunctory manner. "He who prays without making an effort," says the Imam, "is like one who shoots arrows without a bow." As noted earlier, the sincerity (ikhlas) demanded by the Imam's conception of the oneness of God calls for the integration of the soul, and it is in prayer that the deepest dimensions of the soul are expressed, cultivated, and integrated. The prayer must therefore be accomplished not merely with the tongue or the body, but with all that one is.

Elsewhere, Ali (ع) points to the key supererogatory practice by which the spiritual station of nearness is attained. He does so in a commentary on the words of a Quranic verse, "… men whom neither commerce nor trade diverts from the remembrance of God" (An-Nur: 36).

> Truly God has made the remembrance (al-dhikr) a polish for the hearts, by which they hear after suffering from deafness, and see after being blind … There have always been slaves of God … with whom He held intimate discourse through their thoughts and spoke with them through the essence of their intellects. They diffused illumination through the awakened light in their hearing and their seeing and their hearts, calling unto the remembrance of the days of God.

The dhikr is of the first importance in the Imam's outlook, both as a principle of awareness of ultimate reality and as a concrete means of attaining that awareness. By the word dhikr the Imam means both a methodic practice of invoking a divine Name and a principle of permanent awareness of God that embraces all modes of worship, meditation, and reflection. It is to be understood not only as being aware of God or remembering God, but also as an intense mode of prolonged, prayerful meditation on ultimate reality, represented both symbolically and sacramentally by one or more of the divine Names. This remembrance is not the learning of new things from scratch. It is the recollection of ultimate reality — of the immutable, unchanging principles and divine attributes that are inherent in the very substance of our intellects, by which everything can be understood, and which are ultimately rooted in the divine nature of our Creator. This aspect of remembrance receives fuller treatment in the chapter that follows. The relationship between the remembrance of God and the cultivation of justice is made clear in this sermon, for the Imam describes those illuminated by the dhikr:

> Truly there are people who belong to the dhikr; they have adopted it in place of the world, such that "neither commerce nor trade" distracts them from it; they spend the days of their life in it … they instruct people about justice and themselves are steadfast therein.

It is those souls who truly belong to the dhikr who are not only steadfast in justice but also able to instruct others about it. Putting first things first, they can show how to place all things in their proper order. Fervent, lived spirituality is therefore not opposed to dedicated activity in the world. It infuses that activity with an ethical depth that springs from direct contact with the divine — a contact articulated by prayer in general and by the dhikr in particular. Just as the sincerity of a good intention is proven by the effort to realize it, so the sincerity of prayer is proven, and made effective, through the sustained effort to prolong and intensify it, taking your body to its limits. What this has to do with justice is plain. If justice is grasped as a quality rooted in the Real (al-Haqq), then nearness to the Real cannot but draw one nearer to justice and to all positive qualities, whether spiritual, intellectual, or moral. The relationship between worship and justice must therefore be firmly established if the conception of justice is to be called sacred. From this angle, justice is both cause and consequence of worship. On the one hand, justice requires that everything be given its due, and God must accordingly be given His due, which entails, sacramentally, worship and prayer. On the other hand, justice arises ethically as a consequence of that worship, as do all the virtues, in proportion to the nearness God grants His worshipper and in accordance with the radiant repercussions of that nearness.

What the Imam offers in his stress on prayer, together with its essence, the remembrance of God, is a devotional principle that illuminates and, in a sense, sublimates Plato's philosophical position. It might be seen as making explicit in spiritual terms what remains implicit in Plato's teaching. After discussing the question of justice at great length, Socrates comes to the crux of the matter, the nature of the Sovereign Good, which is of paramount concern to the ideal ruler, the guardian, whose moral and intellectual formation lies at the heart of the dialogue's practical side:

> … the highest object of knowledge is the essential nature of the Good, from which everything that is good and right derives its value for us … I need not tell you that, without that knowledge, to know everything else, however well, would be of no value to us …

Socrates declines Glaucon's entreaties to describe the nature of this Good, offering instead to speak of its offspring. This leads him to draw an analogy between the Good and the Sun: what the Sun is to visibility, the Good is to intelligibility and being. He proceeds with the famous allegory of the cave and then describes the course of education that would turn the attention of his prospective rulers from the world of shadows to the world of real objects — a course comprising mathematics, arithmetic, geometry, solid geometry, astronomy, harmonics, and dialectic. Having passed successfully through all its stages, "when they are fifty, those who have come safely through and proved the best at all points in action and in study must be brought at last to the goal. They must lift up the eye of the soul to gaze on that which sheds light on all things; and when they have seen the Good itself, take it as a pattern for the right ordering of the state and of the individual, themselves included." Yet Plato nowhere states what this gazing actually means, nor how it is to be achieved, nor by what means — intellective, contemplative, or methodic.

At an important point in the Republic, Glaucon presses Socrates on the definition of the Sovereign Good: "But, Socrates, what is your account of the Good? Is it knowledge, or pleasure, or something else?" Socrates refuses to give a direct answer, saying after some further discussion, "I am afraid it is beyond my powers; with the best will in the world I should only disgrace myself and be laughed at." Very much in the manner of Glaucon, Dhilib al-Yamani provocatively asked Ali (ع) whether he had seen the object of his devotion. To this the Imam replied, "I would not be worshipping a lord whom I have not seen." Dhilib then asked, "O Commander of the Faithful! How did you see Him?" The Imam replied with a sentence that serves as one of the leitmotifs of this book: "O Dhilib! Eyes see Him not through sight's observation, but hearts see Him through the verities of faith."

The polishing of the heart brought about by remembrance, by ذکر, bears directly on this, for the very word evokes the essence of Plato's approach to knowledge as recollection, anamnesis. Remembrance in this sense is not the learning of something new from scratch, but the recollection of ultimate reality — of the immutable divine principles and attributes inherent in the very substance of our intellects, by which everything else can be understood. Yet Plato in none of his dialogues makes direct reference to the devotional, methodic, or contemplative counterpart of his educational, ethical, and intellective endeavor. There is no explicitly stated link between remembrance of the forms or ideas that engender true knowledge and the gazing upon the Good, the contemplation of that which sheds light on all things. It is not merely knowing and remembering the forms, but coming to know the Bestower of Forms, which in Islam is named by the divine Name al-Musawwir. Whether there was any spiritual method in Plato's teaching — and if there was, why he did not divulge it — remains a matter of speculation. One answer may be gathered from a statement in Plato's famous Seventh Letter, where he denies that any exposition can be given of the true reality of philosophy, and points instead to the disciplined way of life and rigorous daily routine that the subject demands if philosophy in the deepest sense is to be realized. "No treatise by me concerning it exists or ever will exist. It is not something that can be put into words like other branches of learning; only after long partnership in a common life devoted to this very thing does truth flash upon the soul, like a flame kindled by a leaping spark, and once it is born there, it nourishes itself thereafter." This returns to the importance of active spirituality for the practice of authentic virtue. If the Real, indefinable in its essence, is the foundation of all good, then the means of assimilating the Real existentially, and not merely comprehending it mentally, cannot be set aside. Plato's philosophical approach to the Good can be augmented and deepened by an appreciation of Ali (ع)'s means of drawing near to the Real, for in the Imam's perspective intellectual comprehension and spiritual devotion are inseparable and complementary. Integral, deep-rooted justice emerges as one of the fruits of this drawing near, just as, for Plato, gazing on that which sheds light on all things, the Good itself, yields the capacity to take the Good as a pattern for the right ordering of the state and of the individual.

These pages have sketched the outlines of a spiritual approach to the theme of justice as it presents itself principally in the Imam's letter to Malik al-Ashtar. The surface of this important subject has only been skimmed. Yet the Imam's illumination of the principle of justice, addressed in the first instance to a prospective governor of Egypt in the first century of the Islamic era, is by no means outmoded. Whether one operates in an avowedly Islamic or an overtly secular environment, whether the rule be autocratic or democratic, whether political institutions be strong or weak, wherever individuals are vested with power and authority, and by that very token exposed to the temptations that power offers, the approach to justice articulated in the Imam's ethos will not be irrelevant. This ethos does not presuppose any particular form of government. It engages the universal theme of moral responsibility, but does so in terms of that which transcends the level of morality, offering insights drawn from a direct vision of ultimate spiritual realities. The principles contemplated through this vision surpass the domain of politics, and for that very reason are able to penetrate deeply and to refashion, from above, the moral substance of political consciousness. Although the Imam's perspective is particularly pertinent to the meeting point of spirituality, morality, and governance within Islamic discourse and practice, its relevance extends to every context in which a sense of the sacred plays a part in the shaping of moral sensibility and the cultivation of political responsibility.

The Imam's letters and discourses are a vast and largely untapped source of inspired ideas, able to illuminate the role of spiritual principles in forming ethical values and shaping the quality of political practice. In particular, any integral Islamic approach to politics and society must reckon with the requirements and fruits of worship, taking that word in its widest sense. Sincere worship transforms the notion of the Absolute into a concrete reality, imparting to the soul an existential impetus and a spiritual resource that supports, stabilizes, and deepens one's moral life. What is derived from consciousness of the divine Reality is not so much a philosophy of ethics as a spiritual morality — an existential orientation that is at once the consequence of a lived spirituality and the cause of its continuous, dynamic, and ever-deepening realization of spiritual truth, the Real as such, al-Haqq. This means that the haqq, the right due to each person or group, will be given in accordance with the principle of justice, that of putting each thing in its proper place, وَضَعَ الشَّئُی حَقَّ مَحَلِّہِ. Virtue, from such a perspective, is a form of ethical realism, where realism denotes an assimilation of spiritual reality, and morally correct behavior translates that realism into action across every plane, individual, social, and political.

Should it be objected that this perspective is hopelessly utopian, the harsh demands of politics and the sublime ideals of spirituality being poles apart, the reply is this. If no effort is made to grasp the deeper dimensions of Islamic piety and spirituality, then any ostensibly Islamic discourse — whether in politics, sociology, ethics, or any other field — will be reduced to an outer shell, stripped of the inner life that gives it all its meaning and, more importantly, its transformative power. For Islamic concepts to be grasped aright, they must be assimilated not merely by the mind but by the heart, failing which they remain mere abstractions. As the Imam insists, it is the heart, the inmost point of consciousness, that sees the true nature of things. This is why the vision of God as if one could see Him lays bare the crucial relationship between worship and virtue, between spirituality and ethics, and equally between devotion to the Creator and kindness towards His creation. One cannot have the one without the other, for to conduct oneself as though one could see God is to live in the consciousness of standing constantly in the divine presence, since even if we cannot see Him, He sees us. Without this vision there is no ihsan in the ethico-spiritual sense discussed earlier, and without ihsan the very integrity of the Islamic way of life is fatally undermined. It is precisely the denial and subversion of this tradition that bears ultimate responsibility for the atrocities committed by a tiny minority of Muslims in our times — people who betray the highest ideals of the Islamic ethical tradition by resorting to unbridled violence in its name, as though one might hurt creation in order to please the Creator. Without ihsan, religion is left acutely vulnerable, turned into an ideology, driven by individual passion and open to political manipulation. It is no surprise that those most prone to terrorism in the name of Islam have emerged from the currents most hostile to the ihsani or mystical tradition.

This returns to the devotional practices that are all too often regarded as the preserve of a minority — viewed as either mystical or misguided, depending on one's standpoint — rather than understood as a God-given means of narrowing the gap between what one aspires to and what one is: of moving from the actual towards the ideal, of making concrete what would otherwise remain abstract, of living what is only thought about, and of rendering existentially galvanizing what might otherwise be merely theoretically compelling. While the principles established here are universal in their reach and application, it would be wrong to try to decontextualize the Imam's perspective by dismissing, as so much unnecessary superstructure, his repeated, insistent, and uncompromising emphasis on the imperative of prayer. The principle of justice requires that all the elements of one's life — devotion, worship, ethics, action — be bound together in a harmonious, indissoluble, and interconnected whole, in accordance with the ideal of tawhid. And tawhid means precisely this integration, the making of many into one, so that when a person's theory and practice have themselves become one, that person has become a true bearer of that oneness. There can be no question of detaching the domain of the virtues from that of spirituality, for in the Imam's perspective the only true virtue is one that is rooted in, sustained by, and oriented towards the divine Reality. A virtue that is not so rooted, even one that happens by coincidence to mirror an Islamic value, is baseless and without spirit. Cut off from its source, it becomes situational and self-serving, open to compromise the moment circumstances warrant, and ceases to be a virtue at all, dwindling into a mere series of pragmatic adaptations to shifting conditions. Justice, together with all the other virtues, can only be brought to fruition in a soul, and in a society, permeated and penetrated by spirituality, the essence of which is the principle and practice of the remembrance of God. And this remembrance, this dhikr, is not the learning of something entirely new. It is a recollection of the ultimate Reality — a recollection of the immutable principles and unchanging qualities inherent in the very substance of our intellects, principles by which everything else can be understood, and which are ultimately rooted in the divine nature of our Creator. Remembrance of this kind is nothing less than the cognitive and philosophical foundation of ethical thought in Islam. In the last analysis, it is the remembrance of God that determines the quality of human virtue. It is to the spiritual realization intended and cultivated by this remembrance that the following chapter is addressed.

chapters.chapter_key: dhikr: the polish of the heart
chapters.before_md:
The subject of this chapter is the meaning of dhikruLlah, 'the remembrance of God', one of the most fundamental principles in Islamic spirituality. It is approached in two ways: through the sayings of the Imam, read essentially as commentaries on the Quranic idea of dhikruLlah, and through the doctrines that have grown up within the mystical traditions of Islam. To speak of Ali (ع) is to speak of the very heart of Islamic spirituality. His influence is felt wherever spirituality has flourished in Islam — in the more clearly defined disciplines of Sufism and Shii 'Irfan, and equally in the realms of futuwwa (spiritual chivalry), the craft guilds, music, poetry and the arts. As the gate to the city of prophetic wisdom, he leaves his mark on all the noblest expressions of the spirit of Islam.

Within the Sufi tradition especially, the connection with the Imam is uniquely deep. Shii or Sunni, Arab or Persian, Turk or Malay, Mauritanian or Bosnian — whatever their background, the Sufi orders are united in the figure of Ali ibn Abi Talib (ع). He stands at the summit of all the chains of affiliation (salasila, sing. silsila) by which the masters trace their spiritual lineage back to the Prophet. This unifying role appears just as clearly in relation to the deepest internal division within Islam, that between Sunnism and Shiism. The two traditions share vast common ground in essential beliefs and practices; beyond this, they are drawn together in a direct and living way by a shared orientation, both looking toward sanctity (walaya) and gnosis (marifa) as the goal of the religious life. Seyyed Hossein Nasr writes: 'Islamic esotericism or gnosis crystallized into the form of Sufism in the Sunni world, while it poured into the whole structure of Shiism, especially during its early period.' The esoteric core of Islam thus expresses itself in Sunni Sufism and in Shiite 'Irfan with different accents. It takes on different forms and modes of expression, yet its attunement to the essence of tawhid is never fundamentally altered. According to Sayyid Haydar Amuli, one of the great figures in whom Shiism and Sufism meet, the true Shii cannot but be a Sufi' once he sounds the mystical depths of the Imams' teachings; and conversely, the Sufi is a Shii once he recognizes that the deepest roots of Sufism lie in the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt. These are the first poles (aqtab, sing. qutb) of the spiritual tradition, through whom the mystical blessings of the Prophet were passed down within an initiatic setting. For Amuli, the differences of outward form between the two traditions are dissolved in the fire of walaya — sanctity, which is the true substance and goal of both alike. And for both, Ali (ع) is the wali Allah, the 'friend and saint of God', par excellence.

The way Ali (ع) is regarded within the Sufi tradition is captured well by Ali Hujwiri, author of the first manual of Sufism written in Persian, the Kashf al-mahjub: 'Among them [the Sufis] is the son of Muhammad's uncle, he who drowned in the ocean of trying affliction, and was consumed in the fire of loving passion (ghariq-i bahr-i bala' wa hariq-i nar-i wala), the leader of the saints and the pure ones (muqtada-yi awliya wal-asfiya). In this Path he holds a place of tremendous honour and elevated degree. He had complete mastery over the precise expression of the principles of the supernal realities, such that Junayd said of him, "Ali is our master as regards principles and affliction (shaykhuna fil-usul wal-bala)." ... That is, Ali (ع) is the Imam of this Path in respect of both theoretical knowledge and practical application (andar 'ilm wa muamalat imam-i in tariqat), for the adepts of Sufism call the knowledge of this Path its "principles", while its practice is summed up in the endurance of affliction.'

The 'endurance of affliction' recalls the Imam's description of the sages as those who 'befriend that by which the ignorant are estranged'. One reading of that compressed phrase is this: among the things the sages befriend and the ignorant flee is prayer — and more particularly the act of pure concentration on the Absolute, which shuts out every other thought. Such concentration is a kind of death, in which the ego and all its concerns are, as it were, 'sacrificed' before the divine Reality on which the whole attention is fixed. The remembrance of God can be understood in two ways at once: as the fulfillment of that concentration, and as the path leading to the summit of spiritual realization — the effacement of the self before the sole reality of God.

The body of Ali (ع)'s teachings sheds remarkable light on the idea, the principle and the practice of dhikruLlah — a theme of central importance in both the Quran and the Sunna of the Prophet. His sayings form a valuable commentary on those Quranic verses that speak of dhikr; and, since the dhikr stands at the center of Sufi practice and doctrine, they help explain why the Sufis regard the Imam as the first spiritual Pole (qutb) of Sufism after the Prophet himself. The close bond between remembrance and spiritual realization is illumined both by the Imam's sayings and by the writings of the Sufi tradition, especially those of the school of Ibn al-Arabi — known in the tradition as al-Shaykh al-akbar, the greatest Master', for his towering influence on later Sufi thought. These writings can be read as doctrinal echoes of the dense, often compressed pronouncements of the Imam. Taken together, his sayings and the Sufis' elaborations bring key aspects of Islamic spirituality into sharp focus.

The term dhikr calls for attention first, along with the reason for its prominence in Islamic devotional practice. Its meaning is extremely rich, and no single English word can carry its full range. It covers remembrance, recollection, invocation, repetition, incantation, recitation; and also memory, mention, telling, relating a story, praise, glorification, celebration, fame, eminence, honor, exhortation and warning; and it can even denote the Quran itself, or any book of revelation or religion. The definition that comes closest to the spiritual principle the word expresses is the one given by al-Raghib al-Isfahani in his Quranic dictionary. He writes that dhikr is that by means of which 'man preserves that knowledge (marifa) which he has attained, so it is akin to memory (hifz), except that memory is spoken of in respect of its function of acquisition (ihraz), whereas dhikr is spoken of in respect of its function of rendering present (istihdar). Dhikr is also used to refer to the presence of a thing in one's consciousness (lit. "heart") or in one's speech. Thus, it is said that there are two types of dhikr: dhikr of the heart and dhikr of the tongue, and each comprises two further kinds: a dhikr which follows forgetfulness, and a dhikr which does not follow forgetfulness but which, on the contrary, expresses a continuous remembering.'

Much in this definition agrees with the Imam's outlook. The key point is that when the thing remembered — 'rendered present' to consciousness — is God, the importance of dhikruLlah as a principle becomes plain. DhikruLlah is to be understood first and foremost as a principle of awareness, a deep taking-in of the divine presence; but it must also be understood as an action, a practice or set of practices, and so as a spiritual discipline. It can therefore be grasped both as the end and as the means to that end — both as spiritual awareness and as the methodical practice that cultivates that awareness. It is within the Sufi tradition that this relationship, between the practice of the dhikr and the awareness it aims at, is worked out most fully. There the dhikr appears both as a contemplative discipline centered on the methodical invocation or repetition of a Name of God, and as the cognitive result and mystical fruit of that discipline.

The dhikr is thus the spiritual method of the Sufis above all others — a discipline that helps to realize within the heart what is already present to the mind, turning an abstract, notional grasp of certain ideas into a direct perception of spiritual realities. Insofar as dhikruLlah is understood as the permanent awareness of the divine Reality, it can be presented as the very essence of religion itself: it is that which 'once again binds' (re-ligare) the human being to God, and so it is the reason for being of all religious rites and practices. If prayer is the core of religious practice, dhikruLlah is, as the Quran states simply, akbar — that is, 'greater' or 'greatest':

> ٱتْلُ مَآ أُوحِىَ إِلَيْكَ مِنَ ٱلْكِتَبِ وَأَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ ۖ إِنَّ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ تَنْهَىٰ عَنِ ٱلْفَحْشَآءِ وَٱلْمُنكَرِ ۗ وَلَذِكْرُ ٱللَّهِ أَكْبَرُ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ مَا تَصْنَعُونَ

'Truly, prayer keepeth [one] away from lewdness and iniquity, and the remembrance of God is greater' (Al-'Ankabut: 45).

Many sayings of the Prophet testify to the pre-eminence of the remembrance of God. It is related that the Prophet asked his companions: 'Shall I not tell you about the best and purest of your works for your Lord, and the most exalted of them in your ranks, and the work that is better for you than giving silver and gold, and better for you than encountering your enemy, with you striking their necks and them striking your necks?' Those he addressed replied: 'What is that, O emissary of God?' He said, 'The perpetual invocation of God, exalted and glorious (dhikruLlah azza wa jalla daiman).'

Ali (ع) affirms the same: 'Perpetuate the dhikr, for truly it illumines the heart, and it is the most excellent form of worship (huwa afdal al-ibada).' The dhikr receives much emphasis in the Shii tradition, which records many sayings of the early Imams on the merits of invoking the Names of God and various sacred phrases. Imam Jafar al-Sadiq described his followers specifically in terms of dhikr: 'Our Shia are those who, when alone (idha khalau), invoke and remember God much.' The khalwa — the spiritual retreat in which one seeks to be 'alone' with God — is described by 'Allama Tabatabai, one of the foremost masters of Shii gnosis in the twentieth century: As to the particular spiritual retreat (khalwat-i khass) it is distancing oneself from people ... it is especially required during certain types of verbal invocations (adhkar-i kalamiyya) ... and is considered essential by the masters of the path.'

Within the Sufi tradition, the following statement on the dhikr by Shaykh Ahmad al-Alawi may be taken as fully representative:

Remembrance is the mightiest rule of the religion ... The law was not enjoined upon us, neither were the rites of worship ordained but for the sake of establishing the remembrance of God ... In a word, our performance of the rites of worship is considered strong or weak according to the degree of our remembrance while performing them.

Al-Ghazali raises the question of why the dhikr should be the most meritorious practice, when it is so simple to perform beside all the other acts of worship, which demand so much effort. His answer is that this superiority can only be fully understood through the 'science of unveiling' ('ilm al-mukashafa). What can be said from the standpoint of the practical religious sciences (ilm al-muamala) is that the most effective dhikr is the one performed continuously, with the presence of the heart (hudur al-qalb). This is the aim of the dhikr, and it is this that takes precedence over all acts of worship; indeed, it is through this that the other acts of worship gain their dignity; this is the ultimate fruit of the practical acts of worship.' The principle of dhikruLlah thus touches the highest levels of religious practice, contemplative discipline and spiritual realization, and so the very heart of Islamic spirituality. For all their variety across time and place, and all their differing perspectives and emphases, the Sufis are unanimous that dhikruLlah lies at the center of their way. And for all their differences of name, orientation, school of thought or manner of practice, the Sufi orders are united in the pivotal figure of Ali (ع) as the one who connects every later master of the spiritual path to the Prophet himself. This coming-together of the Imam and the dhikruLlah is far from accidental. The Imam's clarifying of the meaning of the dhikr, together with his own initiation of disciples into its methodical practice, is a key part of his role as spiritual guide — the wali Allah, or the Pole (qutb) of his age — and it is therefore central to his esoteric function within the spiritual tradition of Islam, in both its Sunni and Shii forms.

As for this esoteric function, very little firm historical information survives about the Imam's initiatic role in it — that is, his actual initiation of disciples into the practice of invocation, known in the tradition as talqin — just as little survives about his own initiation into the esoteric practice by the Prophet. This is hardly surprising, since the practice is, precisely, esoteric: it is not laid upon everyone as an obligatory rite. Within both Sufism and Shii 'Irfan, the invocation is instead granted to those with a particular vocation, those who have received a calling' to practice something beyond the obligatory rites binding on all. Even so, there are historical accounts that offer prima facie evidence of the Imam's role in transmitting the dhikr. The people described in the earliest sources as devoted to the dhikr as a particular practice were known as close associates, if not disciples, of the Imam. His role in this initiatic domain is stressed in the orally transmitted sources of the Sufi way, and set down in several written sources as well. These preserve reports of the dhikr passing from the Prophet to the Imam, and from him to several other disciples, who went on to initiate others into what later came to be called the way of tasawwuf.

Sound historical material on the earliest use and transmission of dhikruLlah may be scarce, but there remains a body of extremely important literary evidence: the sayings recorded in the Nahj al-balagha and the Ghurar al-hikam, along with the supplications attributed to the Imam. Taken together, these sayings form a coherent corpus — a distinct body of doctrine that offers a rich source of philosophical reflection, spiritual meditation and metaphysical insight into the nature and meaning of this practice, which holds so central a place in the mystical tradition of Islam.

These sayings shed light not only on the meaning of the practice of dhikr but also on the philosophy and the theory of knowledge that underlie it; and they give precious glimpses of the fruits of the practice, its fulfillment in spiritual realization. On one side, the Imam's sayings are an important source of commentary on the Quranic verses that touch this theme; on the other, they clearly foreshadow the more elaborate doctrines of the dhikr found in the later Sufi and 'Irfani traditions. They thus serve as a bridge, joining what came before the Imam — prophetic revelation — with what came after him: the work of mystical elaboration. The texts and manuals of the mystical tradition seem to make explicit what was, more often than not, implicit in the Imam's sayings. The mystics drew out esoteric truths that the Imam had conveyed in sayings that were concise, often paradoxical and compressed, yet always intellectually demanding and spiritually fruitful. Reflection on these sayings — read within the context of the Quran and the Sunna they illuminate, and in the light of the later Sufi doctrine they anticipate — can bring one closer to a proper understanding of the role of dhikruLlah in the practical, operative and visionary dimensions of Islamic spirituality.

The best place to begin reflecting on those sayings is the Imam's comment on the dhikr in sermon 213 of the Nahj al-balagha. There the Imam first quotes words from verse 37 of Sura 24 of the Quran, called al-Nur ('The Light'), which speaks of the invocation of God's Name, and then comments on them. The words are these: 'men whom neither trade nor merchandise diverts from the remembrance of God'. This fragment belongs to the 'verse of light' that comes just before it, the ayat al-nur so rich in mystical symbolism, and this connection gives the Imam's comment a much deeper resonance. The Imam surely knew that reciting the words of verse 37 would bring the earlier verses to his listeners' minds; by not quoting the verse of light in full, he only sharpened the effect of the omission, and such hints, implications, evocations and allusions are a mark of Arabic balagha. His words, then, are best held alongside the verse of light set out in full:

God is the light of the heavens and the earth. A similitude of His light is a niche wherein is a lamp; the lamp is enclosed in a glass; the glass is as it were a shining star. [The lamp] is lit [by the oil of] a blessed olive tree, neither of the East nor of the West. The oil well-nigh shineth forth, though fire touch it not. Light upon light! God guideth to His light whom He will; and God striketh similitudes for mankind; and God knoweth all things (An-Nur: 35).

After this verse come the following two:

In houses which God has allowed to be elevated, and that His Name be remembered therein, He is glorified in the mornings and in the evenings by men whom neither trade nor merchandise diverteth from the remembrance of God, and from establishing the prayer, and from the bestowing of alms ... (An-Nur: 36-7).

After reciting the words 'men whom neither trade nor merchandise diverteth from the remembrance of God', the Imam begins his sermon:

Truly, God has made the remembrance (al-dhikr) a polish for the hearts, by which they hear after being deaf, and see after being blind and yield after being resistant ... There have always been slaves of God ... with whom He held intimate discourse through their thoughts and spoke with them through the essence of their intellects. They diffused illumination through the awakened light in their hearing and their seeing and their hearts, calling unto the remembrance of the days of God ... Indeed, there is a special group (ahl) who belong to the dhikr; they have adopted it in place of the world, such that 'neither trade nor merchandise' distracts them from it. They spend the days of their life in it ... It is as though they had left this world for the Hereafter, and they are there, witnessing what is beyond this world ...

The weight of this passage lies in the Imam's description of the dhikr as a 'polish for hearts' (jila 'an lil-qulub), placed beside his mention of the awakened light' in the hearing, sight and hearts of those who have applied that polish to their hearts. The link between the heart's illumination and the verse of light is plain. The remembrance of God discloses the heart's latent light, and the light within shines together with the light from on high: 'light upon light'. Once the heart is illumined, every other faculty shares in the radiance the invocation produces, and so, again, there is further 'light upon light'. The very word given for 'polish', jila, can itself be read as an implicit commentary on the light verse, for it derives from the verb jala, whose primary meaning is 'to become clear', to be exposed to view, disclosed, brought to light. The Quran speaks of 'the night when it enshroudeth in darkness, and the day when it shineth forth in brightness' (idha tajalla) (Al-Layl: 1-2), and likewise: 'By the day, as it bringeth to light [the sun] (idha jallaha) (Ash-Shams: 3). The consciousness that lies hidden within the heart is brought to light' through the polishing worked by the remembrance of God.

What is at stake here is the clarifying of the organ of consciousness, the spiritual 'heart'. This clarifying does two things at once: it enables the heart to work as a mirror that reflects truths from above, and it uncovers the heart's own hidden depths, disclosing truths from within — the concealed contents of consciousness the Imam calls the 'buried treasures of the intellect' (dafain al-uqul). The dhikr is offered as a means of purifying this spiritual mode of perception, the 'heart', which is not the same as the rational faculty, and still less the same as the organs of sense, as Chapter 1 discussed.

The Quran points to the deeper significance of the heart and its distinctive mode of 'vision': 'Have they not travelled in the land, that they might have hearts with which to comprehend, and ears with which to hear? Indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but blind are the hearts that are in the breasts' (Al-Hajj: 46). The eye's outward sight reaches only the surface of things, whereas the vision proper to the heart is an insight that passes beneath that surface to the reality concealed there. And again: 'They have hearts with which they understand not, eyes with which they see not, ears with which they hear not. They are like cattle, nay, even further astray. They are the heedless' (al-ghafilun) (Al-A'raf: 179). The mention of 'the heedless', the ghafilun, at the end of verse 179 leads back to the dhikr, for the ghafil is the very opposite of the dhakir, the 'rememberer'; and the verse that immediately follows is one of the most important 'methodic' foundations of the mystical practice of dhikr: 'Unto God belong the most beautiful Names, so call Him by them. And leave behind those who desecrate His Names; they will be requited for what they do' (Al-A'raf: 180). These verses affirm plainly the bond between remembrance and the heart: ... Those who believe and whose hearts are at peace in the remembrance of God, is it not in the remembrance of God that hearts are at peace? (Ar-Ra'd: 28); 'Truly, therein is a reminder (dhikra) for him who hath a heart' (Qaf: 37); 'Those are true believers whose hearts quake with awe when God is invoked' (Al-Anfal: 2); 'Is he whose breast God hath opened up to submission (islam), such that he followeth a light from his Lord [like he who remains closed to submission and in darkness]? So woe be to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of God, they are in plain error' (Az-Zumar: 22).

By contrast, the verse that follows refers to hearts that 'soften' to dhikruLlah: 'God hath revealed the most beautiful saying, a Book [containing] similitudes and paired [threats and promises] at which the skins of those who fear their Lord quiver; then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of God' (Az-Zumar: 23).

The Imam's comment on verse 37 of the 'Light' chapter should therefore be read as illuminating all those Quranic verses that speak of the 'understanding' or spiritual vision the heart can reach in principle, and that point to dhikruLlah as the means of turning this capacity into an actual reality. The heart needs to be 'polished' by the invocation of God. The Imam's comment echoes and strengthens a saying of the Prophet frequently quoted in Sufi circles: 'For everything there is a polish (siqala), and the polish of the hearts is the dhikruLlah.'

What is meant here is a real discipline — a practice, an action, or a regular series of actions — though this does not in any way rule out the sense of dhikr as awareness, as a state of recollectedness in the divine presence, a disposition of soul shaped by the consciousness that 'if you cannot see Him, He sees you'. The 'polishing' can be understood in two ways: as the work of purifying thought through reflection and meditation, and as a regular methodic practice — whether glorification (tasbih), magnification (tamjid), praise (tahmid), sanctification (taqdis), the declaration of divine unity (tahlil), or the dhikr in the strict sense, the invocation of God's Names, by which the 'rust' of forgetfulness is removed. In his comment Ali (ع) also speaks of a particular group who 'belong' to the dhikr, calling them an ahl. The Prophet likewise spoke of the ahl al-dhikr: 'God has angels who rove the pathways, seeking out the ahl al-dhikr, and when they find a group of people (qawm) invoking God, they call out to one another, "Come to that which you desire!"

Later, one of the greatest members of the qawm — one of the names by which the Sufis refer to themselves — gives poetic expression to the image of the heart polished by the dhikr. It is the custom of kings, Rumi tells in the Mathnawi, to seat the Sufis right before them, for they are a mirror for the soul, and better than a mirror: breasts polished by invocation and meditation, so that the mirror of the heart receives the pure, virginal image.

Another aspect of the heart's polishing deserves reflection: the nature of the 'vision' known by a heart that is purified by the dhikr and given life by faith. As the Imam sees it, this vision is divinely inspired; it is nothing less than the spiritual vision of God already mentioned: 'Eyes see Him not through sight's observation, but hearts see Him through the verities of faith.'

In another saying, the Imam calls 'pure hearts' the 'places' from which God can be seen: 'so whoever purifies his heart sees God'. The bond between the purification of the heart and the remembrance of God is confirmed in this saying: 'Where are they whose actions are accomplished purely for God, and who purify their hearts [so that they become] places for the remembrance of God?'

Taken together, these sayings of the Imam on the dhikr's effect upon the heart can be read as a commentary on the important hadith qudsi cited in Chapter 2: 'My slave never ceases to draw near to Me through supererogatory acts (nawafil) until I love him. And when I love him, I am his hearing by which he hears, his sight by which he sees, his hand by which he grasps, and his foot by which he walks.' The Sufis regard this 'divine utterance' as defining a foundational principle of their metaphysical doctrine while at the same time pointing to the goal of their mystical practice.

A mutual confirmation stands between the Imam's saying and the hadith qudsi. Through the dhikr — the supererogatory act above all others — a person's perceptions and actions are mysteriously assimilated to the divine Reality, and the result is that the heart attains spiritual vision. Once this happens, the heart, as the centre of consciousness, can no longer be regarded only in its relative, human dimension. Its inmost essence, or secret (sirr), belongs in truth to the divine, and this alone can see as God sees and, in the end, 'see' God Himself. As the Sufi master Abu Talib al-Makki wrote, 'None sees Him to whom nothing is similar but Him to whom nothing is similar.' If God enters into the human acts of perception that belong to the outward senses, then all the more does the supreme act of spiritual awareness, the vision of God, prove to be not a vision of God by man but a vision of God by God, worked through the individual's 'heart' rather than by it. The Imam says, 'Know God through God (irafuLlah biLlah).' In the final analysis, then, it is God who both 'sees' and is 'seen'. On a typical Sufi reading of the Quranic verse 'by a witnesser and that which is witnessed' (Al-Buruj: 3), it is God Himself who is both the 'witnesser' (shahid) and the 'witnessed' (mashhud). Al-Kashani, for example, writes in his esoteric exegesis — until quite recently wrongly attributed to Ibn al-Arabi — that the human witness is effaced in his witnessing, so that it is God who witnesses Himself through the individual whose separative consciousness is extinguished, such that 'He is the identity of the witness, there being no difference between the two except in terms of notional expression.'

The final section takes up the ultimate fruits of invocation in terms of spiritual realization through self-effacement. The concern for now is a more relative aspect of the heart's vision of God: the way the reality of God is made clear and present to the heart through the 'verities of faith'. The agent here is the inner dimension of human consciousness, and the object 'perceived' is the divine Reality. In other words, profound faith reveals the objective presence of God — a presence that is everywhere and cannot be taken away, and that constitutes the ontological reality of all existing things. As the Imam's famous Dua Kumayl puts it, noted earlier: 'By Thy tremendousness (azmatika) which has filled all things ... by Thy Names which have filled the foundations of all things, by Thy knowledge which encompasses all things, by the light of Thy face, through which all things are illumined ...' (emphasis added).

Nothing can exist without the 'foundation' — the ontological infrastructure, as it were — that the Name, or combination of Names, of God supplies for it. What constitutes the true being and the positive qualities of each manifested thing is therefore, in the end, a divine Name or combination of Names. To see 'things' correctly means seeing the divine attributes manifested by and through them, and so perceiving them as existential reflections of principial realities, as so many tajalliyyat, or theophanies — self-disclosures of the divine Reality. The 'heart' purified by invocation comes to see God everywhere.

This vision of the divine in all things rests on two principles affirmed in the Quran: the first concerns the divine 'object', that is, the objective, metaphysical nature of reality; the second concerns the human subject and the mystical assimilation of that reality. On the one hand, nothing that exists, not even the most outward aspects of material existence, can be excluded from the divine Reality, for 'He is the First and the Last, and the Outward and the Inward' (Al-Hadid: 3), and 'Wherever ye turn there is the Face of God' (Al-Baqarah: 115); on the other hand, 'We shall show them Our signs on the horizons and in their own souls, until it be clear to them that He is the Real' (Fussilat: 53). Everything around us thus provides a sign pointing back to its Creator.

The heart polished and purified by the dhikr can decipher these signs and so 'see' God everywhere and in everything; yet the possibility of such a vision in no way reduces the divine Reality to the level of the things of sense. As noted earlier, the first sermon of the Nahj al-balagha proclaims that 'God is with every thing, but not through association; and other than every thing, but not through separation.' This 'withness' (maiyya) of God carries no relativizing of God, no association or conjoining (muqarana) of the divine Reality with created things, and no lessening of divine transcendence. The play of ideas here can be read as a commentary both on the Quranic verses that proclaim divine immanence — the presence of God to and within all things — and on those that stress divine transcendence, surpassing and incomparable to all things. God may be 'absolutely' close to us, yet we are infinitely far from Him. On the one hand, 'We are closer to man than the neck-artery' (Qaf: 16) — He is as near to us as our own jugular vein — and on the other, ... there is none comparable unto Him (Al-Ikhlas: 4).

Nothing that exists can stand wholly apart from the all-encompassing reality of God, and yet that reality shares no common measure with anything that exists. His oneness both includes all things and excludes them. To affirm God's immanence within the world — His being 'with every thing' — therefore takes nothing away from His transcendence; and to affirm His transcendence above the world — His being 'other than every thing' — does not make Him absent from it. The oneness of God implies all of this, just as it rules out any merely numerical oneness, as was briefly discussed in the first chapter. In the Imam's perspective, God is One not in the sense of a countable 'one,' a single unit or entity among others, but in the sense that His oneness admits no 'other.' In his words, 'That which has no second does not enter into the category of numbers.'

This can be read as an esoteric commentary on the Quranic verse 'Say: He, God is One' (Al-Ikhlas: 1). The opposite of this divine oneness is the multiplicity of gods implied in the error of shirk, and this conception refines that error, turning it into a statement about being rather than mere theology. The act of shirk — of associating 'partners' with God — is thereby carried to a higher register and shown to imply more than the affirmation of false deities: it attributes to God a merely numerical oneness. To reduce His oneness to number is to confine it within the wholly relative category of determinate entities. Each such entity is a single unit, and on this view God would be no more than one being among other similar beings. But the Imam insists that God 'has no second'; there is no other 'being' in being but Him. To call Him 'one' in the ordinary sense is itself imprecise, for it implies that a second could follow in sequence. He is better described as unique. No entity or unit that appears to exist can, in reality, be compared with His being, which is one in an infinitely all-encompassing sense and unique in an absolutely exclusive sense: a oneness that includes all reality and excludes all alterity. This radical idea of a oneness that wholly excludes any 'otherness' in Being implies that created entities are so many false gods — precisely to the extent that their apparent 'oneness' in existence is set beside God's true oneness, or rather His 'one-and-onliness.'

In another sermon, Ali (ع) turns to divine immanence, this time focusing on the kind of awareness the human intellect can have of the divine Reality — which returns to the question of what vision of God is possible for a human being:

"Praise be to God who is present in the hidden inwardness of things, and whose being is indicated by the signs of manifest things. The eye of the onlooker cannot behold Him, so the eye of one who does not see Him cannot deny His reality, nor can the heart of one who affirms His reality see Him. He is utmost in elevation, so no thing is more elevated than He; but He is also close in His nearness, so no thing is closer than He ... God has not made the intellects capable of defining His qualities, but He has also not veiled the intellects from essential knowledge of Him."

This passage says, on the one hand, that human intellects cannot define, still less know, the divine attributes; and on the other, that "essential knowledge" of Him is attainable. The apparent contradiction resolves in another key dimension of dhikr: that of recollection, remembrance, recognition. One is re-collecting — gathering again — fragments of a knowledge that already exists but has been forgotten. One recognizes what one has always known, and for exactly this reason one is able to know it once more. This does not mean the knowledge is made of parts to be reassembled, which would be empirical knowledge. The remembrance here is more like an awakening, an illumination that dawns as the clouds of inborn forgetfulness are dispelled.

This approach to knowledge through remembrance recurs throughout the Imam's sayings. In Sermon 1 of the Nahj, for instance, comes the phrase, "Foremost in religion is knowledge of Him (awwal al-din marifatuhu)." The word awwal literally means "the first," and can be understood as the starting-point, the foundation, and so the foremost element of religion. The word marifa means not merely knowledge but also carries the sense of "recognition." The implication is plain: the basis of all religious orientation is man's pre-existing knowledge of the divine Reality. One re-cognizes what one has always known at the deepest level of consciousness; one ac-knowledges what one already knows but had seemingly forgotten.

Further on in the same sermon, God sent to mankind "His messengers, dispatching prophets in succession, in order to claim from them [His creatures] the fulfilment of the covenant of His creation; to remind them of His forgotten graces; to remonstrate with them through communication [of His revelation]; to unearth for them the buried treasures of the intellects ..." (dafain al-uqul).

The "buried treasures" can be identified with the knowledge of divine realities ingrained in man's deepest nature — those realities to which humanity was made to bear witness at the dawn of creation: "And when thy Lord brought forth from the children of Adam, from their loins, their seed, and made them testify of themselves, 'Am I not your Lord?' They said, 'Yea, we testify.' [This was] lest ye say on the Day of Resurrection, 'Truly, of this we were unaware'" (Al-A'raf: 172).

These divine realities can also be understood in relation to the divine spirit breathed into man at the creation of the human soul: "Then He fashioned [man] and breathed into him of His Spirit" (As-Sajdah: 9); to the "names" taught by God to Adam: "And He taught Adam the names, all of them ..." (Al-Baqarah: 31); and to the fitra, the primordial nature of man, patterned upon the divine nature: "... the nature of God (fitrat Allah), that according to which He created man" (Ar-Rum: 30). The primordial nature of the human soul can thus be seen to contain the very element — knowledge of God — to which all of humanity is made to bear witness in the pact (mithaq) named in the verse above. This identification of the fitra with the knowledge of God is made explicit by Imam Muhammad al-Baqir, in a saying quoted by al-Khui as a commentary on that sentence of the first sermon. Al-Baqir was asked about the meaning of the words in the Quran, "the nature of God, that according to which He created man." He answered, "He created them [such that their primordial nature was] in conformity with tawhid, at the covenant regarding knowledge of Him, [when they testified] that He is indeed their Lord."

Knowledge of God, then, essentially defines human nature; and it is for this reason that the human intellect cannot be veiled, as the Imam said, from "essential knowledge of God." Yet even though this knowledge is ingrained in human nature, forgetfulness (ghafla) has become man's second nature. In Quranic terms, the very passage of time smothers the heart and so hardens it: "Hath not the moment come for the believers, that their hearts be humbled to the remembrance of God, and to what hath been revealed of the truth; and that they not become as those who were given the Book aforetime. Then the term was prolonged for them, so their hearts were hardened; and many of them are evil-doers" (Al-Hadid: 16).

The verse speaks both of this hardening of the heart over time — which can be identified with the ghafla of second nature — and of its opposite: the heart's being present, here and now, to the dhikruLlah. To remedy forgetfulness, more is needed than a simple factual reminder, some piece of information, some element of formal, conceptual, discursive knowledge. No amount of empirical data, coming wholly from outside, can bring man to knowledge of God. Rather it is integral remembrance — a spiritual awareness welling up from within and crystallizing on contact with revelation from without — that makes the innate knowledge of God present once again to heart and mind, the knowledge that is "buried" deep in the intellect. There is no common measure between this consciousness of God and ordinary empirical knowledge of phenomena. The Imam expresses the gap between the two kinds of knowledge in sayings such as, "Praise be to God who is well-known (maruf) without being seen." A further formulation sharpens the paradox: "By things their Creator manifests Himself to the intellects; and by things He is guarded from the sight of the eyes." This opens onto a complex theme in the Imam's perspective: the nature of the "veil" formed by created phenomena, and how it is to be understood in the light of the infinite and inalienable reality of God.
