The first response to that question begins with a limit. On his own, the individual cannot make the leap from remembrance to forgetfulness. A conscious person, concentrating on the act of invocation, cannot render himself unconscious of himself in the course of it. The Imam's phrasing is exact: the soul is to be forgotten 'in' the remembrance. Any attempt to will oneself into unconsciousness springs from a conscious will, and so entrenches self-consciousness rather than effacing it. The point, then, is not to force oneself to forget oneself while invoking God. It is to concentrate on the Name so completely that no room is left in one's consciousness — no 'space', mental or existential — for anything but the Named, the reality being invoked. A first measure of self-effacement thus follows naturally from total concentration.

The full consummation of self-effacement in fana, however, comes as a divine grace, surpassing all individual effort — even though the act of invocation is understood to attract that grace, or to strip from the heart the 'rust' that hides one's own nothingness before the sole reality of God, 'that which has no second'. This part of the response can be gathered into an esoteric reading of the Quranic words, ... thou wilt not forget, unless God willeth it so (Al-A'la: 6-7). Al-Kalabadhi, author of one of the most important early manuals of Sufism, opens his chapter on dhikr with words that echo the Imam's: 'The haqiqa of the dhikr is this: that you forget everything other than the madhkur (the Invoked) in the dhikr. For He says: "So remember thy Lord when thou hast forgotten" (Al-Kahf: 24). That is, when you have forgotten what is not God, then you have remembered God.'

The second response can be framed through the principle of inverse analogy. Human invocation is analogous to divine invocation — a kind of reflection of it — and, like any reflected image, it both shares in what it reflects and inverts it. In sharing, human invocation brings the invoker a greater fullness of consciousness and a fuller participation in being. In inverting, it reaches its consummation in what looks like the very opposite: the effacement of the individual in the object invoked. Yet the opposition is only apparent. In truth this effacement fulfills that same process, though its last stage takes a quantum leap — the negation of the very limits that constitute individuality. Insofar as the individual is limited, and insofar as limitation is itself a negation, the negation of this negation amounts to pure affirmation: the affirmation of unconditional, supra-individual being. On the plane of the self, this negation of negation reflects the negation of nothingness expressed in Ibn al-Arabi's line, 'Praise be to Him who engendered things from nothing, then negated it.'

Here the Imam's enigmatic saying returns: 'I am the death of the dead.' It recalls the words Rumi places in the Imam's mouth in these lines of his Mathnawi:

He said, 'I am wielding the sword for God's sake, I am the servant of God, I am not under the command of the body.

I am the Lion of God, I am not the lion of my passion: my deed bears witness to my religion.

In war I am (manifesting the truth of) thou didst not throw when thou threwest: I am (but) as the sword, and the wielder is the (divine) Sun.

I have removed the baggage of self out of the way, I have deemed (what is) other than God to be non-existence.

I am a shadow, the Sun is my lord; I am the chamberlain, I am not the curtain (which prevents approach) to Him.

I am filled with the pearls of union, like a (jewelled) sword: in battle I make (men) living, not slain.

The cosmic unfolding of creation, the movement from God to man, requires the negation of that relative nothingness which is pregnant with the possibilities of being; the realization of God by man requires the negation of that same 'nothingness' that God breathed into being. Ibn al-Arabi's treatise Extinction in Contemplation names what is at stake: 'the extinction of that which never was ... and the subsistence of that which never ceased to be.' The Quranic verses clearly implied are these: 'Everything thereon perisheth (fan), and there subsisteth (yabqa) only the Face of thy Lord, possessor of glory and bounty' (Ar-Rahman: 26-27).

Yet all things, insofar as they exist, have two aspects or 'faces': the divine aspect, which is the true being of the thing, and the created aspect, which is 'nothing'. The 'Face' of the Lord that alone subsists is therefore not merely the divine Reality above and beyond all things, but that same reality within all things. This is the import of al-Ghazali's esoteric commentary on the Quranic verse, 'Everything perisheth except His Face' (Al-Qasas: 88). Al-Ghazali comments:

[it is] not that it perisheth at some particular moment, but rather it is forever perishing, since it cannot be conceived except as perishing. For each thing other than God is, when considered in and by itself, pure nothingness; and if considered from the face (wajh) to which existence flows to it from the Prime Reality, it is viewed as existing, but not in itself, solely from the face which accompanies Him Who gives it existence. Therefore, the divine face is the sole thing in reality.

He then ties the mystical realization of this oneness to the invocation of God and to the forgetting of the self within it, and so offers a valuable commentary on the meaning of this total dissolution of self-consciousness. The Sufis who verify this oneness through mystical 'taste' (dhawq), he writes, are 'drowned in oneness', so that they become 'dumbfounded':

No capacity remained within them save to recall Allah; yea, not so much as the capacity to recall their own selves ... when this state prevails, it is called in relation to him who experiences it Extinction, nay Extinction of Extinction, for the soul has become extinct to itself, extinct to its own extinction; for it becomes unconscious of itself and unconscious of its own unconsciousness, since were it conscious of its own unconsciousness, it would be conscious of itself.

Also pertinent is the statement al-Qushayri attributes to Abu 'Uthman, which sheds light on another dimension of the unconsciousness realized through invocation: Whoever has not tasted the loneliness of unconsciousness will not find the food of the intimacy of remembrance.' Here losing consciousness of oneself is equated with 'loneliness', while becoming fully conscious of God through invocation yields 'intimacy'. True intimacy with the divine Reality can be found only by stripping the self of its false 'intimacy' — that self-satisfied, habitual self-centeredness which is the shadow cast by self-awareness. It is this awareness of self that, in the Imam's statement, must be forgotten. Such higher forgetfulness can arise only on the basis of the remembrance of God, for only the source of Being, unconditional Consciousness, and eternal Life can extinguish, eclipse, or efface the relative existence, partial consciousness, and apparent life of the individual. This, the haqiqa of the dhikr, is expressed with perfect economy in the Imam's own words: ... forget your own soul in your remembrance.

The state of fana, the highest degree of this 'forgetting' of oneself, is therefore a grace. However great his effort, the individual cannot attain it. Yet this implies no abandonment of effort by the invoker. On the contrary, as the Sufi tradition amply attests, fana is bound up with the practice of dhikr, being its very climax. After this state, or hal, of extinction comes the station, or maqam, of subsistence, baqa: a return of consciousness to the self — a self now transfigured by the knowledge of reality impressed upon the soul in the state of fana. For only in fana is the ultimate 'vision' of absolute oneness attained, a vision that leaves no room for the ontological duality inseparable from individuality. To posit the 'individual' is to posit its correlate, the Lord, and so to affirm duality.

Al-Kashani makes this point in his commentary on the Quranic verse, 'Remember Him as He hath guided you' (Al-Baqarah: 198), where he traces the guided ascent through the degrees of the dhikr. The first is the dhikr of the tongue, which corresponds to the soul (al-nafs); then that of the heart (al-qalb), corresponding to the divine acts, those which manifest His graces; then that of the 'secret' (al-sirr), corresponding to the vision of the divine acts together with 'the unveiling of the sciences of the manifestation of the divine qualities'; then that of the spirit (al-ruh), corresponding to 'the contemplation of the lights of the manifestations of the divine qualities, with an apprehension of the light of the Essence'; then comes the dhikr of 'the hidden' (al-khafi), which is 'the contemplation of the beauty of the Essence along with the subsistence of duality'; and finally the dhikr of the Essence, 'which is essential vision, attained through the removal of duality.'

The same point emerges from the counsel of Ibn 'Ataillah, which shows how the dhikr generates receptivity to the divine presence and to the grace by which alone the individual can truly forget' himself — becoming, in al-Ghazali's phrase, 'unconscious of his own unconsciousness':

Do not abandon the invocation because you do not feel the Presence of God therein. For your forgetfulness of the invocation of Him is worse than your forgetfulness in the invocation of Him. Perhaps He will take you from an invocation with forgetfulness (ghafla) to one with vigilance (yaqaza), and from one with vigilance to one with the Presence of God (hudur), and from one with the Presence of God to one wherein everything but the Invoked (al-Madhkur) is absent. 'And that is not difficult for God.'

In his commentary on the Hikam, Ibn 'Ajiba adds: So, in the measure that one is extinguished in the Name, one is extinguished in the Essence.' This follows from the principle that the Name is the Named. In another treatise, a commentary on a poem by Shushtari on the divine Name Allah, he states this cardinal tenet of the invocatory discipline in Sufism more plainly. The poem's first line reads, referring to the letters of which Allah is composed: 'The alif before two lams, then a ha': coolness of the eyes. Ibn 'Ajiba comments: The "coolness of the eyes", this is joy, for tears of joy, as one knows by experience, are cool. The author means this: this Name is the joy of my heart, its happiness, its beatitude.' He then cites some lines from al-Hallaj on the letters of the Name Allah, adds a verse of his own, and follows with this comment: 'The Name is not other than the Named, for joy cannot come from anything but the essence of a thing, not from the name as such.'

This sums up the doctrine that the Name and the Named are identical — the rationale for the Sufi practice of dhikruLlah. Yet here a difficulty arises. However well the Imam's pronouncements on the dhikr agree with these later Sufi expressions of the underlying principles, this particular stress on the identity of the Name and the Named appears, on the surface, to stand in tension with numerous sayings of the Shii Imams which deny that the Name is the Named. Imam Jafar al-Sadiq, for instance, is reported as saying:

The Name of Allah is other than Him. For everything to which the name of a thing is applicable is a creation, hence other than God. For whatever the tongue expresses, or is worked on by the hand, is a creation ... everything described is created, and the Creator of things cannot be described within the limits of a named object.

Allah has ninety-nine Names. If the Name were the Named, then every one of the Names would be a god. But Allah is the one meaning, or spiritual reality, mana, indicated by the Names, and all of them are other than Him.

This apparent contradiction can be resolved in two ways. First, one must attend closely to what 'Name' means in each of the two contexts: that of doctrinal distinction, in which the Absolute is rigorously distinguished from the relative and the Essence from all forms; and that of methodic concentration, in which the Absolute is taken to be the reality of the very form through which it reveals itself. One can then turn to one of the most esoteric aspects of the Shii Imams' conception of themselves: their references to their own selves as the 'most beautiful Names' (al-asma al-husna).

As regards the meaning of 'Name', Ibn al-Arabi offers a precise definition: [T]he Names have two connotations; the first connotation is God Himself who is what is named, the second that by which one Name is distinguished from another ... As being essentially the other, the Name is the Reality, while as being not the other, it is the imagined Reality. Each Name is, on one side, identified with every other Name by virtue of its essential identity with the Named — the one Essence that is the source of all the Names. On the other side, each Name has its own specific meaning and quality, the relationship by which the one Reality engages the created cosmos. In this second respect each Name is distinguished from the others, and distinction implies limitation, hence relativity and, in the end, a kind of illusion before the one and only Reality. In this sense the Name takes on the character of 'imagined Reality'. For Ibn al-Arabi, the Names have no separate ontological entities of their own; they all revert to the one and only Reality, that of the divine Essence. This dissolves the problem, raised in Imam Jafar's saying, of different Names implying different 'gods'.

In the lexicon of Sufi terms Lataif al-ilam fi isharat ahl al-ilham (Subtle Disclosures in the Allusions of the Folk of Inspiration), attributed to al-Kashani, one finds a definition of the divine Names that also helps to distinguish these two connotations. Under the term 'Names of the Divinity', the text reads:

These are, in the terminology of the Sufis, expressive of the manifest aspect of being, in respect of its determination within a specific meaning. For every divine Name is the manifest aspect of being, which, in turn, is identical to the Essence, but not as the Essence is in itself; rather, in respect of its specification and determination within a particular meaning, or what one might call a 'quality'. For example, the Name al-Hayy ('The Living') is a Name of manifest, determined being, but in respect of its specification and determination as a particular meaning, it is Life. So in regard to being itself, al-Hayy is identical to the Essence, whilst in regard to its determination as a particular meaning, it is other than the Essence. If you have understood what we have said, you will know what is meant by the saying: the Name is not identical to the Essence, the Named, neither is it other than It.

The Name and the Named differ in name and in thought, and by that measure the Name is not the Named; yet they are also spiritually joined, and by that measure the Name is the Named. A further distinction lies beneath this one. The spoken form of the Name must be told apart from the Name understood as an attribute of the Essence. Taken as an attribute, the Name is nothing but the divine quality it points to, and that quality is in turn identical to the Essence. Taken as a spoken word, it is only the 'name' of this Name — a verbal form and nothing more. Qaysari, another major commentator on Ibn al-Arabi, draws out this distinction in the introduction to his commentary on the Fusus al-hikam.

When the Essence is considered together with a particular quality and in relation to one of Its theophanies, it is named by a Name. 'The Compassionate' has an essence, which is compassion; 'The All-Conquering' has an essence, which is all-conquering power. These spoken Names are Names of Names, and this is how the saying is to be understood: the Name is identical to the Named.

Jalal al-Din Ashtiyani, a contemporary authority on Shii 'Irfan, wrote a vast commentary on Qaysari's introduction. After citing this passage he makes an important observation, one that carries the discussion back to two earlier points: the principle of extinction through the invocation of the Name, and the claim that the Imams themselves are the most beautiful Names. The saints, Ashtiyani writes, often speak of the Names as one with the Named because they have in mind the referent (misdaq), which is the sifa, the divine attribute or quality: The sifat are in one respect the specifications of the Essence, while in the station of unicity they are annihilated in the Essence, and are thus identical to the Essence.'

This account of how the Name, the sifa, and the Essence stand to one another mirrors, on the objective and universal plane, the path the soul travels inwardly and mystically when it is extinguished in and by the invocation of the Name. Such extinction is what fana (فنیٰ) means — the perishing of self-centered consciousness before the Absolute. Just as the sifat are 'annihilated' in the Essence, and are therefore absolutely and unconditionally one with it, so the soul extinguished by the Name reaches, in a single act, both its total undoing and its final realization — though no longer as an individual soul. What makes this 'extinction' on the plane of the individual soul amount to 'realization' on the plane of transcendence is the divine theophany alone: the particular divine Name, the 'heart' that is the soul's true being, its mustanad ilahi. Here the deepest truth of tawhid comes to light. The individual no longer affirms that 'there is no god but God', for the individual has been extinguished by the reality that 'there is no reality but the one and only Reality'. God is 'that which has no second'. Just as 'No one has truly said Allah but Allah', so too no one realizes God but God. God alone comes to 'know' or 'be' Himself, and this is one part of the purpose of creation, as the hadith qudsi indicates: 'I was a hidden treasure and I loved to be known.'

In this light the saints (al-awliya) are theophanies made perfectly real in themselves, wholly effaced in that of which they are the manifestation; and it is precisely this effacement in the divine Reality that is the ultimate source of their knowledge of it. This holds all the more for the Prophet himself, the model of all the saints and the 'perfect man', al-insan al-kamil. On this point Sabziwari, in his commentary on the divine Names, cites the saying of Ali (ع), 'We are the most beautiful Names': 'There is no doubt that they are His most exalted indicators and His greatest signs (ala imihil-uzma wa ayatihil-kubra), as the Prophet said, God bless him and his family, "Whoso sees me has seen the Truth (al-Haqq)." He goes on to equate the spiritual station, the inner reality, of the Imams with that of the divine Names and attributes, while insisting that the divine Essence rises above all Names and attributes and remains forever beyond speech, known only to itself. The Prophet, the Imam, the saint, the perfect man' thus display those aspects of the divine nature that can be grasped on the human plane. The higher the divine Essence is raised in transcendence above all Names and attributes, the more brilliantly those Names and attributes are reflected in the mirror that the 'perfect man' provides. The unknowable transcendence of the hidden 'treasure' is, in some measure, offset by the faithful reflection of its communicable aspects in the 'friend of God'.

Identifying the Imam with the divine Name or attribute is worth pondering, for in one respect it would seem to be shirk, the 'association' of a creature, however exalted, with the transcendent Reality. The same charge seems to fall on the ecstatic utterances (shathiyyat) of many of the most celebrated Sufis, such as the anal-Haqq ('I am the Real') of al-Hallaj and the subhani ('Glory to me') of Bayazid. Yet seen from the standpoint of the Imam's own understanding of the divine attributes, a very different picture emerges — one that, far from being tainted by shirk, reaches the deepest application of tawhid. The first sermon of the Nahj al-balagha makes the following remarkable and weighty statements about the attributes of God:

The perfection of purification (ikhlas) is to divest Him of all attributes (sifat) because of the testimony of every attribute that it is other than the object of attribution, and because of the testimony of every such object that it is other than the attribute. So whoever ascribes an attribute to God, glorified be He, has conjoined Him with something else; and whoever so conjoins Him has made Him twofold; and whoever makes Him twofold has fragmented Him; and whoever thus fragments Him is ignorant of Him.

When the Imam says that pure devotion to God requires stripping God of all attributes, what is denied is not the divine attributes themselves. What is denied is the attributes taken as separate, self-standing, or added-on realities, thought of as substantially 'other than' the Essence of God or set apart from it in being. The reality of God's attributes is plainly affirmed in an earlier phrase of the same sermon: 'He whose attribute has no binding limitation (alladhi laysa li-sifatihi hadd mahdud).' What is ruled out is the attempt to confine the reality of any divine attribute within the bounds of human thought and language. No divine attribute can be set apart from the divine nature; and since that nature is infinite, every attribute is likewise infinite in scope, and so lies beyond all the limits that formal conception and verbal definition presuppose.

In one respect, then, the attribute or Name is to be affirmed, and in another it is to be denied: affirmed as not other than the Essence, denied insofar as it is thought of by itself, on its own account. This same understanding of how the attribute or Name stands to the Essence can be applied, mystically, to how the individual soul stands to the divine Reality. On its own account the individual is nothing; but in respect of the divine ground within it — the divine Name, the mustanad ilahi that is its essential reality — it is not other than the unique Real. As Ibn al-Arabi says, 'The final end and ultimate return of the gnostics is that the Real is identical with them, while they do not exist.' This captures perfectly the double aspect of the realized sage's soul: insofar as he is aware that 'he does not exist', he knows that the Real is his true identity. However paradoxical it seems, the mystic's realization of absolute Reality goes hand in hand with the realization of his own non-existence. Ibn al-Arabi expresses these two sides of one and the same realization sparingly. Describing the summit of his spiritual ascent, his miraj, he recounts that God removed from him his 'contingent dimension (imkan), resulting in the attainment of the inner realities of all the Names'. He continues:

Thus I attained in this nocturnal journey the inner realities (maani) of all the Names, and I saw them returning to One Subject (musamma) and One Entity ('ayn): that Subject was what I witnessed and that Entity was my Being. For my voyage was only in myself and pointed to myself, and through this I came to know that I was a pure servant' without a trace of lordship in me at all.

This passage helps explain so many of the ecstatic utterances of the Sufis and the seemingly self-deifying sayings of the Imams. Their personal servitude to God is not denied. On the contrary, it is fully realized through the knowledge of their true identity, for that identity as the Named is reached only when their individuality is effaced. Like the divine attributes, they are mustahlak, annihilated in the divine Essence, so there can be no question of any private laying-claim to the glory of God. When the Imam seems to speak of his own greatness, this is nothing but the greatness of God expressed through him as a mazhar, a place where the divine shows itself — and this exactly in the measure of his own effacement in that greatness.

The same point is borne out by what 'Attar recounts about Imam Jafar al-Sadiq in his Tadhkiratul-awliya'. Someone accused the Imam of being proud, and he replied: 'I am not proud, for pride pertains to the divine greatness. Since I have gone beyond the pride of self, His pride has come and taken the place of my own pride. With pride of self present, there can be no divine greatness, but through the divine greatness, pride will be present.' The divine qualities shine with greater, not lesser, brilliance through the prism of a soul made transparent to the divine Reality — a transparency that comes from the clearing away of all the clouds of egoism and passion.

A holy utterance bears on this: 'My slave draws near to Me through nothing I love more than that which I have made obligatory for him. My slave never ceases to draw near to Me through supererogatory acts (nawafil) until I love him. And when I love him, I am his hearing by which he hears, his sight by which he sees, his hand by which he grasps, and his foot by which he walks.'

In the light of all this, the paradox held in this divine utterance can now be resolved. On the one hand, the thing most beloved to God appears to be the obligatory rites. On the other, it is the supererogatory rites that lead the slave to draw near to God until He loves him — and this love seems the greater, since it ends in the divine entering the human faculties, the uniting realization proper to tawhid. The paradox resolves once one sees that God's 'love' for the obligatory rites is a love turned toward something apart from Himself, whereas His love for the 'slave' — the pure slave effaced in his Lord — is infinitely greater, since it shares in God's love for His own Self-manifestation, and so for Himself. In the beginning God 'loved to be known', and so He created the world. In 'knowing' Himself through the effaced slave, the apparent 'other', His wish to be known is fulfilled through the saint whose greatest glory is precisely his own effacement, poverty, and emptiness of self.

It is in this sense that the following saying of the Imam is to be understood: 'Down from me torrents do pour; up to me no bird can soar.' Torrents pour down from him because, and to the degree that, he is extinguished in the source of the torrent. The image recalls the Quranic description of the 'slaves of God' who, unlike the 'righteous', drink straight from the heavenly spring of Kafur, which is ultimately identified with the divine Essence: 'Truly, the righteous shall drink from a cup flavoured with Kafur, a spring wherefrom the slaves of God drink, making it gush forth abundantly' (Al-Insan: 5-6). These slaves make the spring flow more abundantly because, as al-Kashani explains, 'they are themselves the sources of this spring; there is no duality or otherness. Were it otherwise, it would not be the fountain of Kafur, because of the darkness of the veil of egoity (ana iyya) and duality.'

The highest degree of the dhikr, as al-Kashani defined it, is the dhikr of the Essence, 'which is essential vision, attained through the removal of duality'. The dhikr 'polishes' away not only the impurities of heart and mind but, in the end, through the grace of the madhkur, every trace of duality — above all that root assumption of duality, the individual as such. It removes all subtle or hidden shirk, the 'partners' in being that are nothing before the One 'that has no second', and it sets in place the spiritual principle of tawhid, so that the heart transfigured by the knowledge of the sole Reality comes to see the light of that Reality reflected in all the mirrors of creation. To realize, to 'make real' in the fullest sense, this one and only Reality is, by that very act, to realize the unreality — the merely apparent reality — of everything else.

At this level of realization a measure of bewilderment inevitably accompanies the disclosure of the divine Reality on every side. Because the divine Essence is raised beyond all understanding, it becomes all the more unavoidable that the creature's consciousness be utterly annihilated if that Essence is to be 'realized', if gnosis of it is to be attained. On the one hand, one 'knows' God by knowing that His Essence is unknowable, wholly other, wholly transcendent — the essence of the Creator lying behind the veil that creation itself forms. On the other hand, the very distinction between creature and Creator is effaced once the creature has 'forgotten' itself — not merely as an idea but in its very being, in a state of genuine contemplative extinction. Then it is no longer a matter of one form of self-consciousness replacing another, but of the 'self' being taken out of the reckoning altogether, leaving only pure consciousness as such, which cannot 'belong' to any entity without being reduced to the relativity that entity carries. So consciousness of the Absolute — 'being conscious of the Absolute' — is transmuted into absolute consciousness. The Real is 'realized' not by another but through another, which is why the term used is al-arif biLlah, literally 'the knower through God' rather than simply 'the knower of God'. The Imam says, 'Know God through God.' Knowledge of God at this deepest level is the Real knowing itself through the creature; and to say 'through' implies an unimpeded passage, the creature being marked by perfect faqr — poverty, self-effacement, and, in the end, extinction.

Realization through remembrance, however, means more than the "forgetting" of everything in existence except God; it means discovering that, in reality, there is nothing in being but God. In the Imam's image of the "polish" that remembrance works, the heart, once blind and deaf, is made able to "see" and to "hear." It sees the Face of God wherever it looks, and it hears the cosmic hymn of remembrance and praise that the whole of creation sings, for every creature in existence proclaims the infinite creativity of its Creator. As the Quran says:

> وَلِلَّهِ ٱلْمَشْرِقُ وَٱلْمَغْرِبُ ۚ فَأَيْنَمَا تُوَلُّوا۟ فَثَمَّ وَجْهُ ٱللَّهِ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ وَسِعٌ عَلِيمٌۭ

'Wherever ye turn, there is the Face of God' (Al-Baqarah: 115).

> أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُسَبِّحُ لَهُۥ مَن فِى ٱلسَّمَوَتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ وَٱلطَّيْرُ صَٓفَّتٍۢ ۖ كُلٌّۭ قَدْ عَلِمَ صَلَاتَهُۥ وَتَسْبِيحَهُۥ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمٌۢ بِمَا يَفْعَلُونَ

'Do you not see that God is the one who is glorified by everything in the heavens and the earth, and the birds with wings outstretched; each one indeed knows its prayer and its glorification, and God is All-Aware of what they do' (An-Nur: 41).

A final reflection concerns a passage from the Imam's famous and much-disputed Khutbat al-bayan, 'The Sermon of Clarifying Expression':

I am the Sign of the All-Powerful. I am the gnosis of the mysteries. I am the Threshold of Thresholds. I am the companion of the radiance of the divine Majesty. I am the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden. I am the Face of God. I am the mirror of God, the supreme Pen, the Tabula secreta. I am he who in the Gospel is called Elijah. I am he who is in possession of the secret of God's Messenger.

This extraordinary affirmation of the Imam's inmost reality may appear shocking to the exoteric mentality, and is all too easily misread as a blasphemous self-deification in the manner of Hallaj. One key that unlocks the right understanding of these declarations of "his" true nature is the statement, "I am the gnosis of the mysteries." Once this is grasped, every other statement falls naturally into place. For here the Imam identifies himself not with God, but with the knowledge of God — and not with his own knowledge of God, since that would still be a relative knowledge belonging to him as a relative being. Only knowledge itself, the knowledge God has of Himself, and not the knowledge a human being has of God, can be fully identified with its object. The distinctions between knowledge, knower, and known dissolve only at this transcendent level, just as the distinction between knowledge and being ceases to operate there. Thus the knower is the known when the knowledge in question is the consciousness that the divine Reality has of itself; and individual consciousness reaches this knowledge on one condition alone, the utter extinction of every trace of individual, creaturely selfhood. To "remember" God, one must have "forgotten" oneself. To "be" the knowledge of God is, by a kind of metaphysical reverberation, to "be" everything that God is, for the consciousness that is absolutely at one with the Absolute is nothing other than "the radiance of the divine Majesty." Insofar as this consciousness is one with "the gnosis of the mysteries," and these mysteries (asrar) are all rooted in the ultimate mystery (al-sirr), the one and only Essence of God, it is of necessity one with all the divine attributes. It is in this sense that the Imam can proclaim: "I am the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden."

Similar remarks apply to the claim to be "the Face of God" (wajh Allah). It becomes intelligible only once one grasps that the Imam describes himself as the "mirror" of God. A mirror loses its identity as a mirror when attention is fixed wholly on the object reflected within it, so that the mirror's own surface becomes, as it were, invisible and only the object is seen. Conversely, when the mirror itself is the object of attention, the face reflected within it can no longer be seen. The mirror is thus identified with what it reflects — which in a certain sense is "in" the mirror — without the mirror ceasing to be a mirror, and without the Face ceasing to be absolutely independent of it. The "veil" here is the mirror itself. Directing attention to it as such prevents one from seeing the object it reflects; but once attention is fixed wholly on the image the mirror contains, the mirror ceases to be a veil and instead reveals the object itself. Within this symbolism, forgetting the mirror answers to the effacement of the self, and fixing on the image within it answers to the remembrance of God.

Yet this leads to another paradox: the deepest effacement of individuality goes hand in hand with the most perfect expression of humanity. The "friends of God," who know themselves to be nothing before the Absolute, are precisely those who most faithfully reflect the divine Names and qualities, which belong not to them but to God. This is why the great saints and sages are also exemplars of virtue, whose true foundations are the "most beautiful Names" and attributes of God. The reflections of those divine attributes shine through them most clearly because the mirrors of their hearts have been polished by the remembrance of God, and the most stubborn stains — those imprinted by egotism — have been removed. The creativity of the saint is raised to its highest pitch precisely because the divine qualities reflected by the heart are no longer impeded, from within, by the individualistic coagulations that egotism generates, nor constrained, from without, by the cosmic coagulations of this lower world. For such saints are those whose "hearts are in the Gardens [of Paradise] while their bodies are at work." Their hearts, bound and attached to that divine realm of the abodes and stations of paradise reaching all the way to the divine presence, are already "within" that transcendent realm; they already live more in that spiritual world than in this earthly one. And so, though they labor in this world with their bodies, their outward actions veil their inward transcendence of higher realities: they act, but they are not bound by the fruits of their action.

Such souls have not merely understood this principle; they have been seized by it, existentially, at the very root of their being. It is the principle voiced in the Quranic verse:

> وَمَا هَذِهِ ٱلْحَيَوٰةُ ٱلدُّنْيَآ إِلَّا لَهْوٌۭ وَلَعِبٌۭ ۚ وَإِنَّ ٱلدَّارَ ٱلْآخِرَةَ لَهِىَ ٱلْحَيَوَانُ ۚ لَوْ كَانُوا۟ يَعْلَمُونَ

"And the life of this world is naught but sport and play; and truly, the abode of the Hereafter, that is true life" (Al-'Ankabut: 64).

Their instincts are therefore always attuned to that higher reality. When Ali (ع) was struck by the poisoned sword of Ibn Muljam, the cry that broke from him was not one of pain but of triumph: "I have triumphed, by the Lord of the Kaba!" At the very moment of death there was in him nothing but the remembrance of God, and the Imam passed away, it is said, with his tongue still repeating the words la ilaha illaLlah. His death was thus consummated exactly as his life had been lived, in keeping with the wisdom of the Prophet, who, when asked which of all acts is the most meritorious, replied: "That you die while your tongue is moistened with the invocation of God."

All the rites and practices associated with the chivalric orders of Islam were traced, without exception, back to the Prophet's son-in-law, Ali (ع) ibn Abi Talib, who was thereby established as the supreme source of the virtues of futuwwa, as Muhammad Jafar Mahjub observes in his "Chivalry and Early Persian Sufism." S. H. Nasr writes in a similar vein that Ali (ع), having received the "truth and power" of futuwwa from the Prophet, "became the supreme source of futuwwa in Islam for both Sunnis and Shiites... The personality of Ali, at once sage and knight, contemplative and protector of laborers and craftsmen, has continued to dominate through the centuries over the horizon of futuwwa as it has over much of Sufism." Nasr also draws attention to the organic relationship between futuwwa and the guilds, the asnaf, singular sinf, of craftsmen and artists established throughout the length and breadth of the Muslim world.

It is often said that the Naqshabandi tariqa is the one exception to this rule, tracing its line of descent from the Prophet through the first caliph, Abu Bakr, rather than through Ali (ع). But this affiliation with Abu Bakr pertains to only one of its three principal silsilas. 'Abd al-Majid b. Muhammad al-Khani, himself a Naqshabandi-Khalidi shaykh, calls the first chain (al-silsilat al-ula) the "golden chain," which begins with Ali (ع) and proceeds through the Shii Imams down to Ali (ع) b. Musa, then to Maruf al-Karkhi and the other masters. The second chain (al-silsilatul-thaniya) likewise begins with Ali (ع), proceeding through Hasan al-Basri. Only the third chain, called al-silsilat al-siddiqiyya, proceeds from the Prophet to Abu Bakr (al-siddiq).
